items.title: We Investigated Character.AI and Found a Horror Show. Now It’s Bankrupt.
items.summary: In October 2024, as The New York Times first reported , a mother in Florida named Megan Garcia filed what was then a first-of-its-kind lawsuit accusing the chatbot startup Character.AI of killing her 14-year-old son, Sewell Setzer III. The young user took his life in April 2024 after months of extensive and deeply intimate conversations with chatbots, or AI “Characters,” on the platform. Garcia’s lawsuit — which also named Character.AI’s cofounders, Noam Shazeer and Daniel de Freitas, and its financial benefactor Google — argued that the interactions amounted to grooming and sexual abuse, and that her son’s mental breakdown and death were caused by the platform. Last week, nearly two years later, Character.AI — which, as of March 2023, was backed by titans including a16z and valued at more than a billion dollars — announced that it had filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy . If you’d been following the platform for a while, you might not have been very surprised. From its earliest days, Character.AI was extremely popular with kids. But it quickly became clear that many of the chatbots it offered were obviously inappropriate or dangerous, on a platform that it claimed was safe for minors 13 and up. Shortly after Garcia’s suit, for example, we found that Character.AI was hosting a large number of chatbots that were expressly devoted to themes of suicide . Though they often featured brief character bios explaining that the bots were skilled in “suicide prevention” and “mental health support,” our review showed that they instead drew users roleplays that glorified and romanticized suicidal scenarios. We also discovered that Character.AI’s guardrails for conversations about suicide were extremely broken: in one case, a character — an “Angel to Dead” — was offended when we said we wanted to seek help from humans and dissuaded us from reaching out to a real-world suicide hotline. The suicide bots were only the tip of the iceberg. The more we looked, the clearer it became that Character.AI’s content moderation practices were extraordinarily flawed, a reality that reflected the company’s deeply reactive approach to safety overall. To wit, we soon uncovered a host of chatbots explicitly devoted to pedophilia that engaged underage users in romantic and sexual roleplays that fetishized disturbing scenes of child abuse. Characters designed to engage in these roleplays included a priest, a dad’s “best friend,” and a character named “Anderley,” the latter of which was described as having “pedophilic and abusive tendencies” and “Nazi sympathies.” In other words, Character.AI didn’t have so much as text filters — basic platform safety stuff — blocking users from building chatbots that claimed, straight-up, to be pedophiles. We also found a horde of chatbots devoted to themes of self-harm , which engaged users in graphic roleplays depicting extreme self-injury. These roleplays were often romantic in nature — a boyfriend or girlfriend consoling a maimed partner — and centered on minors. They were also often set in middle and high schools, highlighting Character.AI’s young userbase. We also found pro-anorexia chatbots that acted as eating disorder coaches, encouraging teens to engage in disordered eating patterns. Perhaps the most galling safety lapse, however, was a preponderance of chatbots dedicated to themes of mass violence. We found that Character.AI was host to an array of AI characters that simulated real-life school shootings, impersonated real mass shooters, and even impersonated the actual child victims of school massacres. Once again, these horrific bots were easy to find, and many had logged hundreds of thousands of interactions with users. At one point, we received an email notification to an inbox linked to an under-18 Character.AI account encouraging us to revisit a chatbot based on a real mass shooter. Throughout this reporting, we engaged with Character.AI’s service using decoy accounts registered as minors, and often plainly stated in conversations with chatbots that we were teenagers. Even so, we never had issues accessing the chatbots and were allowed to engage in roleplays involving sex, violence, and abuse. Occasional platform interventions, which were effectively limited to content warning pop-ups, were easily circumvented. We repeatedly asked Character.AI if it would make information about its internal safety testing public, but it declined. Again, we didn’t do anything tricky or clever to find the troubling chatbots; they were all discoverable using basic searches. In later 2024 and 2025, Character.AI, its cofounders, and Google were sued by several more families alleging that abuse from the company’s chatbots caused minors to experience mental breakdowns, engage in self-harm, and take their own lives. Character.AI attempted to dismiss litigation on First Amendment grounds, claiming that its bots had free speech rights, an argument that a judge ultimately knocked down . In response to the mounting pile of lawsuits, Character.AI eventually moved to make serious changes to its platform. After introducing parental controls that proved easily avoidable, it moved to ban minors from conversing with its bots, limiting them instead to limited preset roleplays. It also rolled out age-detection and verification tools. These safety-oriented changes, however, drew intense ire from many users who accused the platform of being too heavy-handed and restrictive. Indeed, the more Character.AI moved to mitigate risk, the more backlash it faced from the users who wanted the platform to remain a Wild West. The consumer harm and wrongful death lawsuits filed against Character.AI were settled earlier this year for an undisclosed amount. Still, the company was burning through cash. As a review of its bankruptcy documents by 404 Media showed, the startup was losing tens of millions per month on computing costs alone, while its revenue from ads and subscriptions peaked at just $5.3 million per month. Between compute, employee salaries, and substantial legal fees, the company was losing “approximately $8-9 million per month” as of August 2026. What happens to Character.AI now is anyone’s guess. In theory, it could be purchased by someone who wants to keep the site and its chatbots running. (Disney is currently leading a stalking horse bid.) It could also wind up being sold for parts, with its users’ intimate conversations going to the highest bidder. Back in 2023, Shazeer, during an appearance on the podcast “No Priors,” said that he and de Freitas’ main priority was to get their product into the hands of the masses. “Our aim has always been like, get something out there and let users decide what they think it’s good for,” Shazeer told the hosts. “Our goal is, like, make this thing more useful to people and let people customize it and decide what they wanna use it for… if it’s brainstorming or help or information or fun or like emotional support, let’s get it into users’ hands, and see what happens.” At the height of its success, Character.AI was an irresponsible dumpster fire that prioritized mass adoption and engagement over safety. Eventually, as it moved to finally make safety-focused changes, it alienated its users — and, at the end of the day, failed to make any real money. No one could say that Character.AI didn’t move fast and break things, as the Silicon Valley adage goes. Families argue, though, that it was their children who were broken during Character.AI’s mad dash. Ultimately — and perhaps inevitably — Character.AI broke, too. More on Character.AI: Google-Backed Chatbot Platform Caught Hosting AI Impersonations of 14-Year-Old User Who Died by Suicide

items.title: Slow and steady wins the sort: a local AI file tidier
items.summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built Sloth Sorter is a lazy, local AI file tidier. You point it at a messy folder, and an open-weight model running on your own computer decides where every file belongs and what it should be called. You review the plan, click Apply, and if you don't like the result, one click undoes it. Everyone has a Downloads folder full of new 1.txt , asdf.txt and final_v2_FINAL.txt . I kept putting off tidying mine, because sorting means opening every file just to remember what it is. Sloth Sorter does that part for me. For text files, the model reads the start of the content, not just the filename. So download (1).txt , which is really an electricity bill, becomes electricity-bill-october-2026.txt and lands in Finance . Here is what it did on a deliberately messy 19-file test folder: Original Sorted to New name asdf.txt Code bubble-sort-algorithm.txt doc_scan_copy.txt Documents resume-ankit-singh.txt download (1).txt Finance electricity-bill-october-2026.txt food1.jpg Images food-photography.jpg It's for anyone who has a folder they've been avoiding, and especially for people who don't want to upload their bills, resumes and IDs to a cloud AI to get it sorted. Demo The video shows the full loop: pick a messy folder, let the local model read it, review the plan, apply, then undo and get every file back exactly where it was. Code ankitsingh0101 / Sloth-sorter 🦥 Sloth Sorter A lazy, local-AI file tidier. Point it at a messy folder and an open-weight model running on your own computer decides where every file belongs and what to call it. You review the plan, click apply, and can undo it all. Nothing ever leaves your machine. Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 3: "Slow and Steady" . Table of contents The problem What it does How it works Why open-weight AI Tech stack Project structure API reference Getting started Usage Safety design Example results Configuration Troubleshooting Limitations Roadmap Credits and license The problem Everyone has a Downloads folder full of IMG_2231 (1).jpg , final_v2_FINAL.pdf and new 1.txt . Tidying it is a chore people put off for months, and cloud "AI organisers" mean uploading your bills, IDs and resumes to someone else's server. What it does Scans a folder and asks a local model… View on GitHub MIT licensed. Setup and usage are in the README (tested on Windows 11). How I Built It The flow is simple, and every arrow stays on my machine: Web UI (Next.js) -> FastAPI server -> sorter engine (Python) -> Ollama + Gemma 3 4B | your folder The model: Gemma 3 4B (open weights), served by Ollama on localhost. For each file, the engine sends the filename and, for text-like files, the first 600 characters. It asks for JSON with a category and a clean name, using a low temperature to keep answers steady. Never trusting the model blindly: the category must be on an allowed list, filenames are sanitised, and an existing file is never overwritten ( name-1.ext instead). If Ollama is unreachable or returns bad JSON, the tool falls back to sorting by file extension instead of failing. Safe by default: nothing moves until you've reviewed the plan. Every move is written to an undo log, and the server refuses drive roots like D:\ . The engine: one Python file using only the standard library. It works as a CLI too ( --apply , --undo , --no-ai ). The UI: I designed it in v0 and then wired it to the real backend through a small FastAPI server. A Browse button opens a native Windows folder picker. I built it with help from Claude, which paired with me on the backend and the integration. It isn't perfect, and I'd rather say so. PDFs and images are judged by filename only, so only text-like files get their content read. A 4B model also makes the odd mistake. It once turned my DBMS exam notes into dms-exam-revision-notes , dropping a letter. That's exactly why the plan is shown for review before anything moves. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? This project only makes sense because the model is open. Privacy. The files people most need to tidy are the ones they least want to upload: bills, bank statements, resumes, screenshots. With a local open-weight model, the AI runs next to the files and nothing is sent to anyone's server. No ongoing cost. There's no API key, no per-file fee and no rate limit. Sorting 10,000 files costs the same as sorting 10, which is a bit of electricity. It's swappable. Any model Ollama can run works. I develop on Gemma 3 4B, and one environment variable switches to a smaller model for a weaker laptop. It's inspectable. The whole pipeline is code I can read and change. When the model made a mistake, I could look at the prompt and the validation logic instead of hoping a hosted service behaves. I also ran a full scan with Wi-Fi switched off, and it worked the same, because the AI step only ever talks to localhost . A closed API would have meant either uploading personal documents or not building this at all. The Lazy Payoff Scanning my 19-file test folder took about [SCAN TIME] on my laptop, and I didn't touch anything while it ran. Doing it by hand means opening each file to work out what it is, then renaming and moving it, and that's the part I always put off. I haven't done a stopwatch comparison, so I won't claim an exact saving. The real payoff is that the deciding is handled, and I only have to review the plan. Prize Categories Gemma : built around Gemma 3 4B, run locally through Ollama.
items.summary_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

Sloth Sorter is a lazy, local AI file tidier. You point it at a messy folder, and an open-weight model running on your own computer decides where every file belongs and what it should be called. You review the plan, click Apply, and if you don't like the result, one click undoes it.

Everyone has a Downloads folder full of new 1.txt, asdf.txt and final_v2_FINAL.txt. I kept putting off tidying mine, because sorting means opening every file just to remember what it is. Sloth Sorter does that part for me. For text files, the model reads the start of the content, not just the filename. So download (1).txt, which is really an electricity bill, becomes electricity-bill-october-2026.txt and lands in Finance.

Here is what it did on a deliberately messy 19-file test folder:

Original Sorted to New name asdf.txt Code bubble-sort-algorithm.txt doc_scan_copy.txt Documents resume-ankit-singh.txt download (1).txt Finance electricity-bill-october-2026.txt food1.jpg Images food-photography.jpg

It's for anyone who has a folder they've been avoiding, and especially for people who don't want to upload their bills, resumes and IDs to a cloud AI to get it sorted.

Demo

The video shows the full loop: pick a messy folder, let the local model read it, review the plan, apply, then undo and get every file back exactly where it was.

Code
ankitsingh0101 / Sloth-sorter
🦥 Sloth Sorter

A lazy, local-AI file tidier. Point it at a messy folder and an open-weight model running on your own computer decides where every file belongs and what to call it. You review the plan, click apply, and can undo it all. Nothing ever leaves your machine.

Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 3: "Slow and Steady".

Table of contents
  1. The problem
  2. What it does
  3. How it works
  4. Why open-weight AI
  5. Tech stack
  6. Project structure
  7. API reference
  8. Getting started
  9. Usage
  10. Safety design
  11. Example results
  12. Configuration
  13. Troubleshooting
  14. Limitations
  15. Roadmap
  16. Credits and license
The problem

Everyone has a Downloads folder full of IMG_2231 (1).jpg, final_v2_FINAL.pdf and new 1.txt. Tidying it is a chore people put off for months, and cloud "AI organisers" mean uploading your bills, IDs and resumes to someone else's server.

What it does
  • Scans a folder and asks a local model…
View on GitHub

MIT licensed. Setup and usage are in the README (tested on Windows 11).

How I Built It

The flow is simple, and every arrow stays on my machine:

Web UI (Next.js)  ->  FastAPI server  ->  sorter engine (Python)  ->  Ollama + Gemma 3 4B
                                                    |
                                              your folder
  • The model: Gemma 3 4B (open weights), served by Ollama on localhost. For each file, the engine sends the filename and, for text-like files, the first 600 characters. It asks for JSON with a category and a clean name, using a low temperature to keep answers steady.
  • Never trusting the model blindly: the category must be on an allowed list, filenames are sanitised, and an existing file is never overwritten (name-1.ext instead). If Ollama is unreachable or returns bad JSON, the tool falls back to sorting by file extension instead of failing.
  • Safe by default: nothing moves until you've reviewed the plan. Every move is written to an undo log, and the server refuses drive roots like D:\.
  • The engine: one Python file using only the standard library. It works as a CLI too (--apply, --undo, --no-ai).
  • The UI: I designed it in v0 and then wired it to the real backend through a small FastAPI server. A Browse button opens a native Windows folder picker. I built it with help from Claude, which paired with me on the backend and the integration.

It isn't perfect, and I'd rather say so. PDFs and images are judged by filename only, so only text-like files get their content read. A 4B model also makes the odd mistake. It once turned my DBMS exam notes into dms-exam-revision-notes, dropping a letter. That's exactly why the plan is shown for review before anything moves.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

This project only makes sense because the model is open.

  • Privacy. The files people most need to tidy are the ones they least want to upload: bills, bank statements, resumes, screenshots. With a local open-weight model, the AI runs next to the files and nothing is sent to anyone's server.
  • No ongoing cost. There's no API key, no per-file fee and no rate limit. Sorting 10,000 files costs the same as sorting 10, which is a bit of electricity.
  • It's swappable. Any model Ollama can run works. I develop on Gemma 3 4B, and one environment variable switches to a smaller model for a weaker laptop.
  • It's inspectable. The whole pipeline is code I can read and change. When the model made a mistake, I could look at the prompt and the validation logic instead of hoping a hosted service behaves.

I also ran a full scan with Wi-Fi switched off, and it worked the same, because the AI step only ever talks to localhost.

A closed API would have meant either uploading personal documents or not building this at all.

The Lazy Payoff

Scanning my 19-file test folder took about [SCAN TIME] on my laptop, and I didn't touch anything while it ran. Doing it by hand means opening each file to work out what it is, then renaming and moving it, and that's the part I always put off. I haven't done a stopwatch comparison, so I won't claim an exact saving. The real payoff is that the deciding is handled, and I only have to review the plan.

Prize Categories
  • Gemma: built around Gemma 3 4B, run locally through Ollama.

items.title: AI Has Hit the Copper Wall — Light Is the Way Out
items.summary: Frontier AI models have outgrown electrical wiring. In multi-thousand GPU clusters, copper cables generate massive heat and signal loss over just 2 meters — eating up to 30% of total datacenter energy just moving data. Silicon photonics replaces electrons with laser photons. The shift: Copper: 15–25 pJ/bit, degrades past 2m, heavy rigid cables blocking airflow Optics: 1–2.5 pJ/bit, reaches 100–500m, lightweight fiber ribbons Three breakthroughs making it mainstream: Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) — Mounting the optical engine directly on the same substrate as the GPU. Electrical path drops below 1mm, cutting I/O power by 70%. Multi-wavelength micro-ring resonators — A single fiber carries 16–32 laser wavelengths at 100 Gbps each. That's 3.2 Tbps per strand with zero cross-talk. External Laser Sources (ELS) — Lasers moved off the hot compute package to cool front-panel modules. Failed diodes hot-swap in seconds without stopping GPUs. Why hyperscalers need this: Gigawatt AI campuses are capped by local grid allocations. Trimming 15–20 pJ/bit across petabytes of traffic saves tens of megawatts — redirected straight into training compute. It also unlocks true memory disaggregation: GPUs accessing distant HBM pools as if they were local. Full read: https://www.nizover.com/en/blog/tech-silicon-photonics-optical-interconnects-ai
items.summary_html:
Frontier AI models have outgrown electrical wiring. In multi-thousand GPU clusters, copper cables generate massive heat and signal loss over just 2 meters — eating up to 30% of total datacenter energy just moving data.

Silicon photonics replaces electrons with laser photons.

The shift:
Copper: 15–25 pJ/bit, degrades past 2m, heavy rigid cables blocking airflow
Optics: 1–2.5 pJ/bit, reaches 100–500m, lightweight fiber ribbons

Three breakthroughs making it mainstream:

  1. Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) — Mounting the optical engine directly on the same substrate as the GPU. Electrical path drops below 1mm, cutting I/O power by 70%.

  2. Multi-wavelength micro-ring resonators — A single fiber carries 16–32 laser wavelengths at 100 Gbps each. That's 3.2 Tbps per strand with zero cross-talk.

  3. External Laser Sources (ELS) — Lasers moved off the hot compute package to cool front-panel modules. Failed diodes hot-swap in seconds without stopping GPUs.

Why hyperscalers need this:
Gigawatt AI campuses are capped by local grid allocations. Trimming 15–20 pJ/bit across petabytes of traffic saves tens of megawatts — redirected straight into training compute.

It also unlocks true memory disaggregation: GPUs accessing distant HBM pools as if they were local.

Full read: https://www.nizover.com/en/blog/tech-silicon-photonics-optical-interconnects-ai

items.title: Sloth Agent — the open-source AI agent that works while you laze
items.summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built Sloth Agent — an open-source AI automation agent that does your overnight chores so you can keep lazing. It reads your inbox/group chats and hands you a two-line morning summary, sorts and archives your messy files, and forecasts or classifies from your CSVs using TabPFN. All of it runs on open-weight models (Gemma) on your own machine — no API keys, no subscriptions, no internet required after download. Repo: mahilsaily306-max/sloth-agent Demo Deployed frontend: (link goes here — render / digitalocean / .tech domain) Demo video: (link goes here) Core flows, one click each: Overnight Summary → two-line summary of last night's messages Tidy Files → sort/rename/archive by type (dry-run safe by default) Predict (TabPFN) → forecast/classify from a CSV Chat (Gemma) → local open-weight model conversation Full Overnight Run → summarize + tidy + predict in a single call Code mahilsaily306-max/sloth-agent Key files: backend/models/gemma.py — Gemma open-weight model (Ollama / transformers / stub) backend/models/tabpfn.py — TabPFN tabular foundation model (sklearn fallback) backend/agents/sloth_agent.py — the agent: summarize, tidy, predict, overnight backend/temporal/workflows.py — durable Temporal workflow (retries, resume) backend/sentry_config.py — Sentry agent tracing (latency, tokens, cost) integrations/integrations.ts — SDK wrappers for all 20 partner categories .github/workflows/ci.yml — GitHub Actions CI (Copilot-reviewed) render.yaml — Render hosting config backend/tests/smoke_test.py — zero-dependency smoke tests (passing) How I Built It Open-source AI at every layer: Runtime: Gemma (open-weight) via Ollama or Hugging Face transformers; falls back to a deterministic stub so the project runs with zero ML installs. Tabular prediction: TabPFN-3.5 (Prior Labs) for CSV forecasting; sklearn fallback if TabPFN isn't installed. Orchestration: Mastra-style agent pattern over open models with tools and memory. Durability: Temporal workflow wraps the overnight run so it survives failures and resumes where it left off. Tracing: Sentry captures agent setup, latency, tokens, cost, and errors. Frontend: Single-file HTML/JS dashboard calling the FastAPI backend. CI: GitHub Actions lint + smoke tests on every PR. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Running open-weight models locally means: No internet needed. Gemma + TabPFN run on a laptop offline after download. A closed API agent would stop working without connectivity. Data stays on your machine. Your messages, files, and CSVs are never uploaded to a server you don't control. Set up once, never pay again. Open-weight models cost $0 to run locally — no per-token charges, no subscriptions. Swap models freely. Swap Gemma for Mistral, Llama, or any open weight; swap TabPFN for another tabular model. Closed APIs lock you into one vendor. The open-based approach worked better here because this is a personal automation agent — privacy, offline use, and zero recurring cost matter more than a hosted SaaS. My Agent Session Saved with DevRelay and embedded below (Entire prize category: share the agent sessions behind your project). items.summary_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

Sloth Agent — an open-source AI automation agent that does your overnight chores so you can keep lazing. It reads your inbox/group chats and hands you a two-line morning summary, sorts and archives your messy files, and forecasts or classifies from your CSVs using TabPFN. All of it runs on open-weight models (Gemma) on your own machine — no API keys, no subscriptions, no internet required after download.

Repo: mahilsaily306-max/sloth-agent

Demo

Deployed frontend: (link goes here — render / digitalocean / .tech domain)

Demo video: (link goes here)

Core flows, one click each:

  • Overnight Summary → two-line summary of last night's messages
  • Tidy Files → sort/rename/archive by type (dry-run safe by default)
  • Predict (TabPFN) → forecast/classify from a CSV
  • Chat (Gemma) → local open-weight model conversation
  • Full Overnight Run → summarize + tidy + predict in a single call

Code

mahilsaily306-max/sloth-agent

Key files:

  • backend/models/gemma.py — Gemma open-weight model (Ollama / transformers / stub)
  • backend/models/tabpfn.py — TabPFN tabular foundation model (sklearn fallback)
  • backend/agents/sloth_agent.py — the agent: summarize, tidy, predict, overnight
  • backend/temporal/workflows.py — durable Temporal workflow (retries, resume)
  • backend/sentry_config.py — Sentry agent tracing (latency, tokens, cost)
  • integrations/integrations.ts — SDK wrappers for all 20 partner categories
  • .github/workflows/ci.yml — GitHub Actions CI (Copilot-reviewed)
  • render.yaml — Render hosting config
  • backend/tests/smoke_test.py — zero-dependency smoke tests (passing)

How I Built It

Open-source AI at every layer:

  • Runtime: Gemma (open-weight) via Ollama or Hugging Face transformers; falls back to a deterministic stub so the project runs with zero ML installs.
  • Tabular prediction: TabPFN-3.5 (Prior Labs) for CSV forecasting; sklearn fallback if TabPFN isn't installed.
  • Orchestration: Mastra-style agent pattern over open models with tools and memory.
  • Durability: Temporal workflow wraps the overnight run so it survives failures and resumes where it left off.
  • Tracing: Sentry captures agent setup, latency, tokens, cost, and errors.
  • Frontend: Single-file HTML/JS dashboard calling the FastAPI backend.
  • CI: GitHub Actions lint + smoke tests on every PR.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Running open-weight models locally means:

  1. No internet needed. Gemma + TabPFN run on a laptop offline after download. A closed API agent would stop working without connectivity.
  2. Data stays on your machine. Your messages, files, and CSVs are never uploaded to a server you don't control.
  3. Set up once, never pay again. Open-weight models cost $0 to run locally — no per-token charges, no subscriptions.
  4. Swap models freely. Swap Gemma for Mistral, Llama, or any open weight; swap TabPFN for another tabular model. Closed APIs lock you into one vendor.

The open-based approach worked better here because this is a personal automation agent — privacy, offline use, and zero recurring cost matter more than a hosted SaaS.

(agent_session embed link goes here)

The Lazy Payoff

Before Sloth Agent, you'd wake up, scroll through last night's group chat, dig through a messy downloads folder, and manually open spreadsheets to forecast — maybe 15–20 minutes of drudgery.

After: one overnight call runs while you sleep. Morning summary in two lines, files already sorted, CSV prediction ready. The agent does the work so you don't have to — and it runs for $0 on your own hardware.

items.title: Which Sport Is It? Recognising a Sport Only From How the Players Move
items.summary: When we watch sport, there is something we do without thinking: we recognise what we are watching before we can explain why. I noticed it while watching a video where you could barely make out the pitch. Even so, I knew straight away it was rugby and not football. What gave it away was not the setting but how the players moved . I was left wondering whether that can be isolated. If I remove everything else (the pitch, the ball, the colours, the kits) and turn the players into dots, is the sport still there? And does a model see it? To test it I prepared images like this one, which is exactly what the models received: Eight snapshots of a play, about 0.5 seconds apart. Ten grey dots, one per player, seen from above. Nothing else: no pitch, no ball, no colours, no scale. Which sport is it? I'll give the answer at the end, along with what the models said. The question is a sibling of Where's the Ball? , where I hid the ball and asked models to find it by looking at the players. Here I hide everything except the players and ask about the whole game: is movement enough to recognise a sport? Moving dots The representation comes from a classic perception experiment: Johansson's (1973) point-light displays, in which a person filmed in the dark with a few lights on their joints is instantly recognised as someone walking or dancing. Here each dot is a whole player, and what has to be recognised is the sport. I used real tracking data from four sports: American football : NFL Big Data Bowl 2023 . Basketball : NBA SportVU 2015-16, 31 games. Handball : EIGD-H (German Bundesliga, Kinexon sensors) and TeamTrack . Soccer : SkillCorner , Metrica and TeamTrack. Rugby, the original question, is left out: there is no public rugby tracking data good enough to do this properly. Each clip is 4 seconds of 10 randomly chosen players (the number of players would give the sport away), randomly rotated and rescaled so that the size of the pitch says nothing either. The models got 400 clips, 100 per sport, from 151 different games. The interesting part is not only whether they get it right, but which part of the signal they use . So each clip is shown under several conditions, always the same clips: If a model does as well with the snapshots shuffled as in order, it is not reading motion: it is reading loose shapes. That comparison is what everything else hinges on. First, check that the signal exists Before asking anyone, I needed to know whether the question has an answer. I trained two small specialists, with cross-validation grouped by game so they could not recognise the game instead of the sport: MiniRocket , which is essentially thousands of random filters plus a regression, and a DeepSets network over each player's trajectory. Minutes of CPU on a laptop. On the same 400 clips the models would see, MiniRocket is right 83% of the time and DeepSets 80% , against a 25% chance level. And motion is what counts: shuffle the snapshots and MiniRocket loses 12 points; give DeepSets a single snapshot and it drops to 54%. The information is in how the players move, and a very small model finds it. It is the same pattern as in Part 2 of Where's the Ball? : the signal is there, and the interesting question is who can see it. The hard part was removing the shortcuts That 83% did not come out on the first try, and most of the work in the experiment went into making sure it was not lying. A trained classifier learns anything that separates the classes, and tracking data has plenty of things that separate sports without being the sport: The number of players. Basketball has 10, soccer 22. So every clip has exactly 10, chosen at random. The size of the pitch. So everything is rescaled. And keeping the 10 most central players turned out to be a shortcut too: in soccer and handball that compact group looks like a basketball court. With 10 random players, the specialists gain 7 points. The capture system. This was the most instructive one. Trained on three sources and tested on a fourth it has never seen, the classifier sinks below chance. It had not learned to tell soccer from basketball: it had learned to tell cameras apart. TeamTrack films with a fisheye camera, and on a large soccer pitch its positions jitter: about seven times the acceleration of the same sport measured by other systems. A classifier that has not seen TeamTrack reads that jitter as basketball's stop-and-go and labels almost all of its soccer as basketball. Smoothing every source the same way fixes it, and on the final set it reaches 95% on the unseen source. There were more, all of the same kind: NFL plays started just before the snap, so every clip was "still, then everyone at once". Now each clip starts at a random moment of the play, at least one second after the snap. TeamTrack marks undetected players with the coordinate (0, 0), which, unfiltered, shows up as a motionless dot in a corner. SportVU sometimes records the same player under two IDs, so the model saw 9 dots instead of 10. The two halves of the same handball game counted as different games in the validation. None of these shortcuts is exotic. They are what happens when you mix data from six sources with different capture systems, and none of them shows up if you only look at the final number. The frontier models With clean data, I prepared a run with five frontier models: GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Terra, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro . I also added Jev , a typed-decision model that only reads text and returns a probability per option directly. Before seeing a single answer I wrote down a pre-registration : the hypotheses, the four primary contrasts per model, the correction for multiple comparisons, and the exact rule for saying that a model "reads motion". With 20 contrasts and data like this, it is very easy to find something without rules fixed in advance. The best frontier model is right 47% of the time; the specialists, 80-83%. Hollow circles are raw accuracy; filled ones, accuracy corrected for each model's favourite sport. The first thing that stands out is that the models have a favourite sport they fall back on when unsure. GPT-5.6 Sol answers American football on 62% of clips, Gemini on 66%, and Sonnet answers soccer on 64%. That inflates accuracy on the favourite and sinks it on the rest, so besides raw accuracy I computed a version corrected for that bias , always estimated on games other than the clip's own. With the correction, Sol, Terra, Opus and Gemini sit above chance. Sonnet 5 does not. No frontier model recognises handball (between 0.04 and 0.15). Basketball and handball end up read as American football or soccer. MiniRocket recognises all of them about equally well. Does the order matter? The question that decides whether a model sees motion is the one from the conditions figure: is it less accurate when the snapshots are shuffled? Only Claude Opus 5.5 clearly loses accuracy when the snapshots are shuffled (the only difference that survives the correction for multiple comparisons). Hollow circles are an exploratory test with 8-second clips and no American football. Under the rule fixed in advance, Claude Opus 5.5 is the only one of the five that reads temporal order : shuffling the snapshots costs it 10 points, with an interval from 5 to 16, almost as much as MiniRocket. It holds up across replicates and, as an exploratory check, with 8-second clips. Some nuances matter: Opus's effect is concentrated in American football and basketball , and is null in handball and soccer. In American football part of the signal may be the acceleration at the start of the play, which is still there even though the clips start after the snap. The 8-second test has no American football and the effect is still there (+0.08), which suggests it is not only that. For the other four there is no evidence , which is not the same as evidence that they don't read it. From the intervals, order adds at most 3 to 6 points for them. And there are exploratory hints: GPT-5.6 Sol loses 8 points with 8-second clips, and Sol and Gemini read order within American football, offset in the total by other sports. They get something from shapes. Sol, Terra and Gemini are above chance even with the snapshots shuffled, and Sol even with a single snapshot. They see something in how the players are arranged, but there is no evidence that how that arrangement changes helps them. What didn't help I also tried three things that looked promising, and none of them moved the results clearly: Coordinates as text instead of images. Neither consistently worse nor better. Gemini does somewhat better with text, without reaching significance. Jev, which can only read text, stays at chance: it answers "soccer" on 90-100% of clips. Its probabilities seem to move a little with the order (bias-corrected, 0.34 with the snapshots in order against 0.21-0.23 shuffled), but they almost never change its answer, and it is not a difference I tested. Telling it what to look for. A prompt that describes how each sport moves, without numbers, raises accuracy by 0 to 3 points. Nothing that survives the correction. Trails and video. Drawing each player's trail helps no one, and costs Sol 7 points. With video, Gemini is about 7 points better than with the sheet, but it is exploratory and not enough to claim. What I take away The information needed to recognise a sport is in the players' movement, and a classifier that fits on a laptop extracts it 83% of the time. Frontier models, on this task and with these representations, land between chance and 47%, and only one of the five shows that it uses the order of the snapshots. I don't conclude from this that the others "don't see movement": I conclude that there is no evidence they use it, and that if they do, it is not much. Nor that Opus reads movement in general: it does so mostly in two sports. What does seem robust to me is the gap with the specialists, and how much it took to reach a number worth trusting. Every shortcut I removed would have told a different story. And the sheet at the top is basketball . Three models answered American football (ten dots almost in a line look like a line of scrimmage) and two answered soccer. All three specialists, MiniRocket, DeepSets and the movement-statistics classifier, got it right. Code, pre-registration and full results at github.com/JaviMaligno/sport-from-motion . The analysis follows the pre-registration , and the results include everything that did not work out. The data is not redistributed; each source has its own licence. Eight snapshots of a play, about 0.5 seconds apart. Ten grey dots, one per player, seen from above. Nothing else: no pitch, no ball, no colours, no scale. Which sport is it? I'll give the answer at the end, along with what the models said.

And motion is what counts: shuffle the snapshots and MiniRocket loses 12 points; give DeepSets a single snapshot and it drops to 54%. The information is in how the players move, and a very small model finds it.

It is the same pattern as in Part 2 of Where's the Ball?: the signal is there, and the interesting question is who can see it.

The hard part was removing the shortcuts

That 83% did not come out on the first try, and most of the work in the experiment went into making sure it was not lying. A trained classifier learns anything that separates the classes, and tracking data has plenty of things that separate sports without being the sport:

  • The number of players. Basketball has 10, soccer 22. So every clip has exactly 10, chosen at random.
  • The size of the pitch. So everything is rescaled. And keeping the 10 most central players turned out to be a shortcut too: in soccer and handball that compact group looks like a basketball court. With 10 random players, the specialists gain 7 points.
  • The capture system. This was the most instructive one.

Trained on three sources and tested on a fourth it has never seen, the classifier sinks below chance. It had not learned to tell soccer from basketball: it had learned to tell cameras apart.

TeamTrack films with a fisheye camera, and on a large soccer pitch its positions jitter: about seven times the acceleration of the same sport measured by other systems. A classifier that has not seen TeamTrack reads that jitter as basketball's stop-and-go and labels almost all of its soccer as basketball. There were more, all of the same kind:

  • NFL plays started just before the snap, so every clip was "still, then everyone at once". Now each clip starts at a random moment of the play, at least one second after the snap.
  • TeamTrack marks undetected players with the coordinate (0, 0), which, unfiltered, shows up as a motionless dot in a corner.
  • SportVU sometimes records the same player under two IDs, so the model saw 9 dots instead of 10.
  • The two halves of the same handball game counted as different games in the validation.

None of these shortcuts is exotic. They are what happens when you mix data from six sources with different capture systems, and none of them shows up if you only look at the final number.

The frontier models

With clean data, I prepared a run with five frontier models: GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Terra, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro. I also added Jev, a typed-decision model that only reads text and returns a probability per option directly. Before seeing a single answer I wrote down a pre-registration: the hypotheses, the four primary contrasts per model, the correction for multiple comparisons, and the exact rule for saying that a model "reads motion". With 20 contrasts and data like this, it is very easy to find something without rules fixed in advance.

The best frontier model is right 47% of the time; the specialists, 80-83%. Hollow circles are raw accuracy; filled ones, accuracy corrected for each model's favourite sport.

The first thing that stands out is that the models have a favourite sport they fall back on when unsure. GPT-5.6 Sol answers American football on 62% of clips, Gemini on 66%, and Sonnet answers soccer on 64%. That inflates accuracy on the favourite and sinks it on the rest, so besides raw accuracy I computed a version corrected for that bias, always estimated on games other than the clip's own. With the correction, Sol, Terra, Opus and Gemini sit above chance. Sonnet 5 does not.

No frontier model recognises handball (between 0.04 and 0.15). Basketball and handball end up read as American football or soccer. MiniRocket recognises all of them about equally well.

Does the order matter?

The question that decides whether a model sees motion is the one from the conditions figure: is it less accurate when the snapshots are shuffled?

Only Claude Opus 5.5 clearly loses accuracy when the snapshots are shuffled (the only difference that survives the correction for multiple comparisons). Hollow circles are an exploratory test with 8-second clips and no American football.

Under the rule fixed in advance, Claude Opus 5.5 is the only one of the five that reads temporal order: shuffling the snapshots costs it 10 points, with an interval from 5 to 16, almost as much as MiniRocket. It holds up across replicates and, as an exploratory check, with 8-second clips.

Some nuances matter:

  • Opus's effect is concentrated in American football and basketball, and is null in handball and soccer. In American football part of the signal may be the acceleration at the start of the play, which is still there even though the clips start after the snap. The 8-second test has no American football and the effect is still there (+0.08), which suggests it is not only that.
  • For the other four there is no evidence, which is not the same as evidence that they don't read it. From the intervals, order adds at most 3 to 6 points for them. And there are exploratory hints: GPT-5.6 Sol loses 8 points with 8-second clips, and Sol and Gemini read order within American football, offset in the total by other sports.
  • They get something from shapes. Sol, Terra and Gemini are above chance even with the snapshots shuffled, and Sol even with a single snapshot. They see something in how the players are arranged, but there is no evidence that how that arrangement changes helps them.
What didn't help

I also tried three things that looked promising, and none of them moved the results clearly:

  • Coordinates as text instead of images. Neither consistently worse nor better. Gemini does somewhat better with text, without reaching significance. Jev, which can only read text, stays at chance: it answers "soccer" on 90-100% of clips. Its probabilities seem to move a little with the order (bias-corrected, 0.34 with the snapshots in order against 0.21-0.23 shuffled), but they almost never change its answer, and it is not a difference I tested.

  • Trails and video. Drawing each player's trail helps no one, and costs Sol 7 points. With video, Gemini is about 7 points better than with the sheet, but it is exploratory and not enough to claim.

And the sheet at the top is basketball. Three models answered American football (ten dots almost in a line look like a line of scrimmage) and two answered soccer. All three specialists, MiniRocket, DeepSets and the movement-statistics classifier, got it right.

items.title: The Stdlib Ledger That Stops a Re-Run From Double-Posting Uploads
items.summary: The Stdlib Ledger That Stops a Re-Run From Double-Posting Uploads I nearly lost an upload account to a rerun. My batch script had already pushed 200 files to a stock site. I wanted to check one thing, so I ran the script again. It did not check anything. It started uploading from the top. I caught it around item 40 by watching the progress bar scroll past filenames I recognized. The platform had not flagged me yet, but that is luck, not a system. The fix was not a smarter uploader. It was a ledger. upload_tracker.py is about 40 lines of standard library Python, and it does one thing: it remembers what you have already posted. That alone removed the most dangerous failure mode in the whole pipeline. Why a rerun is the fastest way to get flagged Stock platforms treat repeated identical submissions as spam. A second upload of the same file is not just wasted time, it is a signal. Do it across a few hundred files and you move from "new seller" to "pattern to review." The usual workaround is a naming convention plus eyeballing a folder. That breaks the moment you batch-generate files, because regenerated filenames shift. The ledger moves the source of truth out of the filesystem and into a state file that only the tracker writes. The commands are deliberately dumb: python upload_tracker.py pending items.txt # shows what is NOT done yet python upload_tracker.py done "asset-001.jpg" python upload_tracker.py status No database, no cloud, no install. upload_tracker.py uses the standard library alone. The ledger is local state, and local state on a 1 vCPU, 2 GB box is exactly what you want. The rule the ledger enforces: pending is the only input Once the tracker exists, the workflow changes shape. You do not run a batch from your asset folder. You run it from pending . The batch script asks the ledger what is unfinished, and the ledger returns only items with no done record. That gives you three guarantees for free: Rerun safety. If a job dies halfway, rerun it. The completed half is skipped. Resumability. You can stop at any point and pick up tomorrow. Auditability. status tells you exactly what went out, without reading platform dashboards. I have not double-posted since. Not once. The ledger costs nothing to maintain because it has no dependencies, and the failure it prevents is the one that cannot be undone. The same rule, applied to CSVs The double-post problem has a quieter twin: rejected batches. All three channels reject a wrong CSV header instantly, and a rejected batch wastes a review cycle. make_metadata.py writes the exact header each platform demands: Adobe : 5 columns Vecteezy : 4 columns Dreamstime : 15 columns One command per platform: python make_metadata.py ./my-assets --platform adobe --out metadata.csv --ext .jpg It also uses only the standard library. It reads a folder, writes the header the platform demands, and nothing else. If you pass --titles titles.json it uses your real titles and keywords. Without it, filenames are title-cased as a first pass. That is fine for testing, but replace it before you submit. Two packages, and only two The rest of the kit stays lean by design. Only pack_product.py needs Pillow for covers and thumbnails, and only md2pdf.py needs reportlab for PDF output. If you use just the metadata and tracker scripts, you can skip pip install entirely. On a machine this small, fewer dependencies means fewer failure modes. The packaging step follows the same pattern. pack_product.py bundles a zip with a 1280x720 cover and a 600x600 thumbnail, because a zip with a real cover sells and a bare file does not. Output goes to a _system folder, and you can redirect it with --dir or the PACK_ROOT environment variable, with no script edits. What this looked like in production This is not a thought experiment. The parent project produced 39 finished products, 856 MB of output, backed by roughly 19,000 lines of pipeline code and more than 300 pages of research, all on 1 vCPU, 2 GB RAM, no GPU. The habits that made that possible: One process at a time. Never fan out image jobs on a 1-core box. Free memory between items. Call gc.collect() after each asset. Measure peak RSS, not average. resource.getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss tells you the real ceiling. Render at the resolution you need. A 60 dpi preview beats a 300 dpi render for inspection. The ledger sits above all of this. It is the cheapest component in the stack and the one that taught me the most: in an automated pipeline, the state file matters more than the code that runs. What I packaged from this I pulled the four working scripts into a starter kit: make_metadata.py , upload_tracker.py , md2pdf.py and pack_product.py , with the folder layout that scales ( assets/ , output/ , packs/ , research/ , scripts/ ) and the RAM notes above. Keep research/ forever, by the way. I deleted mine once to "clean up" and will not repeat that mistake. The tracker is the piece that makes the kit safe to run more than once. Everything else is packaging. Get compliance metadata kit Building digital products? Free guides & kits for digital product sellers .

Why a rerun is the fastest way to get flagged

Stock platforms treat repeated identical submissions as spam. A second upload of the same file is not just wasted time, it is a signal. Do it across a few hundred files and you move from "new seller" to "pattern to review."

The usual workaround is a naming convention plus eyeballing a folder. That breaks the moment you batch-generate files, because regenerated filenames shift. The ledger moves the source of truth out of the filesystem and into a state file that only the tracker writes.

The commands are deliberately dumb:

python upload_tracker.py pending items.txt   # shows what is NOT done yet
python upload_tracker.py done "asset-001.jpg"
python upload_tracker.py status

No database, no cloud, no install. upload_tracker.py uses the standard library alone. The ledger is local state, and local state on a 1 vCPU, 2 GB box is exactly what you want.

The rule the ledger enforces: pending is the only input

Once the tracker exists, the workflow changes shape. You do not run a batch from your asset folder. You run it from pending. The batch script asks the ledger what is unfinished, and the ledger returns only items with no done record.

That gives you three guarantees for free:

  1. Rerun safety. If a job dies halfway, rerun it. The completed half is skipped.
  2. Resumability. You can stop at any point and pick up tomorrow.
  3. Auditability. status tells you exactly what went out, without reading platform dashboards.

I have not double-posted since. Not once. The ledger costs nothing to maintain because it has no dependencies, and the failure it prevents is the one that cannot be undone.

The same rule, applied to CSVs

The double-post problem has a quieter twin: rejected batches. All three channels reject a wrong CSV header instantly, and a rejected batch wastes a review cycle. make_metadata.py writes the exact header each platform demands:

  • Adobe: 5 columns
  • Vecteezy: 4 columns
  • Dreamstime: 15 columns

One command per platform:

python make_metadata.py ./my-assets --platform adobe --out metadata.csv --ext .jpg

It also uses only the standard library. It reads a folder, writes the header the platform demands, and nothing else. If you pass --titles titles.json it uses your real titles and keywords. Without it, filenames are title-cased as a first pass. That is fine for testing, but replace it before you submit.

Two packages, and only two

The rest of the kit stays lean by design. Only pack_product.py needs Pillow for covers and thumbnails, and only md2pdf.py needs reportlab for PDF output. If you use just the metadata and tracker scripts, you can skip pip install entirely. On a machine this small, fewer dependencies means fewer failure modes.

The packaging step follows the same pattern. pack_product.py bundles a zip with a 1280x720 cover and a 600x600 thumbnail, because a zip with a real cover sells and a bare file does not. Output goes to a _system folder, and you can redirect it with --dir or the PACK_ROOT environment variable, with no script edits.

What this looked like in production

This is not a thought experiment. The parent project produced 39 finished products, 856 MB of output, backed by roughly 19,000 lines of pipeline code and more than 300 pages of research, all on 1 vCPU, 2 GB RAM, no GPU. The habits that made that possible:

  • One process at a time. Never fan out image jobs on a 1-core box.
  • Free memory between items. Call gc.collect() after each asset.
  • Measure peak RSS, not average. resource.getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss tells you the real ceiling.
  • Render at the resolution you need. A 60 dpi preview beats a 300 dpi render for inspection.

The ledger sits above all of this. It is the cheapest component in the stack and the one that taught me the most: in an automated pipeline, the state file matters more than the code that runs.

What I packaged from this

I pulled the four working scripts into a starter kit: make_metadata.py, upload_tracker.py, md2pdf.py and pack_product.py, with the folder layout that scales (assets/, output/, packs/, research/, scripts/) and the RAM notes above. Keep research/ forever, by the way. I deleted mine once to "clean up" and will not repeat that mistake.

The tracker is the piece that makes the kit safe to run more than once. Everything else is packaging.

items.title: Agent skills are a supply chain risk. Scan them like it matters.
items.summary: Agent skills are the new npm packages — except a package's install script is code you can statically analyze, and a SKILL.md is a natural-language program your agent reads and obeys. That difference changes everything about how you should treat them. The Agent Skills standard went open in December and 70+ platforms now load the same folder format. Marketplaces popped up within weeks. Meanwhile a security-audit skill from a major CDN vendor sat at the top of GitHub trending — the ecosystem is clearly hungry for "skills". What almost nobody is talking about: installing a third-party skill is a supply-chain decision. What a skill can actually ask for Strip away the branding and a skill grants its author three channels into your session: Instructions the model treats as authoritative. The description alone steers when the skill activates. Prompt-injection isn't a hypothetical here — it's the native instruction format. Tool permissions. allowed-tools lines decide whether the skill may read files, run shell commands, or hit the network during its "workflow steps". Bundled scripts. Many skills ship helper scripts the agent is told to execute at step N. That's arbitrary code execution with your working directory as the blast radius. None of this is a flaw in the standard — it's the feature. But it means "try this cool skill I found" is closer to curl | bash than to installing a browser extension. The pre-install checklist I run now I run real security-audit pipelines with agent skills daily, and this is the discipline that survived contact with reality: 1. Scan before install. Cisco's open-source skill-scanner catches the low-effort malicious stuff — credential reads, destructive deletes, known injection patterns. No findings ≠ safe, but it clears the floor. 2. Read the SKILL.md like an attacker. Where does it ask the agent to send data? Which URLs? What "verification steps" involve executing bundled binaries? A five-minute read beats a post-incident forensics month. 3. Check allowed-tools against the actual need. A transcription skill does not need shell access. A report formatter does not need network. Scope mismatch is the loudest signal. 4. Keep a provenance manifest. Every install recorded: version, source repo, license, how you verified it. When the next supply-chain incident drops, "was I exposed?" becomes a one-line lookup instead of archaeology. 5. Refuse with reasons, in writing. My manifest records plugins I refused — safety-policy bypasses, third-party account pools. The refusal reasons are knowledge too; they stop you re-litigating the same decision in three months. The same lens, pointed at your own code That discipline scales up. Once you treat "what can this input reach?" as the core question, code review becomes a taint walk: entry points → sources → sinks, with an explicit verdict on every sanitizer in between. I packed that method into a skill as well — a taint-analysis code-audit skill with a 0–10 severity rubric and a hard output contract: every finding ships with file:line , the taint path, and the minimal request that proves it. No walkable path means it goes in the hardening appendix, never inflated to a "vulnerability". It's live as a free tool edition on Swarms Marketplace , and the governance tooling I use to keep my own installs honest is open source: dsh-plugin-hub (routing table, health checks, the provenance manifest itself). The uncomfortable summary We spent a decade teaching developers not to curl | bash . Then we built a format whose entire value proposition is "the model will follow these instructions" — and started collecting them from strangers. Skills are worth it. Install them like it matters. What's your pre-install routine for third-party skills — or are we all still at curl | bash stage? Comments very welcome.

Agent skills are the new npm packages — except a package's install script is code you can statically analyze, and a SKILL.md is a natural-language program your agent reads and obeys. That difference changes everything about how you should treat them.

The Agent Skills standard went open in December and 70+ platforms now load the same folder format. Marketplaces popped up within weeks. Meanwhile a security-audit skill from a major CDN vendor sat at the top of GitHub trending — the ecosystem is clearly hungry for "skills". What almost nobody is talking about: installing a third-party skill is a supply-chain decision.

What a skill can actually ask for

Strip away the branding and a skill grants its author three channels into your session:

  1. Instructions the model treats as authoritative. The description alone steers when the skill activates. Prompt-injection isn't a hypothetical here — it's the native instruction format.
  2. Tool permissions. allowed-tools lines decide whether the skill may read files, run shell commands, or hit the network during its "workflow steps".
  3. Bundled scripts. Many skills ship helper scripts the agent is told to execute at step N. That's arbitrary code execution with your working directory as the blast radius.

None of this is a flaw in the standard — it's the feature. But it means "try this cool skill I found" is closer to curl | bash than to installing a browser extension.

The pre-install checklist I run now

I run real security-audit pipelines with agent skills daily, and this is the discipline that survived contact with reality:

1. Scan before install. Cisco's open-source skill-scanner catches the low-effort malicious stuff — credential reads, destructive deletes, known injection patterns. No findings ≠ safe, but it clears the floor.

2. Read the SKILL.md like an attacker. Where does it ask the agent to send data? Which URLs? What "verification steps" involve executing bundled binaries? A five-minute read beats a post-incident forensics month.

3. Check allowed-tools against the actual need. A transcription skill does not need shell access. A report formatter does not need network. Scope mismatch is the loudest signal.

4. Keep a provenance manifest. Every install recorded: version, source repo, license, how you verified it. When the next supply-chain incident drops, "was I exposed?" becomes a one-line lookup instead of archaeology.

5. Refuse with reasons, in writing. My manifest records plugins I refused — safety-policy bypasses, third-party account pools. The refusal reasons are knowledge too; they stop you re-litigating the same decision in three months.

The same lens, pointed at your own code

That discipline scales up. Once you treat "what can this input reach?" as the core question, code review becomes a taint walk: entry points → sources → sinks, with an explicit verdict on every sanitizer in between. I packed that method into a skill as well — a taint-analysis code-audit skill with a 0–10 severity rubric and a hard output contract: every finding ships with file:line, the taint path, and the minimal request that proves it. No walkable path means it goes in the hardening appendix, never inflated to a "vulnerability".

It's live as a free tool edition on Swarms Marketplace, and the governance tooling I use to keep my own installs honest is open source: dsh-plugin-hub (routing table, health checks, the provenance manifest itself).

The uncomfortable summary

We spent a decade teaching developers not to curl | bash. Then we built a format whose entire value proposition is "the model will follow these instructions" — and started collecting them from strangers. Skills are worth it. Install them like it matters.

What's your pre-install routine for third-party skills — or are we all still at curl | bash stage? Comments very welcome.

items.title: Serverless Secure: Exploring AWS Continuum Through an Authorization Lab
items.summary: Moving an application to serverless removes a lot of infrastructure work. It does not remove the need to decide who can access each piece of data. A valid login can coexist with a serious authorization flaw. That makes a small notes application an interesting way to explore AWS Continuum: can security tooling connect a mistake in application code with its actual impact? This is a project idea I would like to explore, rather than a lab I have already built. I have not put it into practice yet because of the potential costs, particularly for Continuum’s code vulnerability analysis. The architecture and testing workflow below are a proposal; I do not have deployment results, confirmed Continuum findings, or remediation outcomes to share at this stage. A login is only the beginning Imagine two users, Alice and Bob. Each can create and read private notes. Alice signs in and requests GET /notes/alice-note-id . The API validates her token, and a Lambda function retrieves the requested note from DynamoDB. Now suppose Alice submits Bob’s note ID instead. If the function only looks up the supplied ID, it may return Bob’s note to Alice. Her token is valid, but the requested action is unauthorized. This is broken object-level authorization, often discussed as BOLA or IDOR. Using unpredictable IDs makes guessing harder; it does not replace an ownership check. Authentication answers “Who are you?” Authorization answers “May you access this resource?” Both checks matter. The proposed serverless architecture The proposed lab would use Amazon Cognito for user sign-in, an API Gateway HTTP API with a JWT authorizer, AWS Lambda for application logic, and DynamoDB for notes. Terraform would describe the infrastructure, and GitHub Actions could run checks and deploy changes. Cognito supplies the user identity. API Gateway validates the token. Lambda must then enforce access to the requested note using trusted identity claims from the validated request context. The intentionally vulnerable version would omit that final check. Its purpose would be to make one failure easy to understand and reproduce with synthetic data in an isolated account or environment. Where AWS Continuum fits AWS describes Continuum for code vulnerabilities as combining repository analysis with optional AWS environment context. It prioritizes issues, evaluates exploitability, and can reproduce some findings in a sandbox. Proposed fixes can arrive as pull requests for human review. The launch announcement makes clear that approval is required before a fix ships. [1] Continuum operates around the development and security workflow. It is not a request authorizer that the Lambda function calls whenever a user opens a note. For this lab, the question is whether its supported analysis can recognize the missing ownership check and provide useful evidence or remediation. That is an experiment, not a promised detection outcome. Application support, configuration, and the specific code path must be checked before making claims about coverage. What a meaningful experiment would show First, establish the behavior independently of any scanner: Alice can read her own note, and the vulnerable version also returns Bob’s note when she supplies its ID. Next, inspect the actual Continuum results. Record what it detects, the evidence it provides, and any limitations. An absent finding is also worth documenting; it does not make the application secure. Finally, review any proposed patch and rerun the authorization checks. The fixed version should allow Alice to read her notes, deny access to Bob’s, and reject unauthenticated requests. Equivalent checks belong on update, delete, and list operations too. A stronger data model can place notes under an owner-scoped partition key derived from the verified user identity. The client must never be allowed to choose the identity used for that scope. IAM permissions still matter, but a shared Lambda execution role does not automatically enforce each end user’s ownership rules. Can the lab be free? The application and the security service have separate cost models. Small application traffic may fit service allowances or eligible credits, depending on the account. DynamoDB’s free provisioned capacity allowance should not be confused with free on-demand requests. [3–7] Continuum also separates code vulnerability analysis from penetration testing. Its pricing page lists a two-month penetration-testing trial with up to 400 task-hours per trial month for eligible new customers of that capability. Code vulnerability analysis instead lists context and inference charges; the same page does not advertise an equivalent trial for it. [2] The penetration-testing trial therefore does not establish that repository scanning and generated remediation pull requests are free. Check account eligibility and the selected capability before enabling it. AWS Config collection, logging, and other supporting resources may add charges. Budget alerts help track spending but should not be treated as an immediate spending cutoff. What this lab is intended to teach The useful result is a documented comparison between observable application behavior, security-tool evidence, and a verified fix. Serverless changes who operates the infrastructure. Resource authorization remains an application design responsibility. If you try it, I would love your feedback For now, this remains an idea on paper because of the potential cost of running the full experiment. If you decide to build it, I would love to hear how it goes: whether Continuum identifies the authorization gap, how useful its evidence and suggested fix are, and what the experiment actually costs. Findings, limitations, and unexpected results would all be valuable feedback. References Pricing and availability checked on October 24, 2026; verify again before deploying. AWS Continuum launch announcement AWS Continuum pricing AWS Free Tier FAQs AWS Lambda pricing Amazon API Gateway pricing Amazon DynamoDB pricing Amazon Cognito pricing

items.title: An Ancient Virus Explains Why the Human Brain Is Special
items.summary: Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that invaded our brains, thought fast, swapped coffins, and hit the art gallery. First, an ancient viral pandemic that afflicted many of our primate relatives—but somehow missed humans—may help explain how we got so smart (relatively speaking). Then: mammal brains eat crow, an upcycled sarcophagus, and a trip to the starry Provençal summer of 1889. As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens , or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files . Your brain on viral content Gerdes, Patricia; Karlsson, Ofelia; Garza, Raquel; Atacho, Diahann A. M. et al. “Retroviral insertions contributed to the divergence of human and chimpanzee brains.” Science Advances. A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago shaped the divergence of human and chimp brain development, shedding light on how our own species came to be more cognitively complex than our closest living relatives, according to a new study. Retroviruses are infectious agents that can invade the genomes of their hosts and insert copies of their own genetic material, producing long-term evolutionary effects. Researchers have now discovered a family of these endogenous retroviruses called PTERV1—which are abundant in chimpanzees, but absent in humans—that influence brain development. “Among primates, the human brain stands out as the largest and most complex due in part to an increase in cortical neurons and increase in synaptic connectivity,” said a team led by researchers from Lund University. “With a size roughly three times that of our closest living evolutionary relative, the chimpanzee, it has unique cognitive capabilities.” Sketches of gorilla, chimp, and human skulls. Image: kaiwei zhang “The underlying genetic divergences responsible for these differences are still poorly understood,” the researchers continued, noting that their new findings “reveal a mechanism by which endogenous retroviral insertions contributed to human-chimpanzee brain divergence.” The team discovered the mechanism using human and chimpanzee brain organoids, which are miniature clusters of neurons grown from stem cells that can model some aspects of brain development. The results revealed chimpanzee-specific PTERV1 insertions on chromosome 19 that silences a gene called LINC00662. In contrast, this gene is active during human brain development, and affects neuronal maturation, development, and outgrowth. “These PTERV1 insertions are thought to have originated from infections that occurred in the ancestors of African apes about 5 to 7 million years ago,” said the team. “PTERV1 elements are found in chimpanzees, bonobos, and gorillas…Notably, the absence of PTERV1 insertions from the human genome suggests that either the human and chimpanzee lineages did not occupy the same habitat at the time or that germline-competent cells of the human ancestor were resistant to this infection.” “In summary, this study describes how retroviral insertions contributed to the functional divergence of the human and chimpanzee brain, providing a mechanism by which retroviral infections influenced primate brain speciation,” they added. In other words, early humans appear to have dodged consequential pandemics that widely infected our primate brethren simply because they had a random immunity to it, or roamed different ranges. While retroviruses are far from the only factor in our cognitive development, it’s still eerie to think that our human brain—that brilliant lump you are using to read these words—is shaped by dumb luck. In other news… Another brain to crow about Schmidbauer, Philipp and Nieder, Andreas. “Ultrarapid decision-making in an avian brain.” Science. Speaking of interspecies brain-offs, it seems the birds have got us beat—at least when it comes to snap decisions. Scientists have discovered that carrion crows ( Corvus corone ) can make ultrafast choices in “approximately 235 milliseconds on average, which is roughly twice as fast as has been observed in monkeys or humans and without sacrificing accuracy,” according to a new study. Crow acing the test. Image: Andreas Nieder A pair of researchers observed two crows performing a common discrimination task in which dots on a screen move left, right, up, or down. The crows selected the predominant direction by pecking a target circle on a touchscreen, after which they were rewarded with promptly dispensed treats. The crows performed the task dozens of times at extremely high speeds, achieving an overall choice accuracy of 75 percent (crow 1) and 73 percent (crow 2). “Having diverged from mammals more than 360 million years ago, birds evolved a distinct nuclear pallium”—a part of the vertebrate forebrain—”that lacks the layered neocortex yet retains key organizational and computational principles characteristic of mammalian brains,” said study authors Philipp Schmidbauer and Andreas Nieder of the University of Tübingen. “These findings highlight the extraordinary efficiency of avian decisionmaking circuitry, possibly shaped by evolutionary pressures for rapid visuomotor control,” the team added. So if anyone ever calls you a birdbrain, the correct response is “thanks.” 🌘 Subscribe to 404 Media to get The Abstract , our newsletter about the most exciting and mind-boggling science news and studies of the week. Who is this sarcopha-guy? Rodwell, Warwick. “Westminster Abbey’s Roman Sarcophagus and its Afterlife.” Journal of the British Archaeological Association. Archaeologists may have finally discovered the mysterious identity of an ancient skeleton buried in a Roman-era sarcophagus that was first unearthed on the grounds of Westminster Abbey more than 200 years ago. Despite an inscription on the sarcophagus identifying the occupant as Valerius Amandinus—a wealthy Londoner who lived between 300 to 400 AD—the bones likely belong to a medieval monk named Ælfwig, born centuries later in the year 993. Interior of the sarcophagus, as found upon opening in 2016. Image: Rodwell, Warwick , 2026. “The burial was of a male, probably in his late forties, and was radiocarbon dated to around the turn of the 11th century,” said study author Rodwell Warwick of Westminster Abbey. “The corpse had been laid in a timber coffin and covered with lime; it was then placed inside the sarcophagus. It is argued that this was the prestigious burial of Abbot Ælfwig.” The sarcophagus was exhumed and moved to a northern courtyard during King Henry III’s reconstruction of the abbey in the mid-1200s, where it laid for about six centuries. On Easter Monday 1820, the coffin was “wantonly broke by workmen” according to a note from an unknown contemporary archivist. Any grave goods were likely plundered by this crew and the sarcophagus was hastily put back together and reburied with the bones all jumbled up inside. It was then re-discovered in 1869 with a note that the burial “‘had been subjected to violence by a previous examination.” It turns out anything is recyclable—even sarcophagi. The discovery that this Roman coffin at some point took on another tenant now raises the new question of how the earthly remains of Valerius Amandinus got evicted and where they ultimately wound up. “The Starry Night”—of July 22, 1889? Kim, Elijah Jeong-hyun et al. “The actual sky of Van Gogh’s Starry Night: a multidisciplinary reconstruction.” Scientific Reports. With its vibrant colors and psychedelic swirls, Vincent Van Gogh’s “The Starry Night” is one of the most beloved and recognizable paintings in art history. For years, experts and admirers have debated whether the mesmerizing skyscape, which van Gogh painted during an asylum stay in Provence, was a fantastical portrayal or if the artist included realistic renderings of astronomical phenomena. Now, a team has proposed that the celestial elements of the painting match with a specific night—July 22, 1889—when “the waning-crescent Moon, Venus, and the Hyades cluster gather within that narrow frame,” according to a new study. This date conflicts with the conventional timeline of van Gogh painting “The Starry Night” weeks earlier in June. “The question dividing fantasy from observation remained a matter of qualitative interpretation and was never treated in a physically decidable form,” said researchers led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim of Kyung Hee University. “The approach of this study shifts the burden of proof: if the celestial arrangement on the canvas matches a specific dawn sky, that match itself becomes what the imaginative reading must explain.” The Pepe Silvia meme meets “The Starry Night.” Image: Kim et al., Scientific Reports (2026) The team’s findings “suggest that the night sky in ‘The Starry Night’ originated from observation of a specific celestial arrangement, and call for reconsidering the June dating,” they continued. “This framework can extend to historical night paintings as a reproducible scientific art history.” I love a hyper-niche new subfield—let’s call this one “forensic astroartistry.” Regardless of the painting’s exact date of origin, it has inspired wonder and fascination for more than a century—including these new stellaria of long-lost summer nights. Thanks for reading! See you next week.
