items.title: Behind the Scenes, Meta’s Board Is Battling With Mark Zuckerberg Over His Out-of-Control AI Spending
items.summary: Meta’s stocks have taken a serious beating lately, with its price shedding more than 13 percent over the past month. That fact isn’t likely to ease pressure in the trillion-dollar megacorp’s board room, as tensions between CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his board of directors reach a boiling point. As the Wall Street Journal phrased it in new reporting, the conflict between Zuckerberg and his board have amounted to a “war over power and money.” Over the past few months, the paper reports, Zuckerberg has demanded a massive stock-heavy pay raise from Meta’s directorate, forcing an impasse so fraught that numerous board members have threatened to resign if the CEO doesn’t back down. According to documents viewed by the WSJ , a negotiation team made up of three members of the board began preparing a contingency plan in early September, to use in the event that Zuckerberg refused to back down from his compensation demands. That standby plan reportedly included “resignation from the board” by the negotiation team as a last resort. Though the squabble is playing out over Zuckerberg’s salary, the source of the conflict traces back to the CEO’s rampant spending on AI . Per the WSJ , the whole remuneration debate was triggered by Meta’s out-of-control AI spending, which dragged the corporation into a negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion in the third quarter of 2026 — the first time the company has fallen into the red since 2012. “More spending, negative free cash flow, not enough revenue being generated from the spend [is] concerning investors that this is just sort of a bit of a money pit,” as senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth Robert Pavlik told Reuters in an interview. In an October 2025 investor meeting, Zuckerberg reportedly said his aggressive gamble on the AI-front was a necessary risk for Meta, despite simultaneously acknowledging that the hyperscale approach to AI had created a dangerous financial bubble. “I think it’s the right strategy to aggressively front-load building capacity so that way we’re prepared for the most optimistic cases,” Zuckerberg told stockholders in 2025. With Meta’s AI products failing security testing and automation implementation — to say nothing of the ongoing Muse safety debacle — it seems Zuckerberg’s AI ambitions are finally hitting the brick wall of financial reality. Meta’s stocks have taken a serious beating lately, with its price shedding more than 13 percent over the past month. That fact isn’t likely to ease pressure in the trillion-dollar megacorp’s board room, as tensions between CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his board of directors reach a boiling point.

As the Wall Street Journal phrased it in new reporting, the conflict between Zuckerberg and his board have amounted to a “war over power and money.” Over the past few months, the paper reports, Zuckerberg has demanded a massive stock-heavy pay raise from Meta’s directorate, forcing an impasse so fraught that numerous board members have threatened to resign if the CEO doesn’t back down.

According to documents viewed by the WSJ, a negotiation team made up of three members of the board began preparing a contingency plan in early September, to use in the event that Zuckerberg refused to back down from his compensation demands. That standby plan reportedly included “resignation from the board” by the negotiation team as a last resort.

Though the squabble is playing out over Zuckerberg’s salary, the source of the conflict traces back to the CEO’s rampant spending on AI.

Per the WSJ, the whole remuneration debate was triggered by Meta’s out-of-control AI spending, which dragged the corporation into a negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion in the third quarter of 2026 — the first time the company has fallen into the red since 2012.

“More spending, negative free cash flow, not enough revenue being generated from the spend [is] concerning investors that this is just sort of a bit of a money pit,” as senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth Robert Pavlik told Reuters in an interview.

In an October 2025 investor meeting, Zuckerberg reportedly said his aggressive gamble on the AI-front was a necessary risk for Meta, despite simultaneously acknowledging that the hyperscale approach to AI had created a dangerous financial bubble.

“I think it’s the right strategy to aggressively front-load building capacity so that way we’re prepared for the most optimistic cases,” Zuckerberg told stockholders in 2025.

With Meta’s AI products failing security testing and automation implementation — to say nothing of the ongoing Muse safety debacle — it seems Zuckerberg’s AI ambitions are finally hitting the brick wall of financial reality.

items.title: A veteran tech investor says 'doom and gloom' over the AI boom is overblown, even though it has shades of the dot-com bubble
items.summary: Paul Wick is the CIO of Seligman Investments. 12/08 There are clear parallels between the AI boom and the dot-com bubble, tech investor Paul Wick says. But solid demand, strong earnings, and less mania make for a "healthier" backdrop, Wick said. Seligman's chief investor brushed off Michael Burry's worries but flagged some trends to watch. The AI boom has shades of the dot-com bubble , but fears of an imminent crash and mass unemployment are overblown, a veteran tech investor says. At the turn of this century , there was an explosion in dot-com startups being formed, and a huge infrastructure buildout with telecoms "aggressively" spending on wired and wireless networks, Paul Wick told Business Insider in an interview this week. The chief investor of Seligman Investments — a group within Columbia Threadneedle Investments that manages over $40 billion of assets and comprises a hedge fund, a mutual fund, and a venture capital arm — said there were clear parallels between that period and the current boom in AI startups and data-center spending . He also noted that energy prices and interest rates jumped then as they've done this year. But Wick noted there isn't the same IPO frenzy now, or the same "frenetic environment" where stocks soar fivefold or tenfold in a day. He also said that by late 2000, a slowdown in IT spending was being forecasted for 2001, whereas enterprise spending on AI remains strong and recent tech earnings have been robust. Simply put, the situation seems "healthier" now than in 2000, he said. Business Insider asked Wick about Michael Burry's warnings this year around AI. "The Big Short" investor has called out aggressive accounting, circular financing, hidden debt, and overinvestment in depreciating assets like microchips as reasons to be skeptical that the boom has legs. Wick said that Burry, known for predicting and profiting from the collapse of the mid-2000s housing bubble, has been "early or downright wrong on many other things." Burry has previously defended his track record, citing his correct predictions and sharing charts showing the timing of his market calls. As for concerns about Nvidia's efforts to grow the AI ecosystem by investing in data center developers and software companies, Wick emphasized that the chipmaker is "extraordinarily profitable." He cast doubt on whether Nvidia should spend its spare cash only on buybacks, rather than bolstering its customers, especially as several of the industry's biggest players are working to develop their own AI chips to reduce their reliance on Nvidia. But he also flagged some industry trends to watch, including enterprise clients opting to use older models or build their own, and token pricing coming under pressure as users embrace open-source models, raising questions over the size of the market opportunity for the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic. Navigating a new world Wick weighed in on how a young person can get ahead in the AI era. "It used to be that a degree in computer science was a ticket to success," he said. A better option today might be to learn a trade, as there's "booming demand" for workers such as electricians and HVAC technicians, and they can make an "incredibly good living" without having to go to a four-year college, Wick said. He also took aim at the "doom-and-gloom notion that AI is going to eviscerate demand " for human labor. He described that worry as a "little premature" as nobody knows for sure how AI will affect entry-level roles in the future, unemployment is yet to soar, and there's always inertia when it comes to businesses and consumers changing their behavior. items.title: Stateful Agentic Engineering Copilots with Letta: Core Memory, Shared State, Semantic Retrieval, Custom Tools, Streaming, and Portable Agent Workflows

In this tutorial, we build a stateful engineering copilot with Letta that demonstrates how agentic memory extends beyond conventional prompt-based conversations. We begin by creating inspectable core memory blocks that the agent can autonomously update, then expose those blocks for programmatic state synchronization and shared access across multiple agents. We further extend the architecture with archival vector memory for semantic retrieval, a custom server-side tool for deterministic risk estimation, streaming for observing agent execution, server-side message history for persistent conversations, and .af export for portability. Together, these components demonstrate a practical memory architecture in which persistent state, retrieval, tools, multi-agent collaboration, and execution traces work as an integrated agentic system. We then inspect server-side conversation history to verify that the interaction state persists independently of the local Python process. We also demonstrate how the agent can be reconnected from a fresh process using only its persistent identifier. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser hr("9. reviewer : {reviewer.id}") print("Inspect them visually in the ADE at https://app.letta.com") We export the complete agent state to an .af file, providing a portable representation of the agent’s memory, tools, and conversation state. We also used custom tools and streaming to extend and observe agent behavior while server-side history and agent export provide persistence and portability. Through this workflow, we established a practical foundation for building engineering copilots that continuously retain context, reason over accumulated knowledge, collaborate across agents, and operate with explicit, controllable memory.        elif kind == "tool_call_message":

           print(" tool call :", getattr(tc, "name", "?"), textwrap.shorten(str(getattr(tc, "arguments", "")), 200))
       elif kind == "tool_return_message":
           print("  tool ret  :", textwrap.shorten(str(getattr(m, "tool_return", "")), 260))
       elif kind == "assistant_message":
           print(" assistant :", as_text(getattr(m, "content", "")))
       elif kind == "approval_request_message":
           print("  approval  : agent is waiting for you to approve a tool call")
   u = getattr(response, "usage", None)
   if u:
       print(f"   ↳ steps={getattr(u, 'step_count', '?')} tokens={getattr(u, 'total_tokens', '?')}")
def chat(agent_id, text, max_steps=12, quiet=False):
   r = flex(
       lambda: client.agents.messages.create(agent_id=agent_id, input=text, max_steps=max_steps),
       lambda: client.agents.messages.create(agent_id=agent_id, input=text),
       lambda: client.agents.messages.create(agent_id=agent_id,
                                             messages=[{"role": "user", "content": text}]),
       label="messages.create",
   )
   if not quiet:
       print(f"\n user      : {text}")
       show(r)
   return r
PREFERRED = ["openai/gpt-4.1", "openai/gpt-4o-mini", "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-20250514"]
try:
   handles = [getattr(m, "handle", None) for m in client.models.list()]
   MODEL = next((h for h in PREFERRED if h in handles), None) or handles[0]
except Exception:
   MODEL = PREFERRED[0]
print(f" connected · model handle = {MODEL}")
hr("1. Create a stateful agent with custom memory blocks")
def make_agent(**kw):
   return flex(
       lambda: client.agents.create(model=MODEL, embedding="openai/text-embedding-3-small", **kw),
       lambda: client.agents.create(model=MODEL, **kw),
       label="agents.create",
   )
copilot = make_agent(
   name=f"copilot-{int(time.time())}",
   description="Engineering copilot with inspectable long-term memory",
   tags=["tutorial", "copilot"],
   memory_blocks=[
       {"label": "persona",
        "value": "I am Mnemo, an engineering copilot. I am terse, concrete, and I never "
                 "invent facts — if I don't know something I say so and then go look it up.",
        "limit": 3000},
       {"label": "human",
        "description": "Durable facts about the engineer I work with: name, role, stack, "
                       "preferences, working style. Update this whenever I learn something stable.",
        "value": "Unknown so far.",
        "limit": 3000},
       {"label": "project_state",
        "description": "Live state of the project we are shipping: milestones, blockers, "
                       "decisions and their rationale. Keep it dense and current; delete stale lines.",
        "value": "(empty)",
        "limit": 5000},
       {"label": "lessons",
        "description": "Hard-won lessons and mistakes to never repeat. Append-only, one line each.",
        "value": "(empty)",
        "limit": 2000},
   ],
)
print("agent id:", copilot.id)
def get_block(agent_id, label):
   return flex(
       lambda: client.agents.blocks.retrieve(agent_id=agent_id, block_label=label),
       lambda: client.agents.blocks.retrieve(agent_id, label),
       label="agents.blocks.retrieve",
   )
def set_block(agent_id, label, value):
   return flex(
       lambda: client.agents.blocks.update(agent_id=agent_id, block_label=label, value=value),
       lambda: client.agents.blocks.modify(agent_id=agent_id, block_label=label, value=value),
       lambda: client.agents.blocks.update(agent_id, label, value=value),
       label="agents.blocks.update",
   )
def dump_memory(agent_id, title="core memory"):
   blocks = flex(lambda: client.agents.blocks.list(agent_id=agent_id),
                 lambda: client.agents.blocks.list(agent_id), label="agents.blocks.list")
   print(f"\n──── {title} ────")
   for b in blocks:
       ro = " [read-only]" if getattr(b, "read_only", False) else ""
       print(f"▸ {b.label}{ro} ({len(b.value or '')}/{getattr(b, 'limit', '?')} chars)")
       print(textwrap.indent(textwrap.fill(b.value or "", 100), "    "))
   return blocks
dump_memory(copilot.id, "core memory at birth")

We set up the Letta client, install the SDK, and add compatibility helpers that handle API variations across Letta versions. We dynamically select an available model and create a stateful engineering copilot with structured core memory blocks. We then inspect the initial memory state to establish the agent’s persistent context.

Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browser
hr("2. Self-editing memory — talk once, then read the block back")
chat(copilot.id,
    "Hi, I'm Priya, staff engineer at Northwind. We're shipping 'Halo', a Rust ingestion "
    "service, on Nov 14. I hate long explanations — give me bullets or code, never essays. "
    "Current blocker: the Kafka consumer rebalances every ~4 minutes under load.")
chat(copilot.id,
    "Update: we traced the rebalance to a 5s max.poll.interval.ms with slow batch commits. "
    "Decision: move commits off the poll loop. Also remember we already tried bumping "
    "session.timeout.ms and it did nothing — don't suggest that again.")
dump_memory(copilot.id, "core memory after 2 turns (note what moved where)")
hr("3. Your code writes into the context window")
live = get_block(copilot.id, "project_state")
set_block(copilot.id, "project_state",
         (live.value or "") + "\n[CI 09:41Z] main is RED: integration/kafka_rebalance_test failing (flaky x3).")
chat(copilot.id, "Anything I should know before I start the day?")
hr("4. Shared memory between two agents")
policies = client.blocks.create(
   label="policies",
   description="Non-negotiable engineering policies. Read-only: obey, never edit.",
   value="1. No direct pushes to main.\n2. Every fix ships with a regression test.\n"
         "3. Customer data never leaves EU regions.",
   limit=2000,
   read_only=True,
)
scratchpad = client.blocks.create(
   label="team_scratchpad",
   description="Shared working notes between the copilot and the reviewer agent. "
               "Both agents read and write here; keep entries prefixed with your name.",
   value="(empty)",
   limit=4000,
)
for bid in (policies.id, scratchpad.id):
   flex(lambda: client.agents.blocks.attach(agent_id=copilot.id, block_id=bid),
        lambda: client.agents.blocks.attach(copilot.id, bid),
        label="agents.blocks.attach")
reviewer = make_agent(
   name=f"reviewer-{int(time.time())}",
   description="Strict code reviewer sharing memory with the copilot",
   tags=["tutorial", "reviewer"],
   block_ids=[policies.id, scratchpad.id],
   memory_blocks=[{"label": "persona",
                   "value": "I am Argus, a paranoid staff reviewer. I look for the failure mode "
                            "everyone else skipped, and I cite the team policies by number."}],
)
print("reviewer id:", reviewer.id)
chat(copilot.id, "Write your proposed fix for the rebalance issue into the team_scratchpad "
                "block so the reviewer can see it. Keep it to 4 lines.")
print("\n what the REVIEWER sees in the shared block (written by the other agent):")
print(textwrap.indent(client.blocks.retrieve(scratchpad.id).value, "    "))
chat(reviewer.id, "Read team_scratchpad and review the proposed fix. Cite any policy it violates, "
                 "then append your verdict to the same block.")
print("\n shared block after the reviewer replied:")
print(textwrap.indent(client.blocks.retrieve(scratchpad.id).value, "    "))
print("\nagents attached to this block:",
     [a.name for a in flex(lambda: client.blocks.agents.list(block_id=scratchpad.id),
                           lambda: client.blocks.agents.list(scratchpad.id),
                           label="blocks.agents.list")])

We demonstrate self-editing memory by providing the copilot with durable information about the engineer, project, decisions, and known failure modes. We also update project state directly from application code and create shared read-only and writable blocks for multi-agent collaboration. We then connect a reviewer agent to the shared memory and observe how both agents exchange persistent working context.

Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browser
hr("5. Archival memory: bulk-load knowledge, then let the agent retrieve it")
KNOWLEDGE = [
   ("Postmortem 2024-08-02: Halo dropped 1.2M events when the consumer group rebalanced during a "
    "deploy. Root cause: commits inside the poll loop blocked past max.poll.interval.ms.",
    ["postmortem", "kafka", "halo"]),
   ("ADR-017: Halo uses at-least-once delivery with idempotent writes keyed on (tenant_id, event_id). "
    "Exactly-once via Kafka transactions was rejected for throughput reasons.",
    ["adr", "architecture", "halo"]),
   ("Runbook: to drain a Halo node, set DRAIN=1, wait for lag<1000, then SIGTERM. Never SIGKILL — "
    "in-flight batches are only checkpointed on graceful shutdown.",
    ["runbook", "ops", "halo"]),
   ("Benchmark 2025-01: rdkafka 2.3 with 8 partitions sustained 240k events/s at p99 32ms on "
    "c6i.4xlarge; the bottleneck was JSON parsing, not the network.",
    ["benchmark", "performance"]),
   ("Priya's preference on file layout: one module per bounded context, integration tests live "
    "next to the module, no tests/ mega-directory.", ["preference", "style"]),
   ("Incident 2025-03-19: an EU tenant's payload was mirrored to us-east-1 for 40 minutes. "
    "Fixed by region-pinning the DLQ. This is why policy 3 exists.", ["incident", "compliance"]),
]
def archive(agent_id, content, tags):
   return flex(
       lambda: client.agents.passages.insert(agent_id=agent_id, content=content, tags=tags),
       lambda: client.agents.passages.create(agent_id=agent_id, text=content, tags=tags),
       lambda: client.agents.passages.create(agent_id=agent_id, text=content),
       label="agents.passages.insert",
   )
for content, tags in KNOWLEDGE:
   archive(copilot.id, content, tags)
print(f"inserted {len(KNOWLEDGE)} passages")
hits = flex(
   lambda: client.agents.passages.search(agent_id=copilot.id, query="losing messages during a deploy"),
   lambda: client.agents.passages.list(agent_id=copilot.id, search="losing messages during a deploy"),
   label="agents.passages.search",
)
print("\n programmatic semantic search for 'losing messages during a deploy':")
for h in list(hits)[:3]:
   print("   •", textwrap.shorten(getattr(h, "content", None) or getattr(h, "text", ""), 150))
chat(copilot.id, "Before I restart a node tonight: is there anything in our history I should "
                "worry about, and what's the safe procedure?")
hr("6. Give the agent a custom tool")
def estimate_release_risk(open_bugs: int, days_to_deadline: int, test_coverage: float) -> str:
   """Estimate the risk of shipping a release on time.
   Args:
       open_bugs (int): Number of open P0/P1 bugs.
       days_to_deadline (int): Calendar days left before the ship date.
       test_coverage (float): Line coverage as a fraction between 0.0 and 1.0.
   Returns:
       str: A risk score from 0-100 and a verdict.
   """
   import math
   pressure = open_bugs / max(days_to_deadline, 1)
   score = max(0.0, min(100.0, 100 * (1 - math.exp(-1.4 * pressure)) * (1.3 - test_coverage)))
   verdict = "SHIP" if score < 35 else ("SLIP ONE WEEK" if score < 70 else "DO NOT SHIP")
   return f"risk_score={score:.1f} verdict={verdict}"
tool = flex(
   lambda: client.tools.upsert_from_function(func=estimate_release_risk),
   lambda: client.tools.create_from_function(func=estimate_release_risk),
   label="tools.upsert_from_function",
)
flex(lambda: client.agents.tools.attach(agent_id=copilot.id, tool_id=tool.id),
    lambda: client.agents.tools.attach(copilot.id, tool.id),
    label="agents.tools.attach")
print("attached tool:", tool.name, "| agent tools:",
     [t.name for t in flex(lambda: client.agents.tools.list(agent_id=copilot.id),
                           lambda: client.agents.tools.list(copilot.id), label="agents.tools.list")])
chat(copilot.id, "We have 9 open P0/P1 bugs, 12 days to the Nov 14 date, coverage is 0.61. "
                "Score the risk with the tool, then record the verdict in project_state.")

We populate archival memory with tagged engineering knowledge and use semantic search to retrieve relevant information without relying on exact keyword matches. We then allow the agent to query this archival knowledge autonomously when answering an operational question. Finally, we create and attach a custom server-side release-risk tool so the agent can perform deterministic calculations and record the resulting decision in memory.

Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browser
hr("7. Streaming the agent's steps")
def stream_chat(agent_id, text):
   print(f" user      : {text}")
   s = flex(
       lambda: client.agents.messages.stream(agent_id=agent_id, input=text),
       lambda: client.agents.messages.stream(agent_id=agent_id,
                                             messages=[{"role": "user", "content": text}]),
       lambda: client.agents.messages.create_stream(agent_id=agent_id,
                                                    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": text}]),
       label="messages.stream",
   )
   for chunk in s:
       kind = getattr(chunk, "message_type", None) or getattr(chunk, "type", "")
       if kind == "reasoning_message":
           print("", textwrap.shorten(getattr(chunk, "reasoning", "") or "", 160))
       elif kind == "tool_call_message":
           print("", getattr(getattr(chunk, "tool_call", None), "name", "?"))
       elif kind == "assistant_message":
           print("", as_text(getattr(chunk, "content", "")))
try:
   stream_chat(copilot.id, "One-line status of Halo, from memory only. No tools.")
except Exception as e:
   print("streaming unavailable on this SDK version:", e)
hr("8. Server-side conversation history")
hist = flex(lambda: client.agents.messages.list(agent_id=copilot.id, limit=8),
           lambda: client.agents.messages.list(copilot.id, limit=8),
           label="agents.messages.list")
for m in hist:
   kind = getattr(m, "message_type", "?")
   body = as_text(getattr(m, "content", "")) or getattr(m, "reasoning", "") or ""
   print(f"  [{kind:<24}] {textwrap.shorten(str(body), 110)}")
print("\n  reconnect from a fresh process with just the id:")
print("    client.agents.messages.create(agent_id='%s', input='...')" % copilot.id)

We use Letta’s streaming interface to observe reasoning, tool calls, and assistant responses as the agent executes a task. We then inspect server-side conversation history to verify that the interaction state persists independently of the local Python process. We also demonstrate how the agent can be reconnected from a fresh process using only its persistent identifier.

Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browser
hr("9. Export / import the agent")
try:
   dump = flex(lambda: client.agents.export_file(agent_id=copilot.id),
               lambda: client.agents.export_file(copilot.id), label="agents.export_file")
   blob = dump if isinstance(dump, (str, bytes)) else json.dumps(dump, default=str)
   path = "/content/copilot.af" if os.path.isdir("/content") else "copilot.af"
   with open(path, "wb" if isinstance(blob, bytes) else "w") as f:
       f.write(blob)
   print(f"exported → {path} ({len(blob)} bytes) — memory, tools and history travel with it.")
   print("re-import later with: client.agents.import_file(file=open(path,'rb'))")
except Exception as e:
   print("export not available on this SDK/deployment:", e)
CLEANUP = False
if CLEANUP:
   for aid in (copilot.id, reviewer.id):
       try: client.agents.delete(aid)
       except Exception as e: print("agent delete:", e)
   for bid in (policies.id, scratchpad.id):
       try: client.blocks.delete(bid)
       except Exception as e: print("block delete:", e)
   print("deleted.")
else:
   hr("Done")
   print(f"copilot  : {copilot.id}\nreviewer : {reviewer.id}")
   print("Inspect them visually in the ADE at https://app.letta.com")

We export the complete agent state to an .af file, providing a portable representation of the agent’s memory, tools, and conversation state. We then include optional cleanup logic that removes the agents and shared blocks created during the tutorial. We finish by displaying the persistent agent identifiers and the Letta ADE location for further inspection.

In conclusion, we now have a complete view of how Letta supports persistent, inspectable agent workflows rather than treating every interaction as an isolated prompt. We saw how core memory maintains high-value state in context, archival memory provides scalable retrieval, shared and read-only blocks coordinate multiple agents, and application code can directly synchronize external state. We also used custom tools and streaming to extend and observe agent behavior while server-side history and agent export provide persistence and portability. Through this workflow, we established a practical foundation for building engineering copilots that continuously retain context, reason over accumulated knowledge, collaborate across agents, and operate with explicit, controllable memory.

Check out the FULL CODES here. All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter. Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well.

items.title: I bought a house in Japan at 23 with 7 friends. We spent less than $20,000 to have a place to escape to.
items.summary: Hilary Tang, second from right, and her college friends bought an abandoned home in Hiroshima, Japan. Courtesy of Hilary Tang Hilary Tang and her college friends bought an akiya in Hiroshima, Japan, for a little over $11,000. The group of friends spent months living at the property while renovating it. They plan to use it mostly for gatherings but are open to renting it out to cover yearly costs. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Hilary Tang, 23, a recent college graduate from Hong Kong who purchased a home in Hiroshima, Japan, with her college friends . The following has been edited for length and clarity. I graduated from Minerva University in San Francisco last May. I was planning to work at a startup in San Francisco, but I decided that I wanted to take a gap year. At Minerva, our cohort is pretty diverse, and I have quite a few friends from Japan. One of my friends had this concept: "There are these akiyas, but no one actually buys them ." I actually never saw any of those videos about akiyas before, but I did know about the 1 euro house in Italy thing. I didn't know there was a similar concept in Japan. My friend was initially planning to buy a house with his high school friends, but they backed out very early on. After they backed out, he asked if we were interested in buying a house . That was in June. We bought the house in late July, and then we got the keys on August 6. At first, we were trying to recruit people, but no one really wanted to. We even tried to recruit outside our school. I tried asking people from Hong Kong, but no one wanted to go somewhere random and buy a house in Japan because there's quite a lot of risk. From the initial six people who bought the house, five people are from my university. Tang and some of the other homeowners. Courtesy of Hilary Tang Then two other people joined, because my friend's friends also came over after we started the renovation. They're from Japan and really liked the house, so they decided to chip in as well. So currently, we have eight people. We always wanted to have eight people in the house — it's just easier if we have a bigger budget. We wanted to buy and renovate the house for less than $20,000 After we assembled the people who decided to buy the house, we had an initial meeting to understand each person's motivations and expectations, because that would determine what kind of house we buy and how we want to treat it. When we were talking about things we would want in the location, something that was common was that, firstly, we all preferred being in nature or easily accessible to nature. Within the group, most of them are Japanese and already live in Tokyo, Osaka, or another big city, so for them, they wanted to have a second house in a more rural area. Secondly, we wanted somewhere that is easily accessible, even internationally. Another friend is planning to work in the US, and there's also a Korean member, so it's better if there's more motivation, or it's easier for us to actually go there if there's an international airport nearby. And thirdly, we wanted somewhere with better weather and with lower earthquake and tsunami risk. Some homeowners at a nearby train station. Courtesy of Hilary Tang We ended up finding a house in Hiroshima. The house itself was 1.8 million yen (or $11,371), but the price was negotiated because the house was initially listed on the website at 3 million yen. We also had to pay the agent fee and other fees, so we spent about 2.3 million yen in total. The house is around 315 square meters (or 3,390 square feet), and almost 500 square meters of land. We have nine Japanese-style rooms, which are rooms with tatami flooring, and two Western-style rooms, which are rooms without tatami flooring. Initially, we wanted to do the whole renovation within $4,000, but since we have more people chipping in, our budget expanded. We still haven't used up our original $20,000 budget. Just for the renovation, we've used around $1,262, as of start of October. We hang out there once a month, but we're also thinking about renting it out We've been staying in the house the entire time we've renovated it, and luckily the house was in better condition than we expected. Some of the homeowners gathering for a meal. Courtesy of Hilary Tang The timeline was so tight that we couldn't actually go there to see the house before we bought it. But the agent did a video tour, and we looked around, and it was quite nice. We also talked to our neighbors, because the person who lived in the house passed away about five years ago, and then afterward it was left vacant. But before he passed away, the neighbors said how the previous owner was really diligent with cleaning stuff; that they always saw him cleaning, even toward the end of his life. When we got there, we realized it was actually a lot more well-maintained than we thought, so we didn't have to do a very big renovation. At first, we thought we'd have to change all the tatami, or rebuild certain parts, or put down certain parts. But it turns out there hasn't been a super big expense that would require us to rebuild the entire thing. We did paint and also repaired some curtains and lights because they weren't working. We added a fire alarm and air conditioning because they only had one or two aircons, and it gets really hot in Hiroshima during the summer and really cold in the winter. Those wooden houses don't insulate very well. When we first got there in August, there were five of us. Then maybe for the first three days, there was always someone new coming, because there are a lot of friends who wanted to come here. So there are always visitors, and they also helped out because there's a lot going on — we even had friends' parents come over as well. Some homeowners and other guests helping with the renovation. Courtesy of Hilary Tang That's been my favorite part. You see sides of people that you don't know. Everyone has some sort of expertise to bring. For example, some people are really good at painting. Our friend helped us paint the bathroom wall — he wanted to paint a Fuji mountain, but none of us really knew how to paint. So I'm really glad he came and helped us paint. There's a girl who went to a lot of auctions growing up, so she specialized in artwork and helped us go through the things the previous owner left behind. It would be nice to do Airbnb and learn about the process and to experience what it's like to manage an Airbnb . Maybe with the house on Airbnb we can cover at least the running costs every year. Still, we want to prioritize us hanging out. Every month we try to gather there, and so far we've been going consistently once a month. We wanted to create a place we could always come back to whenever life gets a little overwhelming, where any of us could take a break, have some space to ourselves, and take time to process whatever was going on in life. We see this house not as an investment , but as a shared place among us. Read the original article on Business Insider

Some of the homeowners gathering for a meal.

Courtesy of Hilary Tang

The timeline was so tight that we couldn't actually go there to see the house before we bought it. But the agent did a video tour, and we looked around, and it was quite nice.

We also talked to our neighbors, because the person who lived in the house passed away about five years ago, and then afterward it was left vacant. But before he passed away, the neighbors said how the previous owner was really diligent with cleaning stuff; that they always saw him cleaning, even toward the end of his life.

When we got there, we realized it was actually a lot more well-maintained than we thought, so we didn't have to do a very big renovation. At first, we thought we'd have to change all the tatami, or rebuild certain parts, or put down certain parts. But it turns out there hasn't been a super big expense that would require us to rebuild the entire thing.

We did paint and also repaired some curtains and lights because they weren't working. We added a fire alarm and air conditioning because they only had one or two aircons, and it gets really hot in Hiroshima during the summer and really cold in the winter. Those wooden houses don't insulate very well.

When we first got there in August, there were five of us. Then maybe for the first three days, there was always someone new coming, because there are a lot of friends who wanted to come here. So there are always visitors, and they also helped out because there's a lot going on — we even had friends' parents come over as well.

Some homeowners and other guests helping with the renovation.

Courtesy of Hilary Tang

That's been my favorite part.

You see sides of people that you don't know. Everyone has some sort of expertise to bring. For example, some people are really good at painting. Our friend helped us paint the bathroom wall — he wanted to paint a Fuji mountain, but none of us really knew how to paint. So I'm really glad he came and helped us paint.

There's a girl who went to a lot of auctions growing up, so she specialized in artwork and helped us go through the things the previous owner left behind.

It would be nice to do Airbnb and learn about the process and to experience what it's like to manage an Airbnb. Maybe with the house on Airbnb we can cover at least the running costs every year.

Still, we want to prioritize us hanging out.

Every month we try to gather there, and so far we've been going consistently once a month.

We wanted to create a place we could always come back to whenever life gets a little overwhelming, where any of us could take a break, have some space to ourselves, and take time to process whatever was going on in life.

We see this house not as an investment, but as a shared place among us.

items.title: The talk show trying to help solve the entry-level job crisis
items.summary: Job hunters can call in to 877UNMPLYD. Maria Korneeva/Getty Images The job market is rough right now; many would-be entry-level workers are still on the hunt. A new Twitch show hopes to help answer labor market questions and offer job seekers advice. So far, they've advised callers on everything from salaries to highlighting unique experience. When Hans Romine finished his architecture degree in 2025, the 24-year-old began looking for work . After about 50 job applications yielded a single interview appointment, he started feeling despondent. That's when a friend told him about a new show called 877UNMPLYD. The show is on Twitch , a streaming platform favored by gamers and fans, but has an unlikely host: Jeremy Zimmer , the former CEO of United Talent Agency, along with digital-savvy producer Rachel Braun. The show offers career advice, discusses labor market news, and fields live call-ins from people looking for work. When Romine called in, he mentioned he'd spent a few months as a recreation supervisor, building morale at an isolated research station in Antarctica. Zimmer and Braun found that the most interesting part of his whole story, and told him to play it up in applications and interviews. Romine took their advice, and when he went in for that interview, he highlighted his experiences out on the tundra. After he landed the job, he called back in to let the hosts know. That's the kind of win Zimmer and Braun hope to replicate. Over their first season, the duo hosted 12 episodes, with one episode filmed live on the streets of New York garnering over 54,000 views. The show is a small experiment in career guidance at a moment when the entry-level job market is getting harder to navigate — especially in New York City . A new report from Partnership for New York City, a nonprofit business advocacy group, found that the number of entry-level jobs has shrunk disproportionately among professions highly exposed to AI; entry-level postings in design, media, and writing fell by 40.6%. Nationally, employment in white-collar industries has fallen, even as output has gone up — indicating that AI might be effectively replacing entry-level white-collar work. That dearth of entry-level opportunities is part of what spawned the show, a partnership between TikTok savant Adam Faze and the economic mobility nonprofit Schultz Family Foundation. Judith Dubin, the head of content at the foundation, said that they'd drilled down on investments in career navigation after recognizing how difficult it is to be graduating from high school or college into the current labor market. "The current job marketplace is so disrupted with the advent of AI," Dubin said. "It's just an additional barrier for young people." In August, Zimmer and Braun set up a desk on a plaza at Baruch College, with a sign that said "Ask a CEO," and fielded questions from students. One student asked for advice on how to negotiate salary expectations, especially in the interview process. Braun said that not all advice-seekers are new grads: One Gen X marketer called in after being laid off, feeling pushed out of the tech industry. Going into the show, Zimmer focused on what it must feel like when getting a job is no longer as simple as putting your head down, working hard, and expecting things to work out. "That age-old mantra doesn't feel as relevant today," Zimmer said. He's been struck by the contrast between callers who are hyper-focused on what they want, eschewing any concern about why that can't happen, and those who are baffled that they've applied for hundreds of jobs and haven't gotten any interviews. He's found both the naivety and the determination of the callers exciting. Braun, the show's other host and a producer, said that AI emerged as a major theme throughout their first season — both the opportunities it presented and the way that it was shaking up the entry-level job hunt. Romine, who landed a job, hopes that employers can once again understand the value of having fresh talent on their teams. But as the labor market continues its entry-level contraction, getting a leg up — even if it's through advice on a Twitch show — is ever more important. "In the meantime, students and graduates need to really figure out how to work the current system and make themselves stand out in such an intense market," Romine said. items.title: Palantir cofounder says his wife calls their AI agent 'Tradbot' after tradwives
items.summary: Christie Hemm Klok for The Washington Post via Getty Images Palantir cofounder Joe Lonsdale's wife has an interesting nickname for their AI agent. She calls it "Tradbot," he said, a name inspired by the social media trend of tradwives. The Lonsdales use their "Tradbot" for help with parenting. What does Joe Lonsdale's AI agent and Ballerina Farm have in common? Lonsdale, who cofounded Palantir before building his venture capital firm, told CNBC on Thursday how his wife, Tayler, uses AI — and the nickname she's given their agent. "My wife has Grok Bot at home," Lonsdale said. "She calls it the 'tradbot' for tradwife." For those unfamiliar, a tradwife is a woman who embraces traditional gender roles , such as supporting her husband with household work and taking a primary role in raising kids. Some of these tradwives become influencers, posting videos of their ornate meals or gifts for their husbands. The Lonsdale family's "tradbot" helps them manage parenting duties for their six children. Lonsdale said the AI agent tells them about health appointments and activities. He asked the "tradbot" to help his two-year-old break up with his binky. "It's telling me when to and when not to give it to him," Lonsdale said. Parents have been employing AI for all kinds of use cases. One mom of two previously told Business Insider that she sends voice memos to Claude to help organize her life. Another said that she built AI agents to help manage schedules and school emails. Business Insider's Amanda Hoover declared mom, dad, and AI the "modern parenting throuple." The debate of how much — if any — AI should be involved in parenting continues to rage online. Lonsdale is a vocal proponent of AI, having invested in it heavily through his venture capital fund, 8VC. During September's AI extinction freak-out, Lonsdale reassured the public : "The world is going to be alright, guys." Clearly, Lonsdale's use of AI has extended beyond the office. "My wife's definitely using it at home," Lonsdale told CNBC, "and we're using it a lot at work as well." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: I work in cybersecurity, but my mom lost $3,000 to online scams. Now, I do 3 things to keep her safe.
items.summary: Jen Eaves works in cybersecurity and her mom still lost thousands to scams. Courtesy of Jen Eaves Jen Eaves' mother is 79 and lost more than $3,000 to online scams. Eaves now monitors her mother's finances and says that was a hard conversation. Digital caregiving is an important part of supporting aging parents, she says. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Jen Eaves , Digital Caregiving & Elder Fraud Advocate at Aura. It has been edited for length and clarity . It's an odd shift in dynamic when you start caring for the people who always cared for you. My mother is 79, and lives with my brother, who handles most of her day-to-day physical care . I'm the one who handles the administrative side of care, like scheduling doctor appointments and keeping her safe online. About six years ago, my mom had a stroke, and while she recovered fairly well, she wasn't the same cognitively as she had been before. Around that time, I began noticing her falling for scams online . Once, she ordered a cure for diabetes, which she has. The product was supposedly being sold by a famous TV doctor. When she showed me the video ad, I could see it was badly done AI , with the supposed doctor's lips not matching his words. There have been other scams and pitfalls, too: online orders that never arrive, or even a legitimate credit card that my mom opened without realizing what she was doing. All in all, she's lost about $3,000 to scams, though I've been able to recover most of it through her bank. I've realized that I need to take a more proactive approach to digital caregiving to protect my mom's finances. Here's what I'm doing. Approaching from a place of help and dignity After my brother and I had taken my mom's keys away, her phone became her connection to the world. I wanted to respect that. While some people have to restrict their older parents' access to phones , that didn't feel right in my case. It was critical to me that my mom kept her dignity and as much independence as possible. At the same time, I saw there was an emotional side to falling for a scam: she would feel frustrated and confused when it happened, and I wanted to spare her those negative emotions. I never want my mom to feel like I'm parenting her. Instead, I pointed out the patterns I was seeing and emphasized I'm here to help if she's willing to let me be involved. The choice, ultimately, is hers. This would be a lot harder if she wasn't willing. Talk about scams My mom wasn't particularly tech savvy , even before her stroke. I've had to educate her about what scams look like. When she shared the famous doctor video, I pointed out the aspects that seemed AI-generated to me. I remind her that if it sounds too good to be true, it probably is. I emphasize that urgency is a big sign of a scam. The bank, I tell her, is never going to call you. Once, she had a scam caller claiming to be Apple support. They asked for her Apple ID and password, which would have given them access to pretty much everything she has online. Because of our conversations, my mom hesitated. She patched me into the call and asked the scammer to explain the situation to me. I was very proud that she recognized the scam and knew to ask me for help. I monitor my mom's accounts I worked in cybersecurity at Aura, which offers a lot of great products for keeping kids safe online. But my experience with my mom made me realize we were missing a whole vulnerable population: older adults. I helped develop Trusted Family Access, which allows family members like me to see alerts from their loved ones' accounts, with permission. This gives me peace of mind that I can catch any issues quickly. It's also made other aspects of caregiving easier, like handling medical appointments, because I have access to all my mom's information in one place. When my mom was scammed, it felt like I was a victim too. I spent hours calling her bank and credit cards to get her money back. If she were to lose her savings, it would impact the whole family. I'm grateful we've found a solution that empowers both of us to keep her finances safe. Read the original article on Business Insider

Jen Eaves works in cybersecurity and her mom still lost thousands to scams.

Courtesy of Jen Eaves

  • Jen Eaves' mother is 79 and lost more than $3,000 to online scams.
  • Eaves now monitors her mother's finances and says that was a hard conversation.
  • Digital caregiving is an important part of supporting aging parents, she says.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Jen Eaves, Digital Caregiving & Elder Fraud Advocate at Aura. It has been edited for length and clarity.

It's an odd shift in dynamic when you start caring for the people who always cared for you. My mother is 79, and lives with my brother, who handles most of her day-to-day physical care. I'm the one who handles the administrative side of care, like scheduling doctor appointments and keeping her safe online.

About six years ago, my mom had a stroke, and while she recovered fairly well, she wasn't the same cognitively as she had been before. Around that time, I began noticing her falling for scams online.

Once, she ordered a cure for diabetes, which she has. The product was supposedly being sold by a famous TV doctor. When she showed me the video ad, I could see it was badly done AI, with the supposed doctor's lips not matching his words.

There have been other scams and pitfalls, too: online orders that never arrive, or even a legitimate credit card that my mom opened without realizing what she was doing. All in all, she's lost about $3,000 to scams, though I've been able to recover most of it through her bank.

I've realized that I need to take a more proactive approach to digital caregiving to protect my mom's finances. Here's what I'm doing.

Approaching from a place of help and dignity

After my brother and I had taken my mom's keys away, her phone became her connection to the world. I wanted to respect that. While some people have to restrict their older parents' access to phones, that didn't feel right in my case.

It was critical to me that my mom kept her dignity and as much independence as possible. At the same time, I saw there was an emotional side to falling for a scam: she would feel frustrated and confused when it happened, and I wanted to spare her those negative emotions.

I never want my mom to feel like I'm parenting her. Instead, I pointed out the patterns I was seeing and emphasized I'm here to help if she's willing to let me be involved. The choice, ultimately, is hers. This would be a lot harder if she wasn't willing.

Talk about scams

My mom wasn't particularly tech savvy, even before her stroke. I've had to educate her about what scams look like. When she shared the famous doctor video, I pointed out the aspects that seemed AI-generated to me. I remind her that if it sounds too good to be true, it probably is. I emphasize that urgency is a big sign of a scam. The bank, I tell her, is never going to call you.

Once, she had a scam caller claiming to be Apple support. They asked for her Apple ID and password, which would have given them access to pretty much everything she has online.

Because of our conversations, my mom hesitated. She patched me into the call and asked the scammer to explain the situation to me. I was very proud that she recognized the scam and knew to ask me for help.

I monitor my mom's accounts

I worked in cybersecurity at Aura, which offers a lot of great products for keeping kids safe online. But my experience with my mom made me realize we were missing a whole vulnerable population: older adults.

I helped develop Trusted Family Access, which allows family members like me to see alerts from their loved ones' accounts, with permission. This gives me peace of mind that I can catch any issues quickly. It's also made other aspects of caregiving easier, like handling medical appointments, because I have access to all my mom's information in one place.

When my mom was scammed, it felt like I was a victim too. I spent hours calling her bank and credit cards to get her money back. If she were to lose her savings, it would impact the whole family. I'm grateful we've found a solution that empowers both of us to keep her finances safe.

items.title: Fish lamps and Windows XP: Inside Frutiger Aero, the nostalgic tech aesthetic captivating Gen Zers
items.summary: Frutiger Aero design combines old-school tech with green and blue natural imagery. Sammy Conti/@bwuubbles on Instagram and TikTok Frutiger Aero, a Gen Z favorite, combines early internet nostalgia with a utopian tech vision. Fans say the aesthetic represents a "future that was promised" by tech but never arrived. Some recent tech releases have hinted at a Frutiger Aero revival. Looking at 22-year-old Sammy Conti's room is like looking into a fishbowl. Shades of blue fill the space, interspersed with neon green and the occasional pop of orange or yellow. Vines, bubbles, and jellyfish hang from the ceiling. Moving lamps are everywhere: lava lamps, bubble lamps, aquarium lamps with roving tropical fish. Then there are objects that feel out of place: a purple Game Boy Advance, Nintendo 64 cartridges, Wii and PlayStation game cases hung like art on a gallery wall, and a DIY mirror in the shape of an old Microsoft Windows logo. The confluence of nature and old-school tech isn't random. It's Frutiger Aero, an aesthetic inspired by the early internet, embraced by Gen Zers who say it represents a future that was promised but never arrived — one where technology is a source of inspiration and fuel for creativity, coexisting with nature and helping us ascend to our highest selves. "You grow up thinking the world is going to be this green utopia where we coexist with nature and have technology and it helps us," Conti told Business Insider. "Then as I started getting older, things became very sleek and modernist, very gray." For Conti, whose Frutiger Aero content has earned her more than 700,000 followers across Instagram and TikTok, the aesthetic represents a promise tech abandoned. "We could have lived in that future," she said. "It could have been taken care of responsibly in a way that doesn't take people's jobs, doesn't pollute the environment, but it's not." View this post on Instagram A post shared by aqua girl 🫧🐠‧₊˚ (@bwuubbles) A corporate tech aesthetic gets a glow-up A fervent online community has formed around the term after it first gained traction in 2023, according to Google Trends data. There's an active Discord and Subreddit, plus millions of views for #frutigeraero on TikTok. Sofi Xian, a researcher and founding member of an online community called the Consumer Aesthetics Research Institute, coined the term Frutiger Aero in 2017 to describe a corporate tech aesthetic prevalent from the mid-2000s through the early 2010s. Some defining characteristics included glossy surfaces, glass or transparent materials, and macro photos of grass. "Frutiger" refers to a specific typeface, while "Aero" was Microsoft's name for the interface design of its Windows Vista operating system, which came out in 2006. "Nobody at the time really thought it was cool," Xian said of the design style. "It was a corporate product. It was sold to us." The "Bliss" image used in Microsoft Windows XP is beloved by Frutiger Aero fans. Kevin Lee/Getty Images The recent embrace of Frutiger Aero remains somewhat of a mystery to Xian, who says the term has blossomed well beyond what she first documented. Her book on the style, "Archaeology of a Promised Future," is set to come out in November. The modern version of the aesthetic still incorporates some of the classic elements, and then some. "Bliss," the iconic photo of rolling green hills beneath a bright blue sky with clouds — the default wallpaper on Windows XP upon its release in 2001 — remains an almost sacred image to Frutiger fans. Conti recently made a pilgrimage to the area in Sonoma County, California, and called it "just as beautiful as it is in the photos." The future that never showed "The future that was promised" is a central theme in the world of Frutiger Aero and is frequently invoked alongside images of clean, glistening skyscrapers set against grassy fields. "It's really a vision of technology that is quite different to what we have," Maria Gemma Brown, a cultural studies researcher at the University of Queensland, told Business Insider. Many young people now see technology as bland, lifeless, addictive, or even sinister. AI is increasingly associated with war, mass surveillance , and environmental degradation. Data centers , one of the most controversial physical manifestations of modern tech, face fierce opposition over environmental concerns. Richy Srirachanikorn, a Ph.D. candidate at Concordia University, has interviewed more than 30 people in the Frutiger Aero community. He said it's about nostalgia for a feeling more than about the specific objects or design that inspired it. "Whatever this aesthetic was as a kid, it made me optimistic, not about the future, but about the present," he said was how the people he interviewed described it. That could help explain why it's especially appealing to Gen Z, a generation rife with concerns about environmental, technological, and financial doom . Srirachanikorn said he found Frutiger Aero is used almost as a "coping mechanism" and the associated online communities as places to take "respite from the uncertainties of the world." Apple computers and laptops around the turn of the century came in translucent materials and bright, eye-catching shades. Getty Images Lovers of Frutiger Aero are also rejecting a broader design shift toward minimalism and neutral colors. In consumer tech, translucent clamshell laptops and bright pink MP3 players have given way to sleek, uniformly gray designs, as if they're explicitly meant to disappear into the background of our lives. "I feel like products had almost a personality. Which color you picked or what design you picked was a loud extension of you," Conti said, adding that now it feels like everything merely wants to "fit in." The old-school tech may also represent a level of agency that feels unattainable now, Srirachanikorn said. In the early 2000s, consumer tech companies may have embraced bright colors and images of nature to make their products more appealing as they still needed us to buy in. Today, their products are almost impossible to escape. Hope for a new bloom Austin Horey, founder of the New York-based brand Unjust Jewelry, makes a range of products inspired by Frutiger Aero and similar strains of nostalgia. He's sold over 10,000 bottles of a Frutiger Aero-inspired fragrance — oceanic, clean, soapy — that comes in a box that, when opened, plays an original Frutiger Aero-inspired song. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Unjust Jewelry® (@unjustjewelry) Horey said not only is there a huge appetite for Frutiger Aero content and products, but that major tech companies seem to be taking notice. His work has been embraced by an icon of the Frutiger Aero movement: Microsoft. When he released a Windows XP bracelet featuring the classic application icons from the operating system, the company partnered with him to make a necklace as well. Fans of Frutiger Aero celebrate every time Big Tech makes a move they think signals a return to the aesthetic, like Xbox introducing a new glossy neon-green logo and the release of the budget-friendly Apple MacBook Neo, which comes in a bright yellow-green. Apple's introduction of the Liquid Glass design last year also set off the Frutiger Aero antennae. Microsoft even posted a TikTok suggesting the design was reminiscent of Windows Vista. Frutiger Aero design combines old-school tech with green and blue natural imagery.

Sammy Conti/@bwuubbles on Instagram and TikTok

  • Frutiger Aero, a Gen Z favorite, combines early internet nostalgia with a utopian tech vision.
  • Fans say the aesthetic represents a "future that was promised" by tech but never arrived.
  • Some recent tech releases have hinted at a Frutiger Aero revival.

Looking at 22-year-old Sammy Conti's room is like looking into a fishbowl.

Shades of blue fill the space, interspersed with neon green and the occasional pop of orange or yellow. Vines, bubbles, and jellyfish hang from the ceiling. Moving lamps are everywhere: lava lamps, bubble lamps, aquarium lamps with roving tropical fish. Then there are objects that feel out of place: a purple Game Boy Advance, Nintendo 64 cartridges, Wii and PlayStation game cases hung like art on a gallery wall, and a DIY mirror in the shape of an old Microsoft Windows logo.

The confluence of nature and old-school tech isn't random. It's Frutiger Aero, an aesthetic inspired by the early internet, embraced by Gen Zers who say it represents a future that was promised but never arrived — one where technology is a source of inspiration and fuel for creativity, coexisting with nature and helping us ascend to our highest selves.

"You grow up thinking the world is going to be this green utopia where we coexist with nature and have technology and it helps us," Conti told Business Insider. "Then as I started getting older, things became very sleek and modernist, very gray."

For Conti, whose Frutiger Aero content has earned her more than 700,000 followers across Instagram and TikTok, the aesthetic represents a promise tech abandoned. "We could have lived in that future," she said. "It could have been taken care of responsibly in a way that doesn't take people's jobs, doesn't pollute the environment, but it's not."

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by aqua girl 🫧🐠‧₊˚ (@bwuubbles)

A corporate tech aesthetic gets a glow-up

A fervent online community has formed around the term after it first gained traction in 2023, according to Google Trends data. There's an active Discord and Subreddit, plus millions of views for #frutigeraero on TikTok.

Sofi Xian, a researcher and founding member of an online community called the Consumer Aesthetics Research Institute, coined the term Frutiger Aero in 2017 to describe a corporate tech aesthetic prevalent from the mid-2000s through the early 2010s. Some defining characteristics included glossy surfaces, glass or transparent materials, and macro photos of grass. "Frutiger" refers to a specific typeface, while "Aero" was Microsoft's name for the interface design of its Windows Vista operating system, which came out in 2006.

"Nobody at the time really thought it was cool," Xian said of the design style. "It was a corporate product. It was sold to us."

The "Bliss" image used in Microsoft Windows XP is beloved by Frutiger Aero fans.

Kevin Lee/Getty Images

The recent embrace of Frutiger Aero remains somewhat of a mystery to Xian, who says the term has blossomed well beyond what she first documented. Her book on the style, "Archaeology of a Promised Future," is set to come out in November.

The modern version of the aesthetic still incorporates some of the classic elements, and then some. "Bliss," the iconic photo of rolling green hills beneath a bright blue sky with clouds — the default wallpaper on Windows XP upon its release in 2001 — remains an almost sacred image to Frutiger fans. Conti recently made a pilgrimage to the area in Sonoma County, California, and called it "just as beautiful as it is in the photos."

The future that never showed

"The future that was promised" is a central theme in the world of Frutiger Aero and is frequently invoked alongside images of clean, glistening skyscrapers set against grassy fields.

"It's really a vision of technology that is quite different to what we have," Maria Gemma Brown, a cultural studies researcher at the University of Queensland, told Business Insider.

Many young people now see technology as bland, lifeless, addictive, or even sinister. AI is increasingly associated with war, mass surveillance, and environmental degradation. Data centers, one of the most controversial physical manifestations of modern tech, face fierce opposition over environmental concerns.

Richy Srirachanikorn, a Ph.D. candidate at Concordia University, has interviewed more than 30 people in the Frutiger Aero community. He said it's about nostalgia for a feeling more than about the specific objects or design that inspired it.

"Whatever this aesthetic was as a kid, it made me optimistic, not about the future, but about the present," he said was how the people he interviewed described it.

That could help explain why it's especially appealing to Gen Z, a generation rife with concerns about environmental, technological, and financial doom. Srirachanikorn said he found Frutiger Aero is used almost as a "coping mechanism" and the associated online communities as places to take "respite from the uncertainties of the world."

Apple computers and laptops around the turn of the century came in translucent materials and bright, eye-catching shades.

Getty Images

Lovers of Frutiger Aero are also rejecting a broader design shift toward minimalism and neutral colors. In consumer tech, translucent clamshell laptops and bright pink MP3 players have given way to sleek, uniformly gray designs, as if they're explicitly meant to disappear into the background of our lives.

"I feel like products had almost a personality. Which color you picked or what design you picked was a loud extension of you," Conti said, adding that now it feels like everything merely wants to "fit in."

The old-school tech may also represent a level of agency that feels unattainable now, Srirachanikorn said. In the early 2000s, consumer tech companies may have embraced bright colors and images of nature to make their products more appealing as they still needed us to buy in. Today, their products are almost impossible to escape.

Hope for a new bloom

Austin Horey, founder of the New York-based brand Unjust Jewelry, makes a range of products inspired by Frutiger Aero and similar strains of nostalgia. He's sold over 10,000 bottles of a Frutiger Aero-inspired fragrance — oceanic, clean, soapy — that comes in a box that, when opened, plays an original Frutiger Aero-inspired song.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Unjust Jewelry® (@unjustjewelry)

Horey said not only is there a huge appetite for Frutiger Aero content and products, but that major tech companies seem to be taking notice. His work has been embraced by an icon of the Frutiger Aero movement: Microsoft. When he released a Windows XP bracelet featuring the classic application icons from the operating system, the company partnered with him to make a necklace as well.

Fans of Frutiger Aero celebrate every time Big Tech makes a move they think signals a return to the aesthetic, like Xbox introducing a new glossy neon-green logo and the release of the budget-friendly Apple MacBook Neo, which comes in a bright yellow-green. Apple's introduction of the Liquid Glass design last year also set off the Frutiger Aero antennae. Microsoft even posted a TikTok suggesting the design was reminiscent of Windows Vista.

A selfie Sammy Conti took with an iPhone 4 she bought on eBay for taking old-school photos.

Sammy Conti

Conti said the colorful MacBook Neo was the most Frutiger Aero product a tech company had released in years. While she's been disappointed in modern tech, the underlying vibe of Frutiger Aero is one of optimism, and she still sees the ideas behind it as something to strive for, "especially as Gen Z moves into these positions of power as we get older."

"I think it's important not to forget what it still could be," she said.

items.title: Forget free lunch. Some workers just want an office bidet.
items.summary: Getty Images; Alyssa Powell/BI The great bidet takeover has reached the workplace. White-collar workers are bartering with their bosses and weighing job offers over bidet access. "It's the superior way to live," one said. Seungmin Hong felt he had two options: Stay at Tesla or have a clean tush. After finishing an engineering internship at the automotive giant last year, the University of Waterloo student was weighing whether to stick around or accept a job offer from much smaller Simbe Robotics. During Hong's final interview at Simbe's San Francisco office, he asked to use the restroom, and there it was: a glistening, inviting bidet. "That cemented in my mind: 'Yeah, this company actually cares about their employees,'" said Hong, who grew up with a bidet in the bathroom of his childhood home. He took the job. Move over espresso machines, ping-pong tables, and nap pods . For workers like Hong, the humble bidet is the ultimate job perk. In recent years, the hygiene-friendly fixtures have gone from novelty to must-have for many US households. Toto, one of the biggest manufacturers in the space, said cumulative global sales of its Washlet bidets surpassed 70 million units last year, up from 50 million in 2019. High-profile fans include Dodgers pitcher Shohei Ohtani , actor Janelle James , and New York mayor Zohran Mamdani . Now, some devotees are pushing to make bidets a standard in offices. Once you get used to one at home, they say, going bidet-less at work is a pain in the rear. Michael Fiore used to sometimes get about halfway through his commute, then turn around and drive back home just so he could use the bidet in his bathroom. About a year ago, he had an epiphany: Why not install a bidet at work, too? So he did. "It's been a total game changer," said Fiore, president of Smith's Gardentown, a retail garden center in Wichita Falls, Texas. "It's the superior way to live." There's just one wrinkle. Employees who were accustomed to using the restrooms available to shoppers have started coming to what Fiore jokingly calls the "executive" bathroom, which is reserved for staff. It houses one bidet-equipped toilet, meaning he now often has to wait to use it himself. "Word has spread," he said. Persuading the boss This past summer, Cynthia Howard asked her boss to install a bidet in the single-seat restroom she shares with about a dozen of her colleagues. The fulfillment specialist at Swifthouse, a logistics company outside Philadelphia, argued it would reduce toilet paper costs, cut employees' restroom time, and improve morale. Swifthouse's founder and CEO, Dave Harriger, said the proposal persuaded him to order a $60 bidet attachment that same day. He said he's pleased that Howard and other employees like it, though he's not a convert himself. "I used it once. I yelped and don't know if I'll use it again," he said. "It's cold water on your butt." Swifthouse CEO Dave Harriger was persuaded by his employee, Cynthia Howard, to order a $60 bidet attachment in the office restroom. Shifthouse Pricier bidet models that sell for thousands of dollars apiece offer warm-water sprays, air dryers, deodorizers, and even Bluetooth speakers. Not every worker is comfortable asking their boss to install the devices in the office. To help those folks out, Jonathan Brown, a data scientist in Orange County, California, launched buttstuff.work earlier this year. The site lets employees register their interest in having bidets at work without directly approaching management. Brown said he has long wondered why Silicon Valley workplaces offer perks like beer taps and catered lunches but not bidets. He plans to share the data his site collects with bidet manufacturers to help them find potential customers. So far, Brown said, about a dozen people, mostly from small businesses and universities, have signed up. His only promotion has been a post on Reddit. "People don't love talking about bathroom stuff at work," said Brown. The bidet goes to work Bidet makers say interest has surged since what Bill Strang, president of corporate strategy at Toto, called "the great toilet paper panic of 2020," when pandemic shortages sent Americans searching for alternatives. Strang and Justin Allen, CEO of Tushy, another bidet maker , said workplaces are a relatively small but growing part of the bidet business. Installing the devices in office restrooms can be challenging, as some require plumbing modifications, code compliance, and a nearby electrical outlet. Allen sees the demand firsthand. The bidets in Tushy's shared office restroom in Brooklyn, New York, are a draw for employees of neighboring companies, he said, adding that a FedEx driver regularly stops by during his route to use the facilities. Cushy tech companies have long dotted their stalls with bidets. Business Insider spoke with workers who spotted them years ago at some Google and Microsoft offices. Now, with awareness and interest spreading, some workplace observers say what was once a nice-to-have perk could become a competitive advantage for employers well beyond Silicon Valley. A recruiting tool Robert Hatta, an executive recruiter and talent consultant in Columbus, Ohio, thinks employers pushing return-to-office mandates would have a much easier time attracting and retaining talent by investing in the fixtures. In a LinkedIn post that drew nearly 150 comments last year, Hatta argued that flimsy toilet paper and a lack of privacy can make office life less appealing. His prescription? Sound-insulated, well-ventilated stalls, preferably equipped with bidets. "It's about respecting people's dignity," Hatta told Business Insider. Going to the bathroom "is an important part of the workday." The state of a workplace's facilities can reveal a lot about its culture, said Lou Downe, director of the School of Good Services, a UK-based provider of leadership training. Details such as free menstrual products, well-maintained soap dispensers, and bidets can offer clues about how much thought an employer puts into its workers' comfort, they said. Seungmin Hong said access to a bidet was a factor in picking his last job. Seungmin Hong Hong, the bidet-loving Tesla alum, has since left Simbe to build his own startup, Simantic. While the company goes through Y Combinator , he and his cofounder are shacking up in an Airbnb. No modifications are allowed, so no bidets. Once Simantic raises its seed round, Hong said he and his cofounder plan to rent some office space. He knows what their first purchase will be. Read the original article on Business Insider
