items.title: How Vision-Language Models Actually See Images: Inside ViT, CLIP, SigLIP & 3D M-RoPE
items.summary: Why an “iPod” sticker fools OpenAI CLIP (64.5%) while Qwen2.5-VL reads it cleanly — measured layer by layer on a 96 GB Blackwell GPU. By Latent AI Labs (@LatentAILabs) TL;DR — How Do Vision-Language Models (VLMs) Actually See Images? Modern Vision-Language Models (such as Qwen2.5-VL , GPT-4o , and Claude 3.5 Sonnet ) process images in three stages : 1. Vision Transformer (ViT) Patch Slicer & 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger: A 560 × 560 RGB photograph ( 940,800 floats) is sliced by a 14 × 14 pixel grid into 40 × 40 = 1,600 patches , projected into 1,280-dimensional vectors , refined through 28 local-window ViT layers ( 112 × 112 px) and 4 global full-attention layers ( Layers 7, 15, 23, 31), and compressed 4-into-1 by a 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger into 400 Visual Word tokens ( 2,048-D) — cutting LLM self-attention pairs 16× ( 2.56M → 160K). 2. Dual Spatial Compass ( 2D ViT RoPE + 3D M-RoPE [16t, 24h, 24w]): Each attention head splits its 64 rotary position frequency pairs into 16 Time ( t) , 24 Height ( h / Row y) , and 24 Width ( w / Column x) dials so a 1D language model natively understands 2D aspect ratios ( NaViT ) and 3D video timelines. 3. Cross-Modal Attention & Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD): In Layers 17–28, cross-modal grounding heads concentrate up to 96.8%–99.8% of their visual attention onto the target object quadrant, while Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) subtracts noisy-image language priors ( ℓ_VCD = (1+α)ℓ(v) − αℓ(v')) to reduce object hallucinations by 41.5% . In 2021, Gabriel Goh and colleagues at OpenAI demonstrated a famous vulnerability in computer vision known as a typographic attack : stick a paper label reading “iPod” onto a green Granny Smith apple, and OpenAI’s CLIP classifies the piece of fruit as an electronic music player. We rebuilt that experiment with a synthetic studio photograph of a green apple and a digital label, and ran it through OpenAI CLIP (openai/clip-vit-base-patch32), Google SigLIP (google/siglip-base-patch16-224), and Alibaba Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct on a 96 GB NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU : Clean Green Apple: CLIP predicts “a photo of a green Granny Smith apple” at 100.00% (cosine = 0.3302), with 0.00% for "a photo of an iPod electronic music player" (cosine = 0.2033). Apple + "iPod" Label: "Green Apple" drops to 35.47% (cosine = 0.2641), and "iPod" takes first place at 64.51% (cosine = 0.2701). Apple + "Pizza" Label: "Green Apple" drops to 19.86% (cosine = 0.2591), and "Pizza" takes first place at 80.07% (cosine = 0.2730). Figure 1: GPU measurement of the "iPod" typographic attack on OpenAI CLIP (64.51% iPod) vs. Qwen2.5-VL-3B on a 96 GB NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU. Image by the author; source apple photo AI-generated with a digital label. Yet when we feed those exact same labeled photographs into a modern 3-billion-parameter Vision-Language Model ( Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct ) and ask what object is in the photo and what word is printed on the sticker, it separates the physical fruit from the text: On the "iPod" apple ( 1,342.7 ms cold start): "This is an apple, and the word written on the paper sticker is 'iPod.'" On the "Pizza" apple ( 240.7 ms warm inference): "This is an apple with a paper sticker that says 'Pizza.'" Even more intriguing: that same Vision-Language Model reads a 4-digit security code ( PIN: 4829 ) off a wide 1120 × 280 shipping manifest accurately, yet looks at a clean geometric diagram of 15 overlapping circles and counts "12" . Why does a printed word hijack CLIP? How does a 1D language model — built to predict the next token in a sequence — represent 2D photographs and 3D video? And why does a model that can read fine print fail to count 15 rings? We hooked directly into Qwen2.5-VL-3B’s 32-layer Vision Transformer (ViT) and 36-layer Language Model on our Blackwell GPU to measure the tensors, cosine similarities, positional IDs, and attention weights layer by layer ( watch the companion 25-minute animated video on YouTube here ). https://medium.com/media/3d3907e7090805703a8975dee4fce162/href Figure 2: How the Vision Transformer slices a 560×560px photograph by a 14×14px grid into 40×40 = 1,600 patches. Image by the author. Experiment 0. Why Does an “iPod” Sticker Fool CLIP? (The ×100.0 Temperature Multiplier) Direct Answer: OpenAI CLIP compresses an entire image into a single 512-dimensional vector and multiplies raw image-text cosine similarities by a learned temperature scale of 100.0 (exp(4.6052)) before applying Softmax. Because written text in web images strongly predicts captions, OCR features from the "iPod" sticker nudge the "iPod" cosine just +0.0060 above "Green Apple" (0.2701 vs. 0.2641), which the ×100.0 Softmax amplifies into a 64.51% vs. 35.47% victory. Here are the exact cosine similarities (cos(θ) = (I · T) / (‖I‖ ‖T‖)) and Softmax probabilities recorded on our GPU for apple_ipod.jpg across all five candidate prompts: 1. "a photo of an iPod electronic music player" Cosine: 0.2701 → Scaled Logit (100 × cos): 27.01 → Softmax Probability: 64.51% 2. How Does a Vision Transformer (ViT) Turn Pixels into Patch Tokens? Direct Answer: A Vision Transformer (ViT) divides an image of resolution H × W by a fixed patch size P × P (14 × 14 pixels in Qwen2.5-VL) to produce a grid of (H/P) × (W/P) spatial patches. For a 560 × 560 image, 560 ÷ 14 = 40, yielding 40 × 40 = 1,600 patches (the sequence length N). A learned linear projection maps the raw RGB pixel values inside each patch into a 1,280-dimensional embedding vector (the feature dimension D), creating a [1,600 × 1,280] ViT input tensor. In classical digital image processing , computer vision slid local 3×3 filters (such as adaptive or Sobel edge filters) across an image pixel by pixel. In 2020, Alexey Dosovitskiy et al. ( "An Image is Worth 16×16 Words" , ICLR 2021) replaced convolutional hierarchies by slicing an image into non-overlapping patches and projecting each patch into a Transformer token. We hooked into the Vision Transformer (vlm.visual) inside Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct on our GPU as it processed a 560 × 560 RGB image (940,800 float values; center pixel (280, 280) = RGB [147, 132, 157], orange fur (140, 220) = [149, 106, 72], snow (480, 280) = [180, 195, 224]): 1. The 14×14 Spatial Grid ( 560 ÷ 14 = 40): Qwen2.5-VL uses a 14 × 14 pixel patch size. Dividing 560 px ÷ 14 px gives 40 patches across and 40 patches down , or 40 × 40 = 1,600 spatial patches (image_grid_thw = [[1, 40, 40]]). 2. Patch Unrolling ( 588 Spatial RGB Values / 1,176 with Temporal Duplication): A single 14 × 14 RGB square holds 14 × 14 × 3 = 588 pixel values. Under the hood, because Qwen2.5-VL uses a unified 3D patchifier (Conv3d with temporal_patch_size = 2) for both photos and video, a static photograph is duplicated across 2 temporal frames so each tube input has 2 × 14 × 14 × 3 = 1,176 values (pixel_values.shape = [1600, 1176]). 3. Linear Patch Projection ( → 1,280-D): The learned projection matrix maps each patch into a 1,280-dimensional visual embedding vector . Keep the two dimensions distinct: 1,600 is the number of patches N in the 40 × 40 grid, while 1,280 is the feature vector length D inside each single patch, forming the [1,600 × 1,280] ViT tensor (L2 norm = 417.01). Figure 3: Multiplying each patch by the learned projection matrix produces a 1,280-D vector; stacking all 1,600 patches forms the [1,600 × 1,280] ViT tensor. Image by the author. 2. How Do Patches Talk? Windowed vs. Global ViT Attention ([7, 15, 23, 31]) Direct Answer: Running full self-attention across 1,600 patches on all 32 ViT layers would require 1,600² = 2.56 million pairs per layer. To keep compute linear in image size, Qwen2.5-VL restricts 28 of its 32 ViT layers to local 112 × 112 pixel windows (8 × 8 = 64 patches per window) and runs full global self-attention only at 4 checkpoint layers ( Layers 7, 15, 23, and 31, 0-indexed) . 28 Windowed Attention Layers ( 112 × 112 px Local Windows): Patches only attend within their local 8 × 8 patch neighborhood (64 patches). Because window size is fixed, compute scales linearly O(N) with pixel count. 4 Global Full-Attention Checkpoints (0-indexed Layers 7, 15, 23, 31): At every 8th layer (fullatt_block_indexes = [7, 15, 23, 31]), window walls are removed and all 1,600 patches attend across the entire image (2.56M pairs), integrating global scene geometry. Figure 4: Windowed vs. Global ViT attention layers and pairwise cosine similarity distribution of the resulting visual tokens. Image by the author. Across the 400 merged visual tokens exiting the vision tower ([400, 2048], including the diagonal), we measured the pairwise cosine similarity distribution: 10th percentile ( p10): 0.1398 (82.0° apart) Median pair ( p50): 0.2886 (73.2° apart) 90th percentile ( p90): 0.5567 (56.2° apart) 99th percentile ( p99): 0.8225 (34.7° tight cluster) 3. CLIP Softmax vs. Google SigLIP Sigmoid: How Vision Models Align with Text Direct Answer: OpenAI CLIP aligns images and text using a batch Softmax (InfoNCE) loss (Softmax(100 · I_i · T_j)), which requires normalizing across every negative example in the batch. Google SigLIP (Zhai et al., ICCV 2023) replaces the batch Softmax with an independent pairwise Sigmoid (1 / (1 + exp(-117.33 · I_i · T_j + 12.93))), turning every (Image_i, Text_j) pair into a standalone binary classification problem with zero global batch normalization. We evaluated both openai/clip-vit-base-patch32 and google/siglip-base-patch16-224 across 5 studio images (Green Apple, 10:10 Clock, Red Fox, Plate & Knife, Vault Receipt) and their 5 matching captions on our GPU (m3_clip_vs_siglip_5x5): Figure 5: Contrastive image-text alignment in CLIP vs. Google SigLIP's independent pairwise sigmoid equation. Image by the author. Measured GPU Comparison: OpenAI CLIP vs. Google SigLIP Scoring Equation & Learned Parameters: • OpenAI CLIP ( ViT-B/32): Softmax(100.0 · I_i · T_j) (scale = 100.0, no bias) • Google SigLIP ( ViT-B/16-224): 1 / (1 + exp(-117.33 · I_i · T_j + 12.93)) (scale = 117.33, bias = -12.93) 5×5 Diagonal Cosine Similarities ( Apple, Clock, Fox, Plate, Receipt): • OpenAI CLIP: 0.3464, 0.3507, 0.3344, 0.3023, 0.2723 • Google SigLIP: 0.1111, 0.0687, 0.1633, 0.1591, 0.1414 5×5 Diagonal Match Probabilities: • OpenAI CLIP (Softmax over 5 captions): 100.0% , 100.0% , 100.0% , 100.0% , 99.99% (max off-diagonal: 0.01%) • Google SigLIP (Independent Sigmoid): 52.44% (Apple; 97.57% on "Granny Smith" prompt), 0.84% (Clock), 99.83% (Fox), 99.72% (Plate), 97.47% (Receipt) — and 0.00% across all 20 off-diagonal cells! Typographic Attack Robustness: • On "iPod" Apple: CLIP flips to 64.51% iPod (35.47% Apple). SigLIP predicts 40.29% Apple vs. 0.97% iPod . • On "Pizza" Apple: CLIP flips to 80.07% Pizza (19.86% Apple). SigLIP predicts 18.07% Apple vs. 3.13% Pizza . Two key engineering takeaways emerge from these numbers: Why SigLIP Resisted the "iPod" and "Pizza" Labels: Even if we convert SigLIP's raw logits back into a Softmax over the candidate labels, "Green Apple" still wins at ~98.6% — showing that SigLIP's robustness comes from its learned ViT-B/16 representations and WebLI training recipe rather than the sigmoid readout alone. Why SigLIP Scored the 10:10 Clock Caption at 0.84%: Because SigLIP learns a strong negative bias (-12.93) so non-matching pairs default to 0.00%, an image-text pair must exceed a cosine threshold of 12.93 / 117.33 = 0.1102 to cross 50% probability. On our descriptive clock caption, SigLIP's cosine was 0.0687 (still the highest in its row, well above all off-diagonals at ≤ 0.004), which maps to 0.84% under the uncalibrated sigmoid threshold. 4. How Does the 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger Cut LLM Attention by 16×? Direct Answer: Feeding all 1,600 ViT patches directly into a 36-layer language model would require 1,600² = 2,560,000 self-attention pairs per layer. To compress the visual sequence before Layer 0 of the LLM, Qwen2.5-VL uses a 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger (vlm.visual.merger) that concatenates every 2 × 2 block of adjacent 14 × 14 px patches (4 × 1,280 = 5,120-D) and projects it through a 2-layer MLP into a single 2,048-D Visual Word token . This reduces token count 4× ( 1,600 → 400) and cuts quadratic self-attention compute 4² = 16× ( 2.56M → 160K pairs) . Figure 6: The 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger concatenates each 2×2 block of 14×14px patches into a 5,120-D vector and projects it through a 2-layer MLP into one 2,048-D Visual Word token. Image by the author. Concatenate 2×2 Spatial Neighbors ( 4 → 1): Four adjacent 14 × 14 px patches covering a 28 × 28 px square are normalized with RMSNorm and concatenated into a 5,120-dimensional vector . 2-Layer MLP Projection ( 5,120-D → 2,048-D): A 2-layer MLP (Linear(5120 → 5120) → GELU → Linear(5120 → 2048)) maps each 5,120-D block into the exact 2,048-dimensional embedding space of the Qwen2.5-3B language model. You can inspect these exact tensor shapes in 10 lines of Python: from transformers import AutoConfig cfg = AutoConfig.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct") v = cfg.vision_config print(v.patch_size, v.temporal_patch_size, v.spatial_merge_size) # -> 14 2 2 print(v.window_size, v.fullatt_block_indexes, v.hidden_size, v.out_hidden_size) # -> 112 [7, 15, 23, 31] 1280 2048 feats = {} vlm.visual.merger.register_forward_hook( lambda m, inp, out: feats.update(pre=inp[0].shape, post=out.shape) ) # 560x560 image -> pre: [1600, 1280], post: [400, 2048] 5. Native Dynamic Resolution (NaViT) vs. Downscaled Square Input Direct Answer: Early vision models forced every image into a fixed 224 × 224 square, distorting aspect ratios and blurring small text. Native Dynamic Resolution ( Patch n' Pack / NaViT , Dehghani et al., NeurIPS 2023) slices images at their native aspect ratio and pixel resolution (rounded to multiples of 28 px), preserving fine OCR details on wide banners and tall documents. We tested a wide 1120 × 280 ( 4:1 aspect ratio) shipping manifest containing tensors_bf16 = 96.0 GB and VAULT PIN: 4829 on our GPU (m4_dynamic_resolution_ocr) under two regimes: Figure 7: Downscaling a 1120×280 manifest into a 140×140 square (25 visual tokens) blurs the digits into "4857", whereas Native Dynamic Resolution (80×20 raw patches → 400 visual tokens) reads "4829" and "96.0 GB". How Does a 1D Language Model Understand 2D Space? (3D M-RoPE [16, 24, 24]) Direct Answer: Standard Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) encodes a single 1D sequence index m across all 64 complex frequency pairs of an attention head (head_dim = 128). 3D Multimodal RoPE (M-RoPE) partitions those 64 frequency pairs into three independent coordinate sections — 16 pairs for Time (t) , 24 pairs for Height (h / Row y) , and 24 pairs for Width (w / Column x) (16 + 24 + 24 = 64 pairs) — stamping every visual token with its exact 3D (t, h, w) coordinate. 3D M-RoPE Partition Inside Every Attention Head (head_dim = 128 -> 64 pairs) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── mrope_section = [ 16 pairs (32D) , 24 pairs (48D) , 24 pairs (48D) ] └── TIME (t) ──┘ └─ HEIGHT (h) ─┘ └─ WIDTH (w) ──┘ We hooked into vlm.model.get_rope_index (position_ids of shape [3, 1, seq_len]) on our GPU (m5_mrope_3d_coordinates) and recorded the exact position IDs for text vs. image tokens: Figure 8: Live GPU trace of the [3, 1, N] M-RoPE position_ids tensor and the Dual Spatial Compass (2D RoPE inside the 32-layer ViT + 3D M-RoPE inside the 36-layer LLM). Image by the author. 1D Text Prompt Tokens ( Tokens 0..4): All three coordinates step together (t = h = w = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]), making M-RoPE mathematically identical to standard 1D RoPE on text. 2D Image Tokens ( Starting at position 15, Row 0, Cols 0..7): • time_t = [15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15] (frozen across the entire static photograph) • height_h = [15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15] (frozen at 15 across Row 0; increments to 16 on Row 1, up to 34 on Row 19) • width_w = [15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22] (increments left-to-right across the columns of Row 0) A Surprising Null Result: Why Flipping Only the LLM’s M-RoPE Didn’t Swap the Image What happens if we leave the 400 visual token vectors untouched, but intercept vlm.model.get_rope_index in-flight and invert the LLM's Height and Width position IDs (h ← 49 - h, w ← 49 - w) on our 4-quadrant composite image (Top-Left: Apple, Top-Right: Clock, Bottom-Left: Fox, Bottom-Right: Plate & Knife)? We expected the LLM’s spatial answers to swap completely. They didn’t: Normal M-RoPE: “In the top-left corner of the image, there is an apple. In the bottom-right corner, there is a plate with a knife next to it.” Inverted LLM M-RoPE ( h, w flipped): "In the top-left corner of the image, there is an apple. In the bottom-right corner, there is a knife." (Flipping width_w alone also left "top-left: apple, top-right: clock" unchanged!) Why didn’t inverting the LLM’s 3D M-RoPE move the apple to the bottom-right? Because as shown in Figure 8 , Qwen2.5-VL actually uses a Dual Spatial Compass : Before the tokens ever reach the LLM, the 32-layer Vision Transformer ( vlm.visual.rotary_pos_emb) applies its own 2D RoPE across all 4 global full-attention layers ( [7, 15, 23, 31]) . Those 4 global ViT layers bake each patch’s 2D quadrant context directly into the 2,048-D feature vectors, and the tokens enter the LLM in raster-scan order (v_001 ... v_400). Flipping only the LLM's M-RoPE position IDs after the ViT has already encoded spatial position creates a slight feature conflict ("plate with a knife" → "a knife"), but the ViT's baked-in spatial features still dominate! 7. Why VLMs Miscount Overlapping Objects & How Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) Works A. Why Does Qwen2.5-VL Count “12” When Shown 15 Overlapping Circles? We fed three 504 × 504 geometric diagrams of overlapping colored rings (36 × 36 raw patches → 18 × 18 = 324 merged visual tokens) into Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct (m8_counting_and_vcd_hallucination): Figure 11: Qwen2.5-VL-3B counts N=4 circles correctly ("4"), but answers "6" for N=8 and "12" for N=15. Image by the author. N = 4 Circles ( 86.7 ms): VLM outputs "4" (Correct). N = 8 Circles ( 83.6 ms): VLM outputs "6" (Under-counts by 2). N = 15 Circles ( 96.9 ms): VLM outputs "12" (Under-counts by 3). A plausible architectural contributor to this failure is the 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger from Section 4: when 15 rings pass through a tight central rosette, multiple ring intersections fall inside the same 28 × 28 px merged token and are mixed by the MLP before the language model begins counting. B. How Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) Suppresses Language Priors In English text corpora, “a white dinner plate and a silver knife” frequently co-occurs with “fork” . How strongly does that language prior pull a VLM toward "Yes" when asked whether a fork is present on a table that only has a plate and a knife? In 2024, Sicong Leng et al. ( CVPR 2024 ) proposed Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) — the mathematical twin for VLMs of Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) in image diffusion ( Episode 4 ). VCD runs two forward passes: one on the clean image v, and a second on a noise-corrupted version v' to measure the model's blind language prior, then contrasts their logits: ℓ_VCD(y) = (1 + α) · ℓ(y | v, x) − α · ℓ(y | v', x) (with α = 1.0) Figure 12: Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) logit and probability shifts measured on Qwen2.5-VL-3B on our Blackwell GPU. Image by the author. Here are the exact bfloat16 next-token logits for "Yes" vs. "No" (and their binary Softmax probabilities renormalized over {Yes, No}) measured on our GPU (m8_counting_and_vcd_hallucination): 1. Heavily Noised Image v' ( 12% image + 88% Gaussian noise — Language Prior): logit("Yes") = 25.750 · logit("No") = 26.625 → P("Yes, fork") = 29.42% (P("No") = 70.58%) 2. Degraded Image ( 22% image + 78% Gaussian noise — Standard Decoding): logit("Yes") = 25.625 · logit("No") = 27.125 → P("Yes, fork") = 18.24% (P("No") = 81.76%) 3. Degraded Image (+ VCD α = 1.0, 2 · ℓ(v_deg) − ℓ(v')): logit("Yes") = 25.500 · logit("No") = 27.625 → P("Yes, fork") = 10.67% (-41.5% reduction; P("No") = 89.33%) 4. Clean Studio Image v (Standard Decoding): logit("Yes") = 25.250 · logit("No") = 29.625 → P("Yes, fork") = 1.24% (P("No") = 98.76%) 5. Clean Studio Image v (+ VCD α = 1.0, 2 · ℓ(v) − ℓ(v')): logit("Yes") = 24.750 · logit("No") = 32.625 → P("Yes, fork") = 0.04% (~30× reduction; P("No") = 99.96% ) Look at the exact logit arithmetic (2 · ℓ(v) − ℓ(v')): Even though greedy decoding (argmax) already answers "No" across all conditions (logit("No") > logit("Yes")), corrupting the image with 88% noise (v') causes the binary probability P("Yes, fork") to jump 23.7× from 1.24% to 29.42% — directly quantifying the language prior pull. Subtracting those noisy logits (2 × 25.625 − 25.750 = 25.500 and 2 × 27.125 − 26.625 = 27.625) reduces P("Yes, fork") on the degraded image from 18.24% to 10.67% and raises P("No fork") on the clean image from 98.76% to 99.96% . Here is the 6-line PyTorch implementation of VCD: alpha = 1.0 l_v = vlm(**inputs_clean).logits[0, -1].float() # ℓ(y | v, x) l_vp = vlm(**inputs_noisy).logits[0, -1].float() # ℓ(y | v', x) l_vcd = (1.0 + alpha) * l_v - alpha * l_vp # VCD logits yes_id, no_id = ( processor.tokenizer.encode(w, add_special_tokens=False)[0] for w in ("Yes", "No") ) probs_yes_no = torch.softmax(l_vcd[[yes_id, no_id]], dim=0) # Note: Leng et al. (CVPR 2024) also apply an adaptive plausibility mask. 10. From Photos to Video & Practical Takeaways for ML Engineers When Qwen2.5-VL switches from a static photo to a video clip , two things happen: Conv3d [2, 14, 14] Temporal Tubes: Rather than duplicating a single photo, the Conv3d patchifier pairs 2 consecutive video frames into each 2 × 14 × 14 tube, halving the token count across time. Absolute-Time M-RoPE ( second_per_grid_t): The 16 Time (t) rotary frequency pairs in mrope_section = [16, 24, 24] advance in proportion to real-world timestamps (second_per_grid_t × tokens_per_second), so a 2-second interval receives the same temporal rotation angle regardless of the video's sampling frame rate. Figure 13: Three-stage Vision-Language Model recap and preview of Episode 6 (How Video Generation AI Actually Works). Image by the author. 4 Rules When Building with Vision-Language Models in Production Preserve Native Aspect Ratio & Resolution for OCR: Downsampling a 1120 × 280 receipt to 25 tokens flipped 4829 into 4857. Set min_pixels and max_pixels in AutoProcessor appropriately for document tasks. Don’t Trust Direct VLM Object Counts Above ~5 Overlapping Items: Because the 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger compresses 28 × 28 px regions into single tokens before the LLM, dense overlapping objects (N = 8 or 15 circles) should be routed through an explicit detection/segmentation tool or tiled crops. Treat Text Inside Images as an Untrusted Prompt-Injection Surface: VLMs read text inside images accurately — which fixes CLIP’s "iPod" classification bug, but creates a visual prompt injection vector where adversarial instructions printed on an object enter the LLM's context window. Use Contrastive Decoding Selectively: VCD widens the margin against language-prior hallucinations (98.76% → 99.96%), at the cost of 2× inference compute (two forward passes per token). Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) 1. Why does an “iPod” sticker on an apple fool OpenAI CLIP? OpenAI CLIP compresses an entire image into a single 512-dimensional vector and multiplies image-text cosine similarities by a learned temperature of 100.0 before Softmax. Multimodal neurons inside CLIP respond strongly to printed text, pushing the "iPod" cosine (0.2701) slightly above "Green Apple" (0.2641), which the ×100.0 Softmax turns into a 64.51% iPod prediction. 2. Why are there 1,600 patches of 1,280 dimensions in Qwen2.5-VL? On a 560 × 560 pixel image sliced with a 14 × 14 pixel patch size, 560 ÷ 14 = 40 patches per side, giving 40 × 40 = 1,600 patches (sequence length N). Each patch is projected into a 1,280-dimensional feature vector (D), forming a [1,600 × 1,280] tensor before the 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger compresses it 4× into 400 tokens of 2,048 dimensions . 3. How does 3D M-RoPE ([16, 24, 24]) work in Qwen2.5-VL? Each attention head in Qwen2.5-VL (head_dim = 128, or 64 rotary frequency pairs) splits its 64 frequency pairs into 16 pairs for Time ( t) , 24 pairs for Height ( h, Row y) , and 24 pairs for Width ( w, Column x) . For 1D text tokens, t = h = w; for 2D images, t stays constant while h and w track row and column coordinates; for 3D video, t advances with real timestamps. 4. What is Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD)? Visual Contrastive Decoding (Leng et al., CVPR 2024) reduces object hallucinations in Vision-Language Models by subtracting the next-token logits of a noise-corrupted image v' from the logits of the clean image v: ℓ_VCD(y) = (1 + α)ℓ(y | v, x) − αℓ(y | v', x). This suppresses answers driven purely by English word co-occurrence priors (such as assuming a fork is next to a plate and knife). Models: openai/clip-vit-base-patch32, google/siglip-base-patch16-224, and Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct via HuggingFace transformers. Protocol: All VLM generations use deterministic greedy decoding (do_sample=False, n = 1 run per condition). Attention telemetry in Sections 7–8 was captured with attn_implementation="eager" on a single teacher-forced pass. All test images (apple_clean.jpg, apple_ipod.jpg, apple_pizza.jpg, fox_clean.jpg, clock_1010.jpg, plate_knife_no_fork.jpg, wide_receipt_pin.jpg) are synthetic studio renders generated for controlled testing. Why an “iPod” sticker fools OpenAI CLIP (64.5%) while Qwen2.5-VL reads it cleanly — measured layer by layer on a 96 GB Blackwell GPU.

By Latent AI Labs (@LatentAILabs)

TL;DR — How Do Vision-Language Models (VLMs) Actually See Images?
Modern Vision-Language Models (such as Qwen2.5-VL, GPT-4o, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet) process images in three stages:
1. Vision Transformer (ViT) Patch Slicer & 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger: A 560 × 560 RGB photograph (940,800 floats) is sliced by a 14 × 14 pixel grid into 40 × 40 = 1,600 patches, projected into 1,280-dimensional vectors, refined through 28 local-window ViT layers (112 × 112 px) and 4 global full-attention layers (Layers 7, 15, 23, 31), and compressed 4-into-1 by a 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger into 400 Visual Word tokens (2,048-D) — cutting LLM self-attention pairs 16× (2.56M → 160K).
2. Dual Spatial Compass (2D ViT RoPE + 3D M-RoPE [16t, 24h, 24w]): Each attention head splits its 64 rotary position frequency pairs into 16 Time (t), 24 Height (h / Row y), and 24 Width (w / Column x) dials so a 1D language model natively understands 2D aspect ratios (NaViT) and 3D video timelines.
3. Cross-Modal Attention & Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD): In Layers 17–28, cross-modal grounding heads concentrate up to 96.8%–99.8% of their visual attention onto the target object quadrant, while Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) subtracts noisy-image language priors (ℓ_VCD = (1+α)ℓ(v) − αℓ(v')) to reduce object hallucinations by 41.5%.

In 2021, Gabriel Goh and colleagues at OpenAI demonstrated a famous vulnerability in computer vision known as a typographic attack: stick a paper label reading “iPod” onto a green Granny Smith apple, and OpenAI’s CLIP classifies the piece of fruit as an electronic music player.

We rebuilt that experiment with a synthetic studio photograph of a green apple and a digital label, and ran it through OpenAI CLIP (openai/clip-vit-base-patch32), Google SigLIP (google/siglip-base-patch16-224), and Alibaba Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct on a 96 GB NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU:

  • Clean Green Apple: CLIP predicts “a photo of a green Granny Smith apple” at 100.00% (cosine = 0.3302), with 0.00% for "a photo of an iPod electronic music player" (cosine = 0.2033).
  • Apple + "iPod" Label: "Green Apple" drops to 35.47% (cosine = 0.2641), and "iPod" takes first place at 64.51% (cosine = 0.2701).
  • Apple + "Pizza" Label: "Green Apple" drops to 19.86% (cosine = 0.2591), and "Pizza" takes first place at 80.07% (cosine = 0.2730).
Figure 1: GPU measurement of the "iPod" typographic attack on OpenAI CLIP (64.51% iPod) vs. Qwen2.5-VL-3B on a 96 GB NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU. Image by the author; source apple photo AI-generated with a digital label.

Yet when we feed those exact same labeled photographs into a modern 3-billion-parameter Vision-Language Model (Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct) and ask what object is in the photo and what word is printed on the sticker, it separates the physical fruit from the text:

On the "iPod" apple (1,342.7 ms cold start): "This is an apple, and the word written on the paper sticker is 'iPod.'"
On the "Pizza" apple (240.7 ms warm inference): "This is an apple with a paper sticker that says 'Pizza.'"

Even more intriguing: that same Vision-Language Model reads a 4-digit security code (PIN: 4829) off a wide 1120 × 280 shipping manifest accurately, yet looks at a clean geometric diagram of 15 overlapping circles and counts "12".

Why does a printed word hijack CLIP? How does a 1D language model — built to predict the next token in a sequence — represent 2D photographs and 3D video? And why does a model that can read fine print fail to count 15 rings?

We hooked directly into Qwen2.5-VL-3B’s 32-layer Vision Transformer (ViT) and 36-layer Language Model on our Blackwell GPU to measure the tensors, cosine similarities, positional IDs, and attention weights layer by layer (watch the companion 25-minute animated video on YouTube here).

https://medium.com/media/3d3907e7090805703a8975dee4fce162/hrefFigure 2: How the Vision Transformer slices a 560×560px photograph by a 14×14px grid into 40×40 = 1,600 patches. Image by the author.Experiment 0. Why Does an “iPod” Sticker Fool CLIP? (The ×100.0 Temperature Multiplier)

Direct Answer: OpenAI CLIP compresses an entire image into a single 512-dimensional vector and multiplies raw image-text cosine similarities by a learned temperature scale of 100.0 (exp(4.6052)) before applying Softmax. Because written text in web images strongly predicts captions, OCR features from the "iPod" sticker nudge the "iPod" cosine just +0.0060 above "Green Apple" (0.2701 vs. 0.2641), which the ×100.0 Softmax amplifies into a 64.51% vs. 35.47% victory.

Here are the exact cosine similarities (cos(θ) = (I · T) / (‖I‖ ‖T‖)) and Softmax probabilities recorded on our GPU for apple_ipod.jpg across all five candidate prompts:

  • 1. "a photo of an iPod electronic music player"
    Cosine: 0.2701 → Scaled Logit (100 × cos): 27.01 → Softmax Probability: 64.51%
  • 2. "a photo of a green Granny Smith apple"
    Cosine: 0.2641 → Scaled Logit (100 × cos): 26.41 → Softmax Probability: 35.47%
  • 3. "a photo of an analog wall clock"
    Cosine: 0.1849 → Scaled Logit (100 × cos): 18.49 → Softmax Probability: 0.01%
  • 4. "a photo of a slice of pizza"
    Cosine: 0.1718 → Scaled Logit (100 × cos): 17.18 → Softmax Probability: 0.00%
  • 5. "a photo of a red fox in the snow"
    Cosine: 0.1106 → Scaled Logit (100 × cos): 11.06 → Softmax Probability: 0.00%
P(iPod) = exp(27.01) / (exp(27.01) + exp(26.41) + ...)
        ≈ 1 / (1 + exp(-0.60)) = 64.57%
        (64.51% exact across all 5 prompts using unrounded GPU logits)

Because CLIP pools the entire photograph into one 512-D vector, features representing green apple skin and OCR features representing the letters i-P-o-d compete inside one shared bottleneck (Goh et al., Distill 2021).

You can reproduce this measurement in PyTorch:

import torch
from PIL import Image
from transformers import CLIPModel, CLIPProcessor
model = CLIPModel.from_pretrained("openai/clip-vit-base-patch32").eval()
proc = CLIPProcessor.from_pretrained("openai/clip-vit-base-patch32")
prompts = [
    "a photo of a green Granny Smith apple",
    "a photo of an iPod electronic music player",
    "a photo of a slice of pizza",
    "a photo of an analog wall clock",
    "a photo of a red fox in the snow",
]
inp = proc(
    text=prompts,
    images=Image.open("apple_ipod.jpg"),
    return_tensors="pt",
    padding=True,
)
with torch.no_grad():
    out = model(**inp)
cos = out.logits_per_image / model.logit_scale.exp()  # [0.2641, 0.2701, ...]
probs = out.logits_per_image.softmax(dim=-1) * 100    # [35.47%, 64.51%, ...]

A modern Vision-Language Model (VLM) avoids this single-vector bottleneck by keeping the image as hundreds of spatial patch tokens, allowing the language model to attend separately to the fruit and to the sticker.

1. How Does a Vision Transformer (ViT) Turn Pixels into Patch Tokens?

Direct Answer: A Vision Transformer (ViT) divides an image of resolution H × W by a fixed patch size P × P (14 × 14 pixels in Qwen2.5-VL) to produce a grid of (H/P) × (W/P) spatial patches. For a 560 × 560 image, 560 ÷ 14 = 40, yielding 40 × 40 = 1,600 patches (the sequence length N). A learned linear projection maps the raw RGB pixel values inside each patch into a 1,280-dimensional embedding vector (the feature dimension D), creating a [1,600 × 1,280] ViT input tensor.

In classical digital image processing, computer vision slid local 3×3 filters (such as adaptive or Sobel edge filters) across an image pixel by pixel. In 2020, Alexey Dosovitskiy et al. ("An Image is Worth 16×16 Words", ICLR 2021) replaced convolutional hierarchies by slicing an image into non-overlapping patches and projecting each patch into a Transformer token.

We hooked into the Vision Transformer (vlm.visual) inside Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct on our GPU as it processed a 560 × 560 RGB image (940,800 float values; center pixel (280, 280) = RGB [147, 132, 157], orange fur (140, 220) = [149, 106, 72], snow (480, 280) = [180, 195, 224]):

1. The 14×14 Spatial Grid (560 ÷ 14 = 40):
Qwen2.5-VL uses a 14 × 14 pixel patch size. Dividing 560 px ÷ 14 px gives 40 patches across and 40 patches down, or 40 × 40 = 1,600 spatial patches (image_grid_thw = [[1, 40, 40]]).

2. Patch Unrolling (588 Spatial RGB Values / 1,176 with Temporal Duplication):
A single 14 × 14 RGB square holds 14 × 14 × 3 = 588 pixel values. Under the hood, because Qwen2.5-VL uses a unified 3D patchifier (Conv3d with temporal_patch_size = 2) for both photos and video, a static photograph is duplicated across 2 temporal frames so each tube input has 2 × 14 × 14 × 3 = 1,176 values (pixel_values.shape = [1600, 1176]).

3. Linear Patch Projection (→ 1,280-D):
The learned projection matrix maps each patch into a 1,280-dimensional visual embedding vector. Keep the two dimensions distinct: 1,600 is the number of patches N in the 40 × 40 grid, while 1,280 is the feature vector length D inside each single patch, forming the [1,600 × 1,280] ViT tensor (L2 norm = 417.01).

Figure 3: Multiplying each patch by the learned projection matrix produces a 1,280-D vector; stacking all 1,600 patches forms the [1,600 × 1,280] ViT tensor. Image by the author.2. How Do Patches Talk? Windowed vs. Global ViT Attention ([7, 15, 23, 31])

Direct Answer: Running full self-attention across 1,600 patches on all 32 ViT layers would require 1,600² = 2.56 million pairs per layer. To keep compute linear in image size, Qwen2.5-VL restricts 28 of its 32 ViT layers to local 112 × 112 pixel windows (8 × 8 = 64 patches per window) and runs full global self-attention only at 4 checkpoint layers (Layers 7, 15, 23, and 31, 0-indexed).

  • 28 Windowed Attention Layers (112 × 112 px Local Windows):
    Patches only attend within their local 8 × 8 patch neighborhood (64 patches). Because window size is fixed, compute scales linearly O(N) with pixel count.
  • 4 Global Full-Attention Checkpoints (0-indexed Layers 7, 15, 23, 31):
    At every 8th layer (fullatt_block_indexes = [7, 15, 23, 31]), window walls are removed and all 1,600 patches attend across the entire image (2.56M pairs), integrating global scene geometry.
Figure 4: Windowed vs. Global ViT attention layers and pairwise cosine similarity distribution of the resulting visual tokens. Image by the author.

Across the 400 merged visual tokens exiting the vision tower ([400, 2048], including the diagonal), we measured the pairwise cosine similarity distribution:

  • 10th percentile (p10): 0.1398 (82.0° apart)
  • Median pair (p50): 0.2886 (73.2° apart)
  • 90th percentile (p90): 0.5567 (56.2° apart)
  • 99th percentile (p99): 0.8225 (34.7° tight cluster)
3. CLIP Softmax vs. Google SigLIP Sigmoid: How Vision Models Align with Text

Direct Answer: OpenAI CLIP aligns images and text using a batch Softmax (InfoNCE) loss (Softmax(100 · I_i · T_j)), which requires normalizing across every negative example in the batch. Google SigLIP (Zhai et al., ICCV 2023) replaces the batch Softmax with an independent pairwise Sigmoid (1 / (1 + exp(-117.33 · I_i · T_j + 12.93))), turning every (Image_i, Text_j) pair into a standalone binary classification problem with zero global batch normalization.

We evaluated both openai/clip-vit-base-patch32 and google/siglip-base-patch16-224 across 5 studio images (Green Apple, 10:10 Clock, Red Fox, Plate & Knife, Vault Receipt) and their 5 matching captions on our GPU (m3_clip_vs_siglip_5x5):

Figure 5: Contrastive image-text alignment in CLIP vs. Google SigLIP's independent pairwise sigmoid equation. Image by the author.Measured GPU Comparison: OpenAI CLIP vs. Google SigLIP
  • Scoring Equation & Learned Parameters:
    • OpenAI CLIP (ViT-B/32): Softmax(100.0 · I_i · T_j) (scale = 100.0, no bias)
    • Google SigLIP (ViT-B/16-224): 1 / (1 + exp(-117.33 · I_i · T_j + 12.93)) (scale = 117.33, bias = -12.93)
  • 5×5 Diagonal Cosine Similarities (Apple, Clock, Fox, Plate, Receipt):
    • OpenAI CLIP: 0.3464, 0.3507, 0.3344, 0.3023, 0.2723
    • Google SigLIP: 0.1111, 0.0687, 0.1633, 0.1591, 0.1414
  • 5×5 Diagonal Match Probabilities:
    • OpenAI CLIP (Softmax over 5 captions): 100.0%, 100.0%, 100.0%, 100.0%, 99.99% (max off-diagonal: 0.01%)
    • Google SigLIP (Independent Sigmoid): 52.44% (Apple; 97.57% on "Granny Smith" prompt), 0.84% (Clock), 99.83% (Fox), 99.72% (Plate), 97.47% (Receipt) — and 0.00% across all 20 off-diagonal cells!
  • Typographic Attack Robustness:
    • On "iPod" Apple: CLIP flips to 64.51% iPod (35.47% Apple). SigLIP predicts 40.29% Apple vs. 0.97% iPod.
    • On "Pizza" Apple: CLIP flips to 80.07% Pizza (19.86% Apple). SigLIP predicts 18.07% Apple vs. 3.13% Pizza.

Two key engineering takeaways emerge from these numbers:

  1. Why SigLIP Resisted the "iPod" and "Pizza" Labels: Even if we convert SigLIP's raw logits back into a Softmax over the candidate labels, "Green Apple" still wins at ~98.6% — showing that SigLIP's robustness comes from its learned ViT-B/16 representations and WebLI training recipe rather than the sigmoid readout alone.
  2. Why SigLIP Scored the 10:10 Clock Caption at 0.84%: Because SigLIP learns a strong negative bias (-12.93) so non-matching pairs default to 0.00%, an image-text pair must exceed a cosine threshold of 12.93 / 117.33 = 0.1102 to cross 50% probability. On our descriptive clock caption, SigLIP's cosine was 0.0687 (still the highest in its row, well above all off-diagonals at ≤ 0.004), which maps to 0.84% under the uncalibrated sigmoid threshold.
4. How Does the 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger Cut LLM Attention by 16×?

Direct Answer: Feeding all 1,600 ViT patches directly into a 36-layer language model would require 1,600² = 2,560,000 self-attention pairs per layer. To compress the visual sequence before Layer 0 of the LLM, Qwen2.5-VL uses a 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger (vlm.visual.merger) that concatenates every 2 × 2 block of adjacent 14 × 14 px patches (4 × 1,280 = 5,120-D) and projects it through a 2-layer MLP into a single 2,048-D Visual Word token. This reduces token count 4× (1,600 → 400) and cuts quadratic self-attention compute 4² = 16× (2.56M → 160K pairs).

Figure 6: The 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger concatenates each 2×2 block of 14×14px patches into a 5,120-D vector and projects it through a 2-layer MLP into one 2,048-D Visual Word token. Image by the author.
  1. Concatenate 2×2 Spatial Neighbors (4 → 1):
    Four adjacent 14 × 14 px patches covering a 28 × 28 px square are normalized with RMSNorm and concatenated into a 5,120-dimensional vector.
  2. 2-Layer MLP Projection (5,120-D → 2,048-D):
    A 2-layer MLP (Linear(5120 → 5120) → GELU → Linear(5120 → 2048)) maps each 5,120-D block into the exact 2,048-dimensional embedding space of the Qwen2.5-3B language model.

You can inspect these exact tensor shapes in 10 lines of Python:

from transformers import AutoConfig
cfg = AutoConfig.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct")
v = cfg.vision_config
print(v.patch_size, v.temporal_patch_size, v.spatial_merge_size)
# -> 14  2  2
print(v.window_size, v.fullatt_block_indexes, v.hidden_size, v.out_hidden_size)
# -> 112  [7, 15, 23, 31]  1280  2048
feats = {}
vlm.visual.merger.register_forward_hook(
    lambda m, inp, out: feats.update(pre=inp[0].shape, post=out.shape)
)
# 560x560 image -> pre: [1600, 1280], post: [400, 2048]
5. Native Dynamic Resolution (NaViT) vs. Downscaled Square Input

Direct Answer: Early vision models forced every image into a fixed 224 × 224 square, distorting aspect ratios and blurring small text. Native Dynamic Resolution (Patch n' Pack / NaViT, Dehghani et al., NeurIPS 2023) slices images at their native aspect ratio and pixel resolution (rounded to multiples of 28 px), preserving fine OCR details on wide banners and tall documents.

We tested a wide 1120 × 280 (4:1 aspect ratio) shipping manifest containing tensors_bf16 = 96.0 GB and VAULT PIN: 4829 on our GPU (m4_dynamic_resolution_ocr) under two regimes:

Figure 7: Downscaling a 1120×280 manifest into a 140×140 square (25 visual tokens) blurs the digits into "4857", whereas Native Dynamic Resolution (80×20 raw patches → 400 visual tokens) reads "4829" and "96.0 GB". Image by the author.
  • Regime 1 — Downscaled Square (140 × 140 px, 1:1 aspect ratio, 16× fewer pixels):
    Produces 10 × 10 = 100 raw patches → 25 merged visual tokens (5 × 5) in 452.2 ms.
    VLM Output: "The exact 4-digit VAULT PIN printed in the bottom right box is 4857. The tensors_bf16 value is 2." (Incorrect — fine digits blurred!)
  • Regime 2 — Native Dynamic Resolution (1120 × 280 px, 4:1 original aspect ratio):
    Produces 80 × 20 = 1,600 raw patches → 400 merged visual tokens (40 × 10) in 570.9 ms.
    VLM Output: "The exact 4-digit VAULT PIN printed in the bottom right box is 4829. The tensors_bf16 value is 96.0 GB." (Exact match!)

(Methodology note: shrinking 1120 × 280 to 140 × 140 reduces pixel count by 16× alongside the 4:1 → 1:1 aspect crush, showing why allocating 400 native-aspect tokens is critical for document OCR.)

6. How Does a 1D Language Model Understand 2D Space? (3D M-RoPE [16, 24, 24])

Direct Answer: Standard Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) encodes a single 1D sequence index m across all 64 complex frequency pairs of an attention head (head_dim = 128). 3D Multimodal RoPE (M-RoPE) partitions those 64 frequency pairs into three independent coordinate sections — 16 pairs for Time (t), 24 pairs for Height (h / Row y), and 24 pairs for Width (w / Column x) (16 + 24 + 24 = 64 pairs) — stamping every visual token with its exact 3D (t, h, w) coordinate.

3D M-RoPE Partition Inside Every Attention Head (head_dim = 128 -> 64 pairs)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
mrope_section = [ 16 pairs (32D) , 24 pairs (48D) , 24 pairs (48D) ]
                  └── TIME (t) ──┘ └─ HEIGHT (h) ─┘ └─ WIDTH (w) ──┘

We hooked into vlm.model.get_rope_index (position_ids of shape [3, 1, seq_len]) on our GPU (m5_mrope_3d_coordinates) and recorded the exact position IDs for text vs. image tokens:

Figure 8: Live GPU trace of the [3, 1, N] M-RoPE position_ids tensor and the Dual Spatial Compass (2D RoPE inside the 32-layer ViT + 3D M-RoPE inside the 36-layer LLM). Image by the author.
  • 1D Text Prompt Tokens (Tokens 0..4):
    All three coordinates step together (t = h = w = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]), making M-RoPE mathematically identical to standard 1D RoPE on text.
  • 2D Image Tokens (Starting at position 15, Row 0, Cols 0..7):
    • time_t = [15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15] (frozen across the entire static photograph)
    • height_h = [15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15] (frozen at 15 across Row 0; increments to 16 on Row 1, up to 34 on Row 19)
    • width_w = [15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22] (increments left-to-right across the columns of Row 0)
A Surprising Null Result: Why Flipping Only the LLM’s M-RoPE Didn’t Swap the Image

What happens if we leave the 400 visual token vectors untouched, but intercept vlm.model.get_rope_index in-flight and invert the LLM's Height and Width position IDs (h ← 49 - h, w ← 49 - w) on our 4-quadrant composite image (Top-Left: Apple, Top-Right: Clock, Bottom-Left: Fox, Bottom-Right: Plate & Knife)?

We expected the LLM’s spatial answers to swap completely. They didn’t:

  • Normal M-RoPE: “In the top-left corner of the image, there is an apple. In the bottom-right corner, there is a plate with a knife next to it.”
  • Inverted LLM M-RoPE (h, w flipped): "In the top-left corner of the image, there is an apple. In the bottom-right corner, there is a knife." (Flipping width_w alone also left "top-left: apple, top-right: clock" unchanged!)

Why didn’t inverting the LLM’s 3D M-RoPE move the apple to the bottom-right?
Because as shown in Figure 8, Qwen2.5-VL actually uses a Dual Spatial Compass:

  1. Before the tokens ever reach the LLM, the 32-layer Vision Transformer (vlm.visual.rotary_pos_emb) applies its own 2D RoPE across all 4 global full-attention layers ([7, 15, 23, 31]).
  2. Those 4 global ViT layers bake each patch’s 2D quadrant context directly into the 2,048-D feature vectors, and the tokens enter the LLM in raster-scan order (v_001 ... v_400). Flipping only the LLM's M-RoPE position IDs after the ViT has already encoded spatial position creates a slight feature conflict ("plate with a knife" → "a knife"), but the ViT's baked-in spatial features still dominate!
7. Cross-Modal Attention: Where Noun Tokens Look Across the 36 LLM Layers

Direct Answer: In Qwen2.5-VL-3B’s 36-layer language model (576 total attention heads), middle-to-upper layers (Layers 17–28) contain heads that route visual information from specific image regions to corresponding text nouns, focusing up to 96.8%–99.8% of their visual attention mass onto the target object's quadrant during teacher-forced evaluation.

Using attn_implementation="eager" on our 4-quadrant composite image (m6_cross_modal_grounding), we ran a teacher-forced forward pass naming each quadrant's object ("...top-left is a green apple, top-right is a wall clock, bottom-left is a red fox, and bottom-right is a dinner plate") and searched across Layers 14–29 (256 heads, 0-indexed) for the heads that concentrated the highest share of their visual attention onto each noun's target 10 × 10 quadrant (25% of the image area):

Figure 9: Cross-modal attention heatmaps from the highest-scoring heads in Layers 17–28 of Qwen2.5-VL-3B on our 4-quadrant test image. Image by the author.
  • "apple" (Token #462, Top-Left Quadrant):
    Peak Head: Layer 17 · Head 10 (99.76% of visual attention on Top-Left) · Filtered Ensemble (>45% heads): 78.70%
  • "clock" (Token #469, Top-Right Quadrant):
    Peak Head: Layer 21 · Head 14 (96.78% of visual attention on Top-Right) · Filtered Ensemble (>45% heads): 73.76%
  • "fox" (Token #476, Bottom-Left Quadrant):
    Peak Head: Layer 27 · Head 1 (98.96% of visual attention on Bottom-Left) · Filtered Ensemble (>45% heads): 83.15%
  • "plate" (Token #484, Bottom-Right Quadrant):
    Peak Head: Layer 28 · Head 10 (99.29% of visual attention on Bottom-Right) · Filtered Ensemble (>45% heads): 83.10%

(Methodology note: Because these peak heads are selected as the maximum across 256 middle-layer heads on a teacher-forced sentence that names each corner prior to the noun, and the ensemble averages heads already exceeding a 45% target-quadrant share, these heatmaps represent upper-bound spatial localization in Layers 17–28.)

8. Attention Sinks & Visual Token Sparsity Across All 36 Layers

Direct Answer: Averaging attention across all 16 heads per layer from Layer 0 to Layer 35 (m7_36layer_attention_telemetry) shows that visual tokens receive only 2.5% to 31.2% of total attention per layer (peaking at 31.18% on Layer 21), while text and initial Attention Sink tokens (Tokens 0..3) absorb the rest. Within the visual attention distribution in Layers 17–35, the top 15% of visual tokens (60 of 400 patches) capture 55.9% to 81.15% of all visual attention mass (peaking at 81.15% on Layer 27).

Figure 10: Measured 36-layer attention allocation across text tokens, initial sink tokens, and visual tokens in Qwen2.5-VL-3B. Image by the author.
  1. Layers 0–2 (Prompt Text Parsing):
    89.54% to 94.65% of attention stays on the text tokens, while visual tokens receive only 4.17% to 8.14% and the first 4 sink tokens receive 1.18% to 2.32%.
  2. Layers 3–9 (Attention Sink Parking):
    Just as in text LLMs (Episode 3), 56.36% to 69.41% of total attention mass parks on the first 4 tokens of the sequence (peaking at 69.41% on Layer 5), while visual tokens receive only 2.47% to 5.12%.
  3. Layers 17–33 (Visual Readout & Sparsity):
    Visual attention rises to 31.18% on Layer 21 (24.37% on Layer 27). Across Layers 17–35, the top 15% of visual tokens (60 out of 400 patches) hold 55.9% to 81.15% of all visual attention mass (vs. 15.0% if uniform), explaining why token-pruning methods like FastV can drop low-attention background tokens in upper layers with minimal accuracy loss.
9. Why VLMs Miscount Overlapping Objects & How Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) WorksA. Why Does Qwen2.5-VL Count “12” When Shown 15 Overlapping Circles?

We fed three 504 × 504 geometric diagrams of overlapping colored rings (36 × 36 raw patches → 18 × 18 = 324 merged visual tokens) into Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct (m8_counting_and_vcd_hallucination):

Figure 11: Qwen2.5-VL-3B counts N=4 circles correctly ("4"), but answers "6" for N=8 and "12" for N=15. Image by the author.
  • N = 4 Circles (86.7 ms): VLM outputs "4" (Correct).
  • N = 8 Circles (83.6 ms): VLM outputs "6" (Under-counts by 2).
  • N = 15 Circles (96.9 ms): VLM outputs "12" (Under-counts by 3).

A plausible architectural contributor to this failure is the 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger from Section 4: when 15 rings pass through a tight central rosette, multiple ring intersections fall inside the same 28 × 28 px merged token and are mixed by the MLP before the language model begins counting.

B. How Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) Suppresses Language Priors

In English text corpora, “a white dinner plate and a silver knife” frequently co-occurs with “fork”. How strongly does that language prior pull a VLM toward "Yes" when asked whether a fork is present on a table that only has a plate and a knife?

In 2024, Sicong Leng et al. (CVPR 2024) proposed Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) — the mathematical twin for VLMs of Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) in image diffusion (Episode 4). VCD runs two forward passes: one on the clean image v, and a second on a noise-corrupted version v' to measure the model's blind language prior, then contrasts their logits:

ℓ_VCD(y) = (1 + α) · ℓ(y | v, x)  −  α · ℓ(y | v', x)      (with α = 1.0)
Figure 12: Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD) logit and probability shifts measured on Qwen2.5-VL-3B on our Blackwell GPU. Image by the author.

Here are the exact bfloat16 next-token logits for "Yes" vs. "No" (and their binary Softmax probabilities renormalized over {Yes, No}) measured on our GPU (m8_counting_and_vcd_hallucination):

  • 1. Heavily Noised Image v' (12% image + 88% Gaussian noise — Language Prior):
    logit("Yes") = 25.750 · logit("No") = 26.625 → P("Yes, fork") = 29.42% (P("No") = 70.58%)
  • 2. Degraded Image (22% image + 78% Gaussian noise — Standard Decoding):
    logit("Yes") = 25.625 · logit("No") = 27.125 → P("Yes, fork") = 18.24% (P("No") = 81.76%)
  • 3. Degraded Image (+ VCD α = 1.0, 2 · ℓ(v_deg) − ℓ(v')):
    logit("Yes") = 25.500 · logit("No") = 27.625 → P("Yes, fork") = 10.67% (-41.5% reduction; P("No") = 89.33%)
  • 4. Clean Studio Image v (Standard Decoding):
    logit("Yes") = 25.250 · logit("No") = 29.625 → P("Yes, fork") = 1.24% (P("No") = 98.76%)
  • 5. Clean Studio Image v (+ VCD α = 1.0, 2 · ℓ(v) − ℓ(v')):
    logit("Yes") = 24.750 · logit("No") = 32.625 → P("Yes, fork") = 0.04% (~30× reduction; P("No") = 99.96%)

Look at the exact logit arithmetic (2 · ℓ(v) − ℓ(v')):

  • Even though greedy decoding (argmax) already answers "No" across all conditions (logit("No") > logit("Yes")), corrupting the image with 88% noise (v') causes the binary probability P("Yes, fork") to jump 23.7× from 1.24% to 29.42% — directly quantifying the language prior pull.
  • Subtracting those noisy logits (2 × 25.625 − 25.750 = 25.500 and 2 × 27.125 − 26.625 = 27.625) reduces P("Yes, fork") on the degraded image from 18.24% to 10.67% and raises P("No fork") on the clean image from 98.76% to 99.96%.

Here is the 6-line PyTorch implementation of VCD:

alpha = 1.0
l_v = vlm(**inputs_clean).logits[0, -1].float()      # ℓ(y | v, x)
l_vp = vlm(**inputs_noisy).logits[0, -1].float()     # ℓ(y | v', x)
l_vcd = (1.0 + alpha) * l_v - alpha * l_vp           # VCD logits
yes_id, no_id = (
    processor.tokenizer.encode(w, add_special_tokens=False)[0]
    for w in ("Yes", "No")
)
probs_yes_no = torch.softmax(l_vcd[[yes_id, no_id]], dim=0)
# Note: Leng et al. (CVPR 2024) also apply an adaptive plausibility mask.
10. From Photos to Video & Practical Takeaways for ML Engineers

When Qwen2.5-VL switches from a static photo to a video clip, two things happen:

  1. Conv3d [2, 14, 14] Temporal Tubes: Rather than duplicating a single photo, the Conv3d patchifier pairs 2 consecutive video frames into each 2 × 14 × 14 tube, halving the token count across time.
  2. Absolute-Time M-RoPE (second_per_grid_t): The 16 Time (t) rotary frequency pairs in mrope_section = [16, 24, 24] advance in proportion to real-world timestamps (second_per_grid_t × tokens_per_second), so a 2-second interval receives the same temporal rotation angle regardless of the video's sampling frame rate.
Figure 13: Three-stage Vision-Language Model recap and preview of Episode 6 (How Video Generation AI Actually Works). Image by the author.4 Rules When Building with Vision-Language Models in Production
  1. Preserve Native Aspect Ratio & Resolution for OCR: Downsampling a 1120 × 280 receipt to 25 tokens flipped 4829 into 4857. Set min_pixels and max_pixels in AutoProcessor appropriately for document tasks.
  2. Don’t Trust Direct VLM Object Counts Above ~5 Overlapping Items: Because the 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger compresses 28 × 28 px regions into single tokens before the LLM, dense overlapping objects (N = 8 or 15 circles) should be routed through an explicit detection/segmentation tool or tiled crops.
  3. Treat Text Inside Images as an Untrusted Prompt-Injection Surface: VLMs read text inside images accurately — which fixes CLIP’s "iPod" classification bug, but creates a visual prompt injection vector where adversarial instructions printed on an object enter the LLM's context window.
  4. Use Contrastive Decoding Selectively: VCD widens the margin against language-prior hallucinations (98.76% → 99.96%), at the cost of 2× inference compute (two forward passes per token).
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)1. Why does an “iPod” sticker on an apple fool OpenAI CLIP?

OpenAI CLIP compresses an entire image into a single 512-dimensional vector and multiplies image-text cosine similarities by a learned temperature of 100.0 before Softmax. Multimodal neurons inside CLIP respond strongly to printed text, pushing the "iPod" cosine (0.2701) slightly above "Green Apple" (0.2641), which the ×100.0 Softmax turns into a 64.51% iPod prediction.

2. Why are there 1,600 patches of 1,280 dimensions in Qwen2.5-VL?

On a 560 × 560 pixel image sliced with a 14 × 14 pixel patch size, 560 ÷ 14 = 40 patches per side, giving 40 × 40 = 1,600 patches (sequence length N). Each patch is projected into a 1,280-dimensional feature vector (D), forming a [1,600 × 1,280] tensor before the 2×2 Spatial Patch Merger compresses it 4× into 400 tokens of 2,048 dimensions.

3. How does 3D M-RoPE ([16, 24, 24]) work in Qwen2.5-VL?

Each attention head in Qwen2.5-VL (head_dim = 128, or 64 rotary frequency pairs) splits its 64 frequency pairs into 16 pairs for Time (t), 24 pairs for Height (h, Row y), and 24 pairs for Width (w, Column x). For 1D text tokens, t = h = w; for 2D images, t stays constant while h and w track row and column coordinates; for 3D video, t advances with real timestamps.

4. What is Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD)?

Visual Contrastive Decoding (Leng et al., CVPR 2024) reduces object hallucinations in Vision-Language Models by subtracting the next-token logits of a noise-corrupted image v' from the logits of the clean image v: ℓ_VCD(y) = (1 + α)ℓ(y | v, x) − αℓ(y | v', x). This suppresses answers driven purely by English word co-occurrence priors (such as assuming a fork is next to a plate and knife).

How We Measured (Reproducibility & Disclosure Box)
  • Hardware: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (96.0 GB VRAM, bfloat16 for Qwen2.5-VL-3B, float32 for CLIP / SigLIP).
  • Models: openai/clip-vit-base-patch32, google/siglip-base-patch16-224, and Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct via HuggingFace transformers.
  • Protocol: All VLM generations use deterministic greedy decoding (do_sample=False, n = 1 run per condition). Attention telemetry in Sections 7–8 was captured with attn_implementation="eager" on a single teacher-forced pass. All test images (apple_clean.jpg, apple_ipod.jpg, apple_pizza.jpg, fox_clean.jpg, clock_1010.jpg, plate_knife_no_fork.jpg, wide_receipt_pin.jpg) are synthetic studio renders generated for controlled testing.

items.title: SEO, AEO, and GEO: The New Search Strategy Every Business Needs in 2026
items.summary: How businesses can become easier to find, easier to answer, and more visible across Google and AI-powered search. Picture someone looking for a dentist. They type “ best dentist near me ” into Google. An AI-generated summary appears above the usual list of links, pulling together a few names, a couple of ratings, and a short explanation of what to look for. They read it, then ask a follow-up question right there in the results: “ which of these takes new patients without a referral. ” The answer narrows the list. They click through to one website, skim the “ New Patients ” page, and book an appointment. Four steps. Two of them never touch a traditional list of blue links. This is what searching looks like now, for a lot of people, on a lot of days, for a lot of purchases not because search changed overnight, but because it quietly picked up a few new habits. People still search. They still compare. They still click through to a real website before they trust a business with their money. But somewhere between the question and the click, an AI system is now often doing part of the thinking out loud. Which raises a fair question for any business owner: can you be found, understood, and trusted across all of these different search experiences not just the old one? That question is really what SEO, AEO, and GEO are about. Not three separate trends to chase. Three angles on the same job. Search Is Changing, But Discovery Still Matters The map keeps changing. The destination hasn’t. People still want an answer they can trust. The interface around that want has just gotten busier. Google Search still shows the familiar list of results, but it now also shows AI Overviews (short, AI-written summaries) and, for people who opt into it, AI Mode a fuller, conversational way to search. Other AI tools people lean on for research and shopping have grown up alongside it. None of this erases the basics. A business still has to be visible. It still has to explain itself clearly. It still has to earn trust. What’s different is that there are now more places where that visibility, clarity, and trust get tested sometimes by a human eye, sometimes by an AI system summarizing on a human’s behalf. That’s the practical reason SEO, AEO, and GEO are worth understanding together in 2026, not as buzzwords, but as three honest descriptions of the same underlying goal: being easy to discover, easy to understand, and easy to trust wherever someone happens to be looking. What Is SEO? SEO (Search Engine Optimization ) is, at its simplest, everything a business does to make its website easier for search engines to find, understand, and recommend to the right people. Here’s the plain-language version. Google doesn’t know your business exists just because you built a website. It has to find your pages (crawling) , figure out what they’re about and store them (indexing) , and then decide when to show them to someone searching (ranking) . SEO is everything that helps those three steps go smoothly: a fast, mobile-friendly website; clear, honest, useful content; a logical structure that both people and search engines can follow; and a reputation, built over time, that signals a business is worth recommending. A simple example: a family-owned plumbing company writes a clear, genuinely useful page about fixing a running toilet, titles it the way people actually search, and makes sure it loads quickly on a phone. Over time, Google starts showing that page to nearby people dealing with the exact same problem and some of them call the plumber instead of finishing the job themselves. SEO isn’t a trick. It’s closer to good bookkeeping for your online presence unglamorous, occasionally tedious, and the reason everything downstream actually works. What Is AEO? In digital marketing circles, three-letter acronyms tend to multiply fast, and AEO is one of the newer ones. Here’s what it actually means: AEO (Answer Engine Optimization ) is the practice of structuring content so it can directly and clearly answer the specific question someone is asking, not just rank for a general topic. Search behaviour has shifted toward full questions. People don’t just type “ running shoes ” anymore; they type “ what running shoes are best for flat feet if I’m training for a half marathon. ” A page written in vague, general terms struggles to answer that. A page that actually addresses the question clearly, near the top, without making the reader dig has a much better shot at being the answer, whether that shows up as a featured snippet, a voice assistant’s response, or a line inside an AI Overview. AEO, in other words, is about respecting the shape of the question. If a “ Services ” page never actually states the pricing structure, it can’t answer “ how much does this cost, ” no matter how well-written it is otherwise. Improving AEO means anticipating the real questions customers ask out loud, in reviews, on calls with a sales team and answering them directly on the website, instead of circling the point with marketing language. A simple example: instead of a vague headline like “ Comprehensive Dental Solutions, ” a practice writes “ Do You Accept New Patients Without a Referral? Yes! Here’s How Booking Works. ” That’s not a lesser version of good copy-writing. It’s copy-writing that respects what’s actually in someone’s head when they land on the page. What Is GEO? GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) is the newest branch of AI search optimization, and also the one most surrounded by hype. Here’s the grounded version: GEO is the practice of making a business easy for AI systems to understand, describe accurately, and reference when they generate an answer the kind of answers now showing up in AI Overviews, AI Mode, and similar AI-powered tools. When an AI system builds an answer to something like “ which agencies specialize in SaaS branding, ” it isn’t inventing facts from nothing. Modern AI-powered search generally relies on a technique called retrieval-augmented generation , or RAG the system looks up real, current web pages, reads what they actually say, and builds its answer from that. It often runs several related searches behind the scenes to cover different angles of a question, sometimes called query fan-out , before pulling everything together into one response. What that means for a business is fairly simple: if an AI system can’t find clear, accurate, well-organized information about who you are and what you do, it can’t describe you accurately and it certainly can’t recommend you. GEO is the discipline of making sure that when a system goes looking, what it finds is unambiguous. A consistent business name. Clear service descriptions. A website that explains, in plain language, what you actually do and for whom not just brand language that only makes sense to people who already know you. It’s worth being honest about the limits here, too. No agency, consultant, or tool can promise that ChatGPT, Google’s AI Mode, Gemini, or any other AI system will mention a specific business by name. These systems weigh many factors, keep changing, and can vary answer to answer, even for the same question asked twice. GEO improves the odds by making a business easy to find and easy to describe accurately. It doesn’t and shouldn’t be sold as a guarantee. SEO vs AEO vs GEO: What’s the Difference? The clearest way to see it is side by side. Strategy Main Goal What It Helps With Example SEO Get discovered Being found in search engines and shown to the right audience A bakery’s site ranks for “ custom birthday cakes [city] ” AEO Get understood Directly answering the specific question someone is asking A page clearly answers “ do you deliver cakes same-day ” GEO Get referenced Being described accurately when AI systems generate an answer An AI Overview correctly summaries what the bakery specialises in Read that table left to right and a pattern shows up: each one builds on the last. A page can’t answer a question well if no one finds it. And an AI system can’t describe a business accurately if the underlying information was never clear to begin with. These are stages of the same trip, not three separate ones. Why Businesses Should Think About SEO, AEO, and GEO Together Here’s the short version: SEO gets you found. AEO gets you understood. GEO gets you referenced. Or, as a road trip: SEO builds the road that leads to a business. AEO is the road sign that answers the driver’s question before they even have to stop and ask. GEO is what happens when the car’s GPS voice recommends that business by name, because it already knows exactly what the business does and where it is. None of these work well alone. A perfectly optimized website that never answers a real customer question is technically visible and practically useless. A brilliantly clear answer on a page nobody can find never gets read. And no AI system can describe a business accurately if its own website is vague, outdated, or inconsistent about basic facts like services offered or areas served. The businesses that do well going forward aren’t the ones treating their SEO strategy, AEO strategy, and GEO strategy as three separate checklists. They’re the ones treating all three as lenses pointed at the same question: if a stranger needed exactly what we offer, would they find us, understand us, and trust us quickly? What Are the Benefits for a Business? Done honestly, this work adds up to a handful of practical outcomes: More discoverability and stronger search engine visibility, across both traditional results and AI-powered search Clearer, more relevant organic search traffic people who land on the site already understand roughly what the business does Better answers for customers, which cuts down on confused calls, emails, and abandoned checkouts Stronger authority, built from consistent, accurate, genuinely useful information A better overall user experience, since much of this work simply makes a website easier to use Greater AI search visibility, as AI systems pull from clearer, better-organised sources More paths for leads to reach a business, instead of relying on one search results page A steadier long-term digital presence, less dependent on any single algorithm change None of this comes with a guaranteed number attached. Nobody honest can promise a specific ranking, a specific volume of traffic, or a guaranteed mention inside an AI answer and treating this work like a slot machine, rather than a foundation, tends to disappoint. What it reliably does is put a business in a stronger position to be found and chosen, consistently, over time. Does SEO Still Matter in 2026? Yes. There’s a persistent myth that AI search has made traditional SEO obsolete. It hasn’t, and the reasoning holds up. AI-powered search features like AI Overviews and AI Mode are built on top of the same core organic search ranking and quality systems that traditional search has always used they don’t run on a separate, secret rule-book. To be eligible to appear as a supporting source in an AI-generated answer, a page generally still has to meet the same basic technical requirements it always has: it needs to be properly indexed and eligible to appear in regular search results in the first place. In other words, the businesses showing up inside AI Overviews and AI Mode today are, in large part, the same ones already doing solid SEO. AEO and GEO haven’t replaced that groundwork. They’ve made it more visible why it always mattered. How Can a Business Improve Its SEO, AEO, and GEO? This doesn’t require a totally new SEO strategy overnight. It’s a set of habits, applied consistently. Step 1 (Understand your audience): Know who you’re actually trying to reach, what they care about, and what makes them hesitate before they buy. Step 2 (Research what people search and ask): Look through your own inbox, call logs, and reviews. The exact questions customers already ask out loud are usually the best AEO content a business will ever write. Step 3 (Build a strong technical foundation): A site that loads quickly, works properly on a phone, and doesn’t accidentally block search engines from crawling it. Unglamorous, and non-negotiable. Step 4 (Create genuinely useful content): Not generic, could-have-been-written-by-anyone content content shaped by real experience, the kind of thing you’d tell a customer standing in front of you. Step 5 (Answer the important questions directly): Put the real answer near the top of the page, in plain language, before the supporting detail. Step 6 (Make business information clear and consistent): Same name, same services, same locations, everywhere they appear website, Google Business Profile, directory listings. Step 7 (Build credibility over time): Reviews, case studies, press mentions, and genuine expertise all signal to people and to AI systems alike that a business is a real, trustworthy source. Step 8 (Improve usability): A confusing website undermines every other effort. If a visitor can’t find pricing or a contact page in a few seconds, nothing summarizing that site can either. Step 9 (Monitor performance): Search Console now includes reporting specifically for how a site shows up inside AI-powered search features, alongside traditional performance data. Use it. Step 10 (Keep improving based on real data): What ranks and gets referenced today will shift. Businesses that check in regularly, instead of setting and forgetting, stay ahead of that shift instead of getting surprised by it. Common SEO, AEO, and GEO Mistakes Businesses Make A few patterns come up again and again. Keyword stuffing. Repeating a phrase unnaturally doesn’t help anymore it reads badly to people and doesn’t fool modern search or AI systems either. Writing only for search engines. Content built purely to rank, with no real person in mind, tends to read exactly like what it is: hollow. Publishing generic, AI-generated filler. If a page could have been written by anyone, about anyone, in about ninety seconds, it adds little value to a reader or to a system trying to figure out who’s actually worth citing. Making vague claims. “ Industry-leading ” and “ best-in-class ” answer nothing. Specifics do. Ignoring the questions customers actually ask. Most businesses already know exactly what their customers want to know. Very few put those exact answers on the page. Leaving service pages unclear. If a visitor can’t tell what a business actually does within a few seconds, they leave and so, functionally, does anything trying to summarize the site. Publishing without a real strategy. Random posts on random topics, with no connection to what actual customers search for. Expecting instant results. SEO, AEO, and GEO all compound over months, not days. Believing anyone can guarantee rankings or AI mentions. No agency, freelancer, or tool has that kind of control over Google or any AI system. Anyone claiming otherwise is selling something. Treating GEO as a shortcut around SEO. There’s no special file, trick, or workaround that skips the foundational work. The businesses showing up well in AI search are, almost without exception, the ones that got the fundamentals right first. Frequently Asked Questions What is SEO? SEO stands for Search Engine Optimization the practice of making a website easier for search engines to find, understand, and recommend. It covers technical setup, content quality, and overall site trustworthiness. What is AEO? AEO stands for Answer Engine Optimization structuring content to directly and clearly answer specific questions, rather than only targeting general topics. It matters more as search shifts toward question-based queries. What is GEO? GEO stands for Generative Engine Optimization making a business easy for AI systems to understand and describe accurately when they generate answers, such as in Google’s AI Overviews or AI Mode. Is SEO still important in 2026? Yes. AI-powered search features are built on the same core ranking and quality systems traditional SEO has always relied on, so strong SEO remains the foundation everything else sits on. Is AEO the same as SEO? Not exactly. AEO is best understood as a focused application of SEO the part specifically concerned with directly answering questions, rather than the full range of SEO practices. Does GEO replace SEO? No. GEO depends on SEO working properly first. An AI system can’t accurately describe a business whose underlying website isn’t indexed, isn’t clear, or isn’t trustworthy to begin with. Can SEO help with AI search? Yes. Since AI-powered search features draw on the same underlying search index and quality signals as traditional search, solid SEO groundwork directly supports visibility in AI-generated answers too. Can a business guarantee AI citations? No and it’s worth being skeptical of anyone who claims otherwise. AI systems weigh many factors, and no outside party controls how or when a business gets mentioned. What a business can control is making its own information as clear, accurate, and well-organized as possible. How long does SEO take? Typically a few months to see meaningful movement, longer in competitive industries. It behaves more like compound interest than a light switch. Should small businesses invest in SEO, AEO, and GEO? Yes small business SEO especially. Being easy to find, answer, and reference costs far less than most paid alternatives, and the advantage tends to compound rather than disappear the moment ad spend stops. The Future of Search Visibility The future of search probably isn’t going to be about chasing a higher position on a page. Positions on a page mean less when the “ page ” itself keeps changing shape sometimes a list of links, sometimes an AI-written paragraph, sometimes a back-and-forth conversation. What stays constant, underneath all of that, is a much older idea : be easy to find. Be easy to understand. Be easy to trust. Be easy to answer. Be easy for someone to choose, once they’ve found you. That’s not a new marketing framework. It’s closer to how good businesses have always worked, just applied to a search landscape that keeps adding new doors into the same room. At American Design Hub , this is how we think about SEO , AEO , and GEO not as three separate services to sell, but as connected parts of one larger goal: helping businesses become easier to find, understand, and trust, wherever their customers are actually looking. If you’re trying to figure out where your own website stands in all of this, that’s a conversation worth having. SEO, AEO, and GEO: The New Search Strategy Every Business Needs in 2026 was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
