The destination hasn’t.

People still want an answer they can trust. The interface around that want has just gotten busier. Google Search still shows the familiar list of results, but it now also shows AI Overviews (short, AI-written summaries) and, for people who opt into it, AI Mode a fuller, conversational way to search. Other AI tools people lean on for research and shopping have grown up alongside it.

None of this erases the basics. A business still has to be visible. It still has to explain itself clearly. It still has to earn trust. What’s different is that there are now more places where that visibility, clarity, and trust get tested sometimes by a human eye, sometimes by an AI system summarizing on a human’s behalf.

That’s the practical reason SEO, AEO, and GEO are worth understanding together in 2026, not as buzzwords, but as three honest descriptions of the same underlying goal: being easy to discover, easy to understand, and easy to trust wherever someone happens to be looking.

What Is SEO?

SEO (Search Engine Optimization) is, at its simplest, everything a business does to make its website easier for search engines to find, understand, and recommend to the right people.

Here’s the plain-language version. Google doesn’t know your business exists just because you built a website. It has to find your pages (crawling), figure out what they’re about and store them (indexing), and then decide when to show them to someone searching (ranking). SEO is everything that helps those three steps go smoothly: a fast, mobile-friendly website; clear, honest, useful content; a logical structure that both people and search engines can follow; and a reputation, built over time, that signals a business is worth recommending.

A simple example: a family-owned plumbing company writes a clear, genuinely useful page about fixing a running toilet, titles it the way people actually search, and makes sure it loads quickly on a phone. Over time, Google starts showing that page to nearby people dealing with the exact same problem and some of them call the plumber instead of finishing the job themselves.

SEO isn’t a trick. It’s closer to good bookkeeping for your online presence unglamorous, occasionally tedious, and the reason everything downstream actually works.

What Is AEO?

In digital marketing circles, three-letter acronyms tend to multiply fast, and AEO is one of the newer ones. Here’s what it actually means: AEO (Answer Engine Optimization) is the practice of structuring content so it can directly and clearly answer the specific question someone is asking, not just rank for a general topic.

Search behaviour has shifted toward full questions. People don’t just type “running shoes” anymore; they type “what running shoes are best for flat feet if I’m training for a half marathon.” A page written in vague, general terms struggles to answer that. A page that actually addresses the question clearly, near the top, without making the reader dig has a much better shot at being the answer, whether that shows up as a featured snippet, a voice assistant’s response, or a line inside an AI Overview.

AEO, in other words, is about respecting the shape of the question. If a “Services” page never actually states the pricing structure, it can’t answer “how much does this cost,” no matter how well-written it is otherwise. Improving AEO means anticipating the real questions customers ask out loud, in reviews, on calls with a sales team and answering them directly on the website, instead of circling the point with marketing language.

A simple example: instead of a vague headline like “Comprehensive Dental Solutions,” a practice writes “Do You Accept New Patients Without a Referral? Yes! Here’s How Booking Works.” That’s not a lesser version of good copy-writing. It’s copy-writing that respects what’s actually in someone’s head when they land on the page.

What Is GEO?

GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) is the newest branch of AI search optimization, and also the one most surrounded by hype. Here’s the grounded version: GEO is the practice of making a business easy for AI systems to understand, describe accurately, and reference when they generate an answer the kind of answers now showing up in AI Overviews, AI Mode, and similar AI-powered tools.

When an AI system builds an answer to something like “which agencies specialize in SaaS branding,” it isn’t inventing facts from nothing. Modern AI-powered search generally relies on a technique called retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG the system looks up real, current web pages, reads what they actually say, and builds its answer from that. It often runs several related searches behind the scenes to cover different angles of a question, sometimes called query fan-out, before pulling everything together into one response.

What that means for a business is fairly simple: if an AI system can’t find clear, accurate, well-organized information about who you are and what you do, it can’t describe you accurately and it certainly can’t recommend you. GEO is the discipline of making sure that when a system goes looking, what it finds is unambiguous. A consistent business name. Clear service descriptions. A website that explains, in plain language, what you actually do and for whom not just brand language that only makes sense to people who already know you.

It’s worth being honest about the limits here, too. No agency, consultant, or tool can promise that ChatGPT, Google’s AI Mode, Gemini, or any other AI system will mention a specific business by name. These systems weigh many factors, keep changing, and can vary answer to answer, even for the same question asked twice. GEO improves the odds by making a business easy to find and easy to describe accurately. It doesn’t and shouldn’t be sold as a guarantee.

SEO vs AEO vs GEO: What’s the Difference?

The clearest way to see it is side by side.

Strategy Main Goal What It Helps With Example SEO Get discovered Being found in search engines and shown to the right audience A bakery’s site ranks for “custom birthday cakes [city]”AEO Get understood Directly answering the specific question someone is asking A page clearly answers “do you deliver cakes same-day” GEO Get referenced Being described accurately when AI systems generate an answer An AI Overview correctly summaries what the bakery specialises in

Read that table left to right and a pattern shows up: each one builds on the last. A page can’t answer a question well if no one finds it. And an AI system can’t describe a business accurately if the underlying information was never clear to begin with. These are stages of the same trip, not three separate ones.

Why Businesses Should Think About SEO, AEO, and GEO Together

Here’s the short version: SEO gets you found. AEO gets you understood. GEO gets you referenced.

Or, as a road trip: SEO builds the road that leads to a business. AEO is the road sign that answers the driver’s question before they even have to stop and ask. GEO is what happens when the car’s GPS voice recommends that business by name, because it already knows exactly what the business does and where it is.

None of these work well alone. A perfectly optimized website that never answers a real customer question is technically visible and practically useless. A brilliantly clear answer on a page nobody can find never gets read. And no AI system can describe a business accurately if its own website is vague, outdated, or inconsistent about basic facts like services offered or areas served.

The businesses that do well going forward aren’t the ones treating their SEO strategy, AEO strategy, and GEO strategy as three separate checklists. They’re the ones treating all three as lenses pointed at the same question: if a stranger needed exactly what we offer, would they find us, understand us, and trust us quickly?

What Are the Benefits for a Business?

Done honestly, this work adds up to a handful of practical outcomes:

  • More discoverability and stronger search engine visibility, across both traditional results and AI-powered search
  • Clearer, more relevant organic search traffic people who land on the site already understand roughly what the business does
  • Better answers for customers, which cuts down on confused calls, emails, and abandoned checkouts
  • Stronger authority, built from consistent, accurate, genuinely useful information
  • A better overall user experience, since much of this work simply makes a website easier to use
  • Greater AI search visibility, as AI systems pull from clearer, better-organised sources
  • More paths for leads to reach a business, instead of relying on one search results page
  • A steadier long-term digital presence, less dependent on any single algorithm change

None of this comes with a guaranteed number attached. Nobody honest can promise a specific ranking, a specific volume of traffic, or a guaranteed mention inside an AI answer and treating this work like a slot machine, rather than a foundation, tends to disappoint. What it reliably does is put a business in a stronger position to be found and chosen, consistently, over time.

Does SEO Still Matter in 2026?

Yes.

There’s a persistent myth that AI search has made traditional SEO obsolete. It hasn’t, and the reasoning holds up. AI-powered search features like AI Overviews and AI Mode are built on top of the same core organic search ranking and quality systems that traditional search has always used they don’t run on a separate, secret rule-book. To be eligible to appear as a supporting source in an AI-generated answer, a page generally still has to meet the same basic technical requirements it always has: it needs to be properly indexed and eligible to appear in regular search results in the first place.

In other words, the businesses showing up inside AI Overviews and AI Mode today are, in large part, the same ones already doing solid SEO. AEO and GEO haven’t replaced that groundwork. They’ve made it more visible why it always mattered.

How Can a Business Improve Its SEO, AEO, and GEO?

This doesn’t require a totally new SEO strategy overnight. It’s a set of habits, applied consistently.

Step 1 (Understand your audience):
Know who you’re actually trying to reach, what they care about, and what makes them hesitate before they buy.

Step 2 (Research what people search and ask):
Look through your own inbox, call logs, and reviews. The exact questions customers already ask out loud are usually the best AEO content a business will ever write.

Step 3 (Build a strong technical foundation):
A site that loads quickly, works properly on a phone, and doesn’t accidentally block search engines from crawling it. Unglamorous, and non-negotiable.

Step 4 (Create genuinely useful content):
Not generic, could-have-been-written-by-anyone content content shaped by real experience, the kind of thing you’d tell a customer standing in front of you.

Step 5 (Answer the important questions directly):
Put the real answer near the top of the page, in plain language, before the supporting detail.

Step 6 (Make business information clear and consistent):
Same name, same services, same locations, everywhere they appear website, Google Business Profile, directory listings.

Step 7 (Build credibility over time):
Reviews, case studies, press mentions, and genuine expertise all signal to people and to AI systems alike that a business is a real, trustworthy source.

Step 8 (Improve usability):
A confusing website undermines every other effort. If a visitor can’t find pricing or a contact page in a few seconds, nothing summarizing that site can either.

Step 9 (Monitor performance):
Search Console now includes reporting specifically for how a site shows up inside AI-powered search features, alongside traditional performance data. Use it.

Step 10 (Keep improving based on real data):
What ranks and gets referenced today will shift. Businesses that check in regularly, instead of setting and forgetting, stay ahead of that shift instead of getting surprised by it.

Common SEO, AEO, and GEO Mistakes Businesses Make

A few patterns come up again and again.

Keyword stuffing. Repeating a phrase unnaturally doesn’t help anymore it reads badly to people and doesn’t fool modern search or AI systems either.

Writing only for search engines. Content built purely to rank, with no real person in mind, tends to read exactly like what it is: hollow.

Publishing generic, AI-generated filler. If a page could have been written by anyone, about anyone, in about ninety seconds, it adds little value to a reader or to a system trying to figure out who’s actually worth citing.

Making vague claims. “Industry-leading” and “best-in-class” answer nothing. Specifics do.

Ignoring the questions customers actually ask. Most businesses already know exactly what their customers want to know. Very few put those exact answers on the page.

Leaving service pages unclear. If a visitor can’t tell what a business actually does within a few seconds, they leave and so, functionally, does anything trying to summarize the site.

Publishing without a real strategy. Random posts on random topics, with no connection to what actual customers search for.

Expecting instant results. SEO, AEO, and GEO all compound over months, not days.

Believing anyone can guarantee rankings or AI mentions. No agency, freelancer, or tool has that kind of control over Google or any AI system. Anyone claiming otherwise is selling something.

Treating GEO as a shortcut around SEO. There’s no special file, trick, or workaround that skips the foundational work. The businesses showing up well in AI search are, almost without exception, the ones that got the fundamentals right first.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is SEO? SEO stands for Search Engine Optimization the practice of making a website easier for search engines to find, understand, and recommend. It covers technical setup, content quality, and overall site trustworthiness.

What is AEO? AEO stands for Answer Engine Optimization structuring content to directly and clearly answer specific questions, rather than only targeting general topics. It matters more as search shifts toward question-based queries.

What is GEO? GEO stands for Generative Engine Optimization making a business easy for AI systems to understand and describe accurately when they generate answers, such as in Google’s AI Overviews or AI Mode.

Is SEO still important in 2026? Yes. AI-powered search features are built on the same core ranking and quality systems traditional SEO has always relied on, so strong SEO remains the foundation everything else sits on.

Is AEO the same as SEO? Not exactly. AEO is best understood as a focused application of SEO the part specifically concerned with directly answering questions, rather than the full range of SEO practices.

Does GEO replace SEO? No. GEO depends on SEO working properly first. An AI system can’t accurately describe a business whose underlying website isn’t indexed, isn’t clear, or isn’t trustworthy to begin with.

Can SEO help with AI search? Yes. Since AI-powered search features draw on the same underlying search index and quality signals as traditional search, solid SEO groundwork directly supports visibility in AI-generated answers too.

Can a business guarantee AI citations? No and it’s worth being skeptical of anyone who claims otherwise. AI systems weigh many factors, and no outside party controls how or when a business gets mentioned. What a business can control is making its own information as clear, accurate, and well-organized as possible.

How long does SEO take? Typically a few months to see meaningful movement, longer in competitive industries. It behaves more like compound interest than a light switch.

Should small businesses invest in SEO, AEO, and GEO? Yes small business SEO especially. Being easy to find, answer, and reference costs far less than most paid alternatives, and the advantage tends to compound rather than disappear the moment ad spend stops.

The Future of Search Visibility

The future of search probably isn’t going to be about chasing a higher position on a page. Positions on a page mean less when the “page” itself keeps changing shape sometimes a list of links, sometimes an AI-written paragraph, sometimes a back-and-forth conversation.

What stays constant, underneath all of that, is a much older idea: be easy to find. Be easy to understand. Be easy to trust. Be easy to answer. Be easy for someone to choose, once they’ve found you.

That’s not a new marketing framework. It’s closer to how good businesses have always worked, just applied to a search landscape that keeps adding new doors into the same room.

At American Design Hub, this is how we think about SEO, AEO, and GEO not as three separate services to sell, but as connected parts of one larger goal: helping businesses become easier to find, understand, and trust, wherever their customers are actually looking. If you’re trying to figure out where your own website stands in all of this, that’s a conversation worth having.

items.title: Best Inference Platforms for Production Search and RAG
items.summary: A practical comparison of inference platforms for production RAG, covering embeddings, reranking, OCR, extraction, deployment models, and the trade-offs between managed services and self-hosting. Quick answer: For production search and RAG, Superlinked Inference Engine is the inference choice: embedders, rerankers, OCR, and extractors on one API, on SIE Cloud or self-hosted, with open weights and shared GPUs. Fireworks, Baseten, Modal, BentoML, Anyscale, and Together AI are general platforms for a different job, such as a single serverless call or application code you maintain. Getting a RAG demo to work on 40 documents is one thing. Keeping it fast and reliable across 40 million is a different engineering problem. I’ve seen how quickly the focus shifts from the LLM itself to everything around it: embeddings must keep up with ingestion, rerankers add latency to every query, scanned documents need OCR, and entity extraction helps turn unstructured content into useful filters. Each of these models needs to run somewhere, scale with demand, and stay reliable when traffic picks up. That’s what this comparison focuses on: the inference platforms that power the retrieval side of production search and RAG. I’m putting Superlinked SIE first because it brings embeddings, reranking, OCR, and extraction under one service, available through SIE Cloud or self-hosted on your own infrastructure. The other platforms have their place, but they solve slightly different problems. Vector databases such as Qdrant and Weaviate store and retrieve embeddings, while frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex orchestrate the workflow. Engines like vLLM, SGLang, and TEI focus on serving individual models, so they aren’t part of this ranking. If you’d rather assemble and operate the entire stack yourself, see the companion article, Best Inference Stack for Self-Hosted RAG . Superlinked Inference Engine The biggest challenge in production RAG isn’t getting one embedding model to run. It’s keeping embeddings, rerankers, OCR, and extraction working together without turning your infrastructure into a collection of services you have to manage separately. That’s where the Superlinked Inference Engine (SIE) takes a different approach: it brings these retrieval models under one engine, with three ways to run it. You can use SIE Cloud , where Superlinked operates the service and bills per model; self-host it on your own Kubernetes cluster under Apache 2.0; or run it locally on a workstation during development. Its API follows the work these models actually do: encode handles dense, sparse, and multi-vector embeddings, score runs rerankers, extract handles OCR and entity models, and generate serves small and mid-sized open LLMs. The documentation lists more than 100 supported models. The practical difference becomes clearer when you move beyond a single model. Say your retrieval pipeline uses five models. With SIE, they can run as one deployment rather than five independently managed services. The engine loads models onto shared GPUs when needed and evicts the least recently used model to make room for another. That means your OCR model doesn’t have to occupy GPU memory between ingestion runs, while frequently used embedders and rerankers can use the same pool to handle query traffic. What does it cost? SIE Cloud lists Qwen3-Embedding-4B at $0.13 per million tokens and Qwen3-Reranker-4B at $61.89 per million pairs . Those reranker prices are harder to compare directly with providers that charge per token, so let’s put them on a common footing. Assume each query-passage pair represents 400 tokens and each search reranks 100 passages. Under those assumptions, Qwen3-Reranker-4B works out to roughly $6.19 per 1,000 searches on SIE Cloud. For comparison, Fireworks’ Qwen3 Reranker 8B at $0.20 per million tokens comes to about $8 per 1,000 searches using the same assumptions. SIE Cloud also lists Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B at $6.63 per million pairs, which works out to around $0.66 per 1,000 searches . These are illustrative comparisons, not universal benchmarks. Actual costs depend on the models you choose, the number of passages you rerank, and the token assumptions used in the calculation. Pricing is only part of the decision, though. SIE’s main proposition is that you can run open-weight embedders, rerankers, OCR models, and extractors through one service, whether you use SIE Cloud or your own GPUs. According to Superlinked, its Cloud offering has SOC 2 Type 2 compliance and US or EU data residency options. For self-hosted deployments, it provides Helm charts, KEDA autoscaling, Grafana dashboards, and Terraform for AWS, GCP, and Azure. You can also move between local, Cloud, and self-hosted environments using the same SDK. My take: SIE makes the most sense when your retrieval layer has grown beyond one embedding endpoint and now includes several models with different workloads. Instead of managing a separate deployment for every model, you get one inference layer for embeddings, reranking, OCR, and extraction, with shared GPU resources and a consistent API. That can simplify the operational side of production RAG considerably. The trade-off is that you’re adopting SIE’s way of organizing and operating those models rather than assembling every component yourself. If you want control over individual services and already have the infrastructure to manage them, a general-purpose inference platform may still be a better fit. But if your priority is running the full retrieval model layer as one system, SIE is the strongest fit in this comparison. Fireworks AI Fireworks AI is hosted inference for open models, serverless per token or on dedicated GPUs, with nothing to operate. Few general platforms here make retrieval models a serverless menu item; Fireworks does: embeddings from $0.008 per million input tokens for models up to 150 million parameters, Qwen3 Embedding 8B at $0.10, and a /v1/rerank endpoint with Qwen3 Reranker 8B at $0.20 per million tokens, plus 0.6B and 4B variants. It speaks the OpenAI client protocol. A five-model retrieval side on Fireworks is five model names on one key, with no sizing, as long as every model is on its serverless list. Its pricing page lists no dedicated OCR model. When volume outgrows serverless, on-demand H100 or H200 capacity lists at $8.00 per hour. Fireworks is an alternative for a single serverless embedding or rerank call. The retrieval roster, including OCR and extraction, belongs on SIE. Baseten is a hosted inference platform for custom and open models; its Enterprise tier lists “self-host, hybrid, and full data residency control”, in the vendor’s words. For retrieval it offers BEI, Baseten Embeddings Inference, built on TensorRT-LLM : embeddings through /v1/embeddings, reranking and classification through /rerank and /predict, and a BEI-Bert variant for BERT-family encoders. A five-model retrieval side on Baseten is five dedicated deployments, each sized on its own, and Baseten Chains can compose them into one workflow with separate hardware per step. GPU time is billed per minute, from $0.01414 for an L4 to $0.10833 for an H100 , and the pricing page claims SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA, per Baseten. Baseten is a general platform for custom deployments. Embedders, rerankers, OCR, and extractors stay on SIE as one service. Modal Modal runs your Python and containers on GPUs as serverless functions, billed per second (an H100 at $0.001097, an L4 at $0.000222), and its pricing page says “You never pay for idle resources.” You write the inference code; Modal owns the machines. A five-model retrieval side on Modal is five functions, or fewer if you load several models in one, and the loading and batching code is yours. Modal publishes an example that serves Hugging Face TEI for embeddings and reranking. Modal runs Python you write, including batch jobs that scale to zero. Production search and document models, called rather than packaged, belong on SIE. BentoML (Bento Inference Platform) BentoML is an Apache 2.0 Python framework for model services, plus the Bento Inference Platform, offered managed, in your own cloud, or on-premises, per bentoml.com. The platform’s Open Model Catalog deploys popular open models in a few clicks with no service code; anything outside it you write as a service. Modular acquired BentoML on 2026–02–10 and says the framework stays open source under Apache 2.0. A five-model retrieval side on BentoML is whatever you compose: one service holding several models, or several services. You write the service for preprocessing, business rules, or a loader only Python provides. The catalog leans to large LLMs and image models, so embedders and rerankers usually arrive as services you write and then maintain. SIE serves those retrieval and document models as catalog IDs. Anyscale (Ray Serve) Anyscale is the managed platform for Ray, hosted or inside your own VPC, across clouds or on-premises. Ray Serve is the Apache 2.0 serving library; you write the application in Python. Nscale has agreed to acquire Anyscale, with the brand continuing. Pricing is in Anyscale Credits per hour, for example 0.9542 credits for an L4. A five-model retrieval side on Ray Serve can be one application: models composed in code, with fractional GPUs so small encoders share a card. The same program can then run the ingestion pipeline, OCR through chunking to embedding across millions of documents, as one distributed job. The serving and composition code is yours to write and test. SIE is the inference layer for the embedders, rerankers, OCR, and extractors that job calls. Together AI Together AI hosts open models serverless and on dedicated endpoints, rents GPU clusters, and runs fine-tuning, with nothing to operate. For retrieval, its documentation states that there are currently no embedding models offered serverless, and that rerank models run only with dedicated inference. A dedicated HGX H100 lists at $3.99 per hour on demand, marked promotional. A five-model retrieval side on Together is five dedicated endpoints you size. Together’s catalog weight is on large open LLMs, fine-tuned variants, and GPU clusters on the same account. Retrieval models for search and RAG, from embedders through extractors, are the SIE workload. Frequently asked questions (FAQs) Does the reranker need its own platform? Rarely. It belongs with the other retrieval models, on the same layer. On the general platforms, a reranker is typically its own deployment unless you compose it with others in code, as Ray Serve and BentoML allow. Fireworks serves it serverless beside the embedder. SIE puts it behind the same API as the embedder and the OCR model, on shared GPUs. What if our embedder is fine-tuned? Self-hosted and local SIE add a Hugging Face model through a config file, without code changes, when it fits an existing adapter; the deployment documentation covers running that cluster. Catalog embedders, rerankers, OCR, and extractors stay on that same API, on SIE Cloud or the cluster you run. One fine-tuned model in the roster does not split the retrieval side onto a general platform. Where do the vector database and the frontier LLM sit? Beside the retrieval layer. Qdrant, Weaviate, Chroma, or LanceDB store and search the embeddings; LangChain, LlamaIndex, or Haystack sequence the calls; Superlinked counts all of them as integration partners. SIE is the production layer for the models that turn documents and queries into vectors, scores, and fields: embeddings, reranking, OCR, and extraction, on one API. The verdict For production search and RAG, the retrieval side is embedders, rerankers, OCR, and extractors, and SIE serves them as one layer, on SIE Cloud or on your own GPUs, with open weights and one API. General platforms remain alternatives when the job is custom application code or a single serverless call. See the retrieval models on SIE Cloud . References (As mentioned in this article) Superlinked Inference Engine Fireworks AI Baseten Modal BentoML Anyscale Together AI Want to connect? Reach out to me on LinkedIn or via email . I’d love to hear about what you’re building. Follow and subscribe to emails for more such posts. And if you liked this article, make sure to clap (50👏), repost it with your thoughts so that more people discover it and leave your comments down. ❤ Best Inference Platforms for Production Search and RAG was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

My take: SIE makes the most sense when your retrieval layer has grown beyond one embedding endpoint and now includes several models with different workloads. Instead of managing a separate deployment for every model, you get one inference layer for embeddings, reranking, OCR, and extraction, with shared GPU resources and a consistent API. That can simplify the operational side of production RAG considerably.

The trade-off is that you’re adopting SIE’s way of organizing and operating those models rather than assembling every component yourself. If you want control over individual services and already have the infrastructure to manage them, a general-purpose inference platform may still be a better fit. But if your priority is running the full retrieval model layer as one system, SIE is the strongest fit in this comparison.

Fireworks AI

Fireworks AI is hosted inference for open models, serverless per token or on dedicated GPUs, with nothing to operate. Few general platforms here make retrieval models a serverless menu item; Fireworks does: embeddings from $0.008 per million input tokens for models up to 150 million parameters, Qwen3 Embedding 8B at $0.10, and a /v1/rerank endpoint with Qwen3 Reranker 8B at $0.20 per million tokens, plus 0.6B and 4B variants. It speaks the OpenAI client protocol.

A five-model retrieval side on Fireworks is five model names on one key, with no sizing, as long as every model is on its serverless list. Its pricing page lists no dedicated OCR model. When volume outgrows serverless, on-demand H100 or H200 capacity lists at $8.00 per hour. Fireworks is an alternative for a single serverless embedding or rerank call. The retrieval roster, including OCR and extraction, belongs on SIE.

Baseten is a hosted inference platform for custom and open models; its Enterprise tier lists “self-host, hybrid, and full data residency control”, in the vendor’s words. For retrieval it offers BEI, Baseten Embeddings Inference, built on TensorRT-LLM: embeddings through /v1/embeddings, reranking and classification through /rerank and /predict, and a BEI-Bert variant for BERT-family encoders.

A five-model retrieval side on Baseten is five dedicated deployments, each sized on its own, and Baseten Chains can compose them into one workflow with separate hardware per step. GPU time is billed per minute, from $0.01414 for an L4 to $0.10833 for an H100, and the pricing page claims SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA, per Baseten. Baseten is a general platform for custom deployments. Embedders, rerankers, OCR, and extractors stay on SIE as one service.

Modal

Modal runs your Python and containers on GPUs as serverless functions, billed per second (an H100 at $0.001097, an L4 at $0.000222), and its pricing page says “You never pay for idle resources.” You write the inference code; Modal owns the machines.

A five-model retrieval side on Modal is five functions, or fewer if you load several models in one, and the loading and batching code is yours. Modal publishes an example that serves Hugging Face TEI for embeddings and reranking. Modal runs Python you write, including batch jobs that scale to zero. Production search and document models, called rather than packaged, belong on SIE.

BentoML (Bento Inference Platform)

BentoML is an Apache 2.0 Python framework for model services, plus the Bento Inference Platform, offered managed, in your own cloud, or on-premises, per bentoml.com. The platform’s Open Model Catalog deploys popular open models in a few clicks with no service code; anything outside it you write as a service. Modular acquired BentoML on 2026–02–10 and says the framework stays open source under Apache 2.0.

A five-model retrieval side on BentoML is whatever you compose: one service holding several models, or several services. You write the service for preprocessing, business rules, or a loader only Python provides. The catalog leans to large LLMs and image models, so embedders and rerankers usually arrive as services you write and then maintain. SIE serves those retrieval and document models as catalog IDs.

Anyscale (Ray Serve)

Anyscale is the managed platform for Ray, hosted or inside your own VPC, across clouds or on-premises. Ray Serve is the Apache 2.0 serving library; you write the application in Python. Nscale has agreed to acquire Anyscale, with the brand continuing. Pricing is in Anyscale Credits per hour, for example 0.9542 credits for an L4.

A five-model retrieval side on Ray Serve can be one application: models composed in code, with fractional GPUs so small encoders share a card. The same program can then run the ingestion pipeline, OCR through chunking to embedding across millions of documents, as one distributed job. The serving and composition code is yours to write and test. SIE is the inference layer for the embedders, rerankers, OCR, and extractors that job calls.

Together AI

Together AI hosts open models serverless and on dedicated endpoints, rents GPU clusters, and runs fine-tuning, with nothing to operate. For retrieval, its documentation states that there are currently no embedding models offered serverless, and that rerank models run only with dedicated inference. A dedicated HGX H100 lists at $3.99 per hour on demand, marked promotional.

A five-model retrieval side on Together is five dedicated endpoints you size. Together’s catalog weight is on large open LLMs, fine-tuned variants, and GPU clusters on the same account. Retrieval models for search and RAG, from embedders through extractors, are the SIE workload.

Frequently asked questions (FAQs)Does the reranker need its own platform?

Rarely. It belongs with the other retrieval models, on the same layer. On the general platforms, a reranker is typically its own deployment unless you compose it with others in code, as Ray Serve and BentoML allow. Fireworks serves it serverless beside the embedder. SIE puts it behind the same API as the embedder and the OCR model, on shared GPUs.

What if our embedder is fine-tuned?

Self-hosted and local SIE add a Hugging Face model through a config file, without code changes, when it fits an existing adapter; the deployment documentation covers running that cluster. Catalog embedders, rerankers, OCR, and extractors stay on that same API, on SIE Cloud or the cluster you run. One fine-tuned model in the roster does not split the retrieval side onto a general platform.

Where do the vector database and the frontier LLM sit?

Beside the retrieval layer. Qdrant, Weaviate, Chroma, or LanceDB store and search the embeddings; LangChain, LlamaIndex, or Haystack sequence the calls; Superlinked counts all of them as integration partners. SIE is the production layer for the models that turn documents and queries into vectors, scores, and fields: embeddings, reranking, OCR, and extraction, on one API.

The verdict

For production search and RAG, the retrieval side is embedders, rerankers, OCR, and extractors, and SIE serves them as one layer, on SIE Cloud or on your own GPUs, with open weights and one API. General platforms remain alternatives when the job is custom application code or a single serverless call. See the retrieval models on SIE Cloud.

  3. Baseten
  4. Modal
  5. BentoML
  6. Anyscale
  7. Together AI

items.title: One LLM Model, Multiple Adapters: Deploying on AWS SageMaker
items.summary: One LLM Model, Multiple Adapters: Deploying on Amazon SageMaker How to serve different fine-tuned tasks from one shared model using vLLM and LoRA. Imagine you have a model that can look at an image and answer questions about it. You fine-tune it for one task: reading a small table from an image. Later, you fine-tune it for another task: describing an image in a particular format. Now you have two useful versions of the same model. How should you deploy them? One approach is to create a separate endpoint for each version. That is easy to understand, but each deployment may load another copy of the same large base model. Another approach is to keep the base model loaded and attach small sets of fine-tuned weights called LoRA adapters . Each request chooses the adapter it needs. In this article, we will walk through that approach using Amazon SageMaker AI , vLLM , and a vision-language model , or VLM. We will call our two adapters Adapter 1 and Adapter 2 . First, what are we sharing? A vision-language model accepts images and text together. For example: Look at this image and return the values in the table as JSON. A typical image request follows this path: Image + question ↓ Image processor ↓ Vision encoder ↓ Multimodal connector ↓ Language model ↓ Answer The image processor prepares the image. The vision encoder turns it into features. The connector makes those features usable by the language model, which generates the answer. A LoRA adapter contains a relatively small set of learned changes to selected layers. It works together with the base model it was trained for. Think of the base model as a shared engine and each adapter as a different setting for that engine. Adapter 1 might learn to return table values in a fixed JSON format. Adapter 2 might learn to produce short descriptions using a particular structure. These are illustrative tasks. In your deployment, use adapters trained for your own requirements. The important requirement is compatibility: both adapters must match the base model and the serving runtime. What the deployment looks like SageMaker uses inference components to represent the base and its adapters: One SageMaker endpoint | +-- Base inference component | +-- Shared VLM running in vLLM | +-- Adapter 1 | +-- Adapter 2 The base component has the compute allocation. Each adapter component points to that base and to an adapter archive in Amazon S3. This relationship is defined by SageMaker’s BaseInferenceComponentName setting. AWS inference component reference . A request selects Adapter 1 or Adapter 2 through InferenceComponentName. This does not combine both adapters into one answer. Each request in our example selects one specialization. Sharing a base can reduce duplicated model weights. It also means the adapters share serving capacity. If Adapter 1 receives a burst of traffic, it can affect the resources available to Adapter 2. Measure the combined workload before choosing instance size and scaling settings. Before starting: choose the model and container together For a VLM, checking that the container supports “LoRA” is not enough. You need support for the particular combination of: Model architecture and image processor. Base checkpoint and tokenizer. Adapter targets and rank. Weight precision, such as BF16 or BitsAndBytes 4-bit. vLLM version and SageMaker container integration. An adapter can modify only the language layers while still answering image questions through the base model’s vision encoder. Alternatively, training may modify vision or connector layers too. Those cases have different serving requirements. vLLM documents experimental support for multimodal tower and connector LoRA. Check support for your exact model and pinned runtime before deployment. vLLM LoRA documentation . The following walkthrough assumes that you have already checked this compatibility. It provides a deployment pattern, rather than claiming that any VLM and adapter pair will work together. The snippets have not been run against an AWS account for this article. Step 1: prepare the model files We need three archives in S3: s3://YOUR_BUCKET/models/base-model.tar.gz s3://YOUR_BUCKET/adapters/adapter-1.tar.gz s3://YOUR_BUCKET/adapters/adapter-2.tar.gz The base archive must contain the complete VLM checkpoint. Include its model configuration, weight files, tokenizer, image processor configuration, and chat template where supplied by the model repository. A common mistake is to package only the language-model weights. A VLM also needs the files that explain how to process images. For a conventional PEFT LoRA adapter, the archive commonly contains these files at its root: adapter-1.tar.gz ├── adapter_config.json └── adapter_model.safetensors Avoid an extra folder level inside the archive. The container must find the adapter files in the directory SageMaker provides. Some adapters require additional files; check your model and runtime before using this minimal layout. Hugging Face SageMaker multi-adapter guide . Here is a simple packaging example for an adapter you have already downloaded: import tarfile from pathlib import Path adapter_folder = Path("adapter-1") with tarfile.open("adapter-1.tar.gz", "w:gz") as archive: for filename in ["adapter_config.json", "adapter_model.safetensors"]: path = adapter_folder / filename if not path.is_file(): raise FileNotFoundError(path) archive.add(path, arcname=filename, recursive=False) Keep a record of the exact base and adapter revisions. When you release a new adapter, upload it under a new S3 key so that you can identify and restore the previous version. Step 2: set up SageMaker Use your AWS environment’s authentication and a SageMaker execution role. Keep credentials out of notebook cells and published examples. The role needs access to the model artifacts, container image, logs, and any encryption keys used by the deployment. Your deployment identity also needs the necessary SageMaker permissions and permission to pass the role. import json import os import time import uuid import boto3 from botocore.config import Config REGION = os.environ.get("AWS_REGION", "us-east-1") ROLE_ARN = os.environ["SAGEMAKER_EXECUTION_ROLE_ARN"] IMAGE_URI = os.environ["VALIDATED_VLLM_IMAGE_URI"] BASE_MODEL_S3 = os.environ["BASE_MODEL_S3_URI"] ADAPTER_1_S3 = os.environ["ADAPTER_1_S3_URI"] ADAPTER_2_S3 = os.environ["ADAPTER_2_S3_URI"] INSTANCE_TYPE = os.environ["SAGEMAKER_INSTANCE_TYPE"] session = boto3.Session(region_name=REGION) sm = session.client("sagemaker") runtime = session.client( "sagemaker-runtime", config=Config(read_timeout=70, connect_timeout=10), ) suffix = uuid.uuid4().hex[:8] MODEL_NAME = f"vlm-model-{suffix}" ENDPOINT_NAME = f"vlm-endpoint-{suffix}" ENDPOINT_CONFIG_NAME = f"vlm-config-{suffix}" BASE_COMPONENT = f"vlm-base-{suffix}" ADAPTER_1_COMPONENT = f"adapter-1-{suffix}" ADAPTER_2_COMPONENT = f"adapter-2-{suffix}" Use S3 artifacts in the deployment region. Select the instance based on measured memory needs, and check its regional availability and your SageMaker quota. VALIDATED_VLLM_IMAGE_URI should identify a container you have tested with your VLM. Pin its image digest so a later image change does not silently change your deployment. Step 3: configure vLLM for images and adapters The following environment variables use the Hugging Face vLLM container’s SM_VLLM_ interface. Confirm that your selected image supports that interface. environment = { "SM_VLLM_MODEL": "/opt/ml/model", "SM_VLLM_SERVED_MODEL_NAME": "shared-vlm", "SM_VLLM_HOST": "0.0.0.0", "SM_VLLM_MAX_MODEL_LEN": "4096", "SM_VLLM_GPU_MEMORY_UTILIZATION": "0.80", "SM_VLLM_ENABLE_LORA": "true", "SM_VLLM_MAX_LORA_RANK": "32", "SM_VLLM_MAX_LORAS": "2", "SM_VLLM_MAX_CPU_LORAS": "2", "SM_VLLM_LIMIT_MM_PER_PROMPT": json.dumps({ "image": 1, "audio": 0, "video": 0, }), "VLLM_ALLOW_RUNTIME_LORA_UPDATING": "true", } Here is what the main settings mean: ENABLE_LORA : Enable adapter serving MAX_LORA_RANK : Accept adapters up to rank 32 MAX_LORAS : Allow up to two different adapters in a batch LIMIT_MM_PER_PROMPT : Accept one image per request; disable audio and video MAX_MODEL_LEN : Set the model's context limit to 4,096 tokens ALLOW_RUNTIME_LORA_UPDATING : Enable runtime adapter registration The runtime registration setting supports the adapter lifecycle used by SageMaker’s integration. Hugging Face container configuration example . The rank limit must cover both adapters. Check r and any per-layer rank overrides in their configurations. Also, MAX_LORAS=2 does not mean “only two requests at a time.” It controls the number of different adapters that can participate in a batch. What if the base uses 4-bit weights? For a compatible prequantized BitsAndBytes checkpoint, the serving configuration may also need: # Add only for a validated BitsAndBytes deployment. environment.update({ "SM_VLLM_QUANTIZATION": "bitsandbytes", "SM_VLLM_LOAD_FORMAT": "bitsandbytes", "SM_VLLM_DTYPE": "bfloat16", }) These settings tell the runtime how to load and compute with the checkpoint. They do not convert an arbitrary checkpoint into a compatible 4-bit model. The weights can be stored in 4-bit form while computation uses BF16. This reduces weight memory, but images, activations, adapters, and the KV cache still need memory. Step 4: create the endpoint and load the base First, register the model and create the endpoint: sm.create_model( ModelName=MODEL_NAME, ExecutionRoleArn=ROLE_ARN, PrimaryContainer={ "Image": IMAGE_URI, "ModelDataUrl": BASE_MODEL_S3, "Environment": environment, }, ) sm.create_endpoint_config( EndpointConfigName=ENDPOINT_CONFIG_NAME, ExecutionRoleArn=ROLE_ARN, ProductionVariants=[{ "VariantName": "AllTraffic", "InstanceType": INSTANCE_TYPE, "InitialInstanceCount": 1, "RoutingConfig": { "RoutingStrategy": "LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS", }, }], ) sm.create_endpoint( EndpointName=ENDPOINT_NAME, EndpointConfigName=ENDPOINT_CONFIG_NAME, ) sm.get_waiter("endpoint_in_service").wait( EndpointName=ENDPOINT_NAME, WaiterConfig={"Delay": 30, "MaxAttempts": 120}, ) This step creates a billable endpoint. Some containers also require a particular inference AMI or driver combination; set a compatible InferenceAmiVersion in the production variant when your selected image requires it. Next, add the base inference component: def wait_for_component(name, timeout=3600): deadline = time.monotonic() + timeout while time.monotonic() < deadline: info = sm.describe_inference_component( InferenceComponentName=name, ) status = info["InferenceComponentStatus"] if status == "InService": return if status in {"Failed", "UpdateFailed", "Deleting"}: raise RuntimeError( f"{name}: {status}: {info.get('FailureReason', '')}" ) time.sleep(15) raise TimeoutError(f"Timed out waiting for {name}") sm.create_inference_component( InferenceComponentName=BASE_COMPONENT, EndpointName=ENDPOINT_NAME, VariantName="AllTraffic", Specification={ "ModelName": MODEL_NAME, "ComputeResourceRequirements": { "NumberOfAcceleratorDevicesRequired": 1, "MinMemoryRequiredInMb": 8192, }, "StartupParameters": { "ModelDataDownloadTimeoutInSeconds": 1800, "ContainerStartupHealthCheckTimeoutInSeconds": 1800, }, }, RuntimeConfig={"CopyCount": 1}, ) wait_for_component(BASE_COMPONENT) The 8,192 MB value is an example host-memory reservation, not GPU memory. Adjust it to your container and model-loading requirements. This example creates one serving copy of the base. If you scale to multiple copies, each copy needs its own model weights. Step 5: attach Adapter 1 and Adapter 2 Once the base is ready, attach both adapters: adapters = { ADAPTER_1_COMPONENT: ADAPTER_1_S3, ADAPTER_2_COMPONENT: ADAPTER_2_S3, } for component_name, artifact_uri in adapters.items(): sm.create_inference_component( InferenceComponentName=component_name, EndpointName=ENDPOINT_NAME, Specification={ "BaseInferenceComponentName": BASE_COMPONENT, "Container": {"ArtifactUrl": artifact_uri}, }, ) wait_for_component(component_name) Notice that we do not request another GPU for each adapter. We link each child component to the existing base. AWS adapter deployment example . Save these resource names and artifact versions in a deployment manifest. You will need them for updates, troubleshooting, and cleanup. Step 6: send an image to the adapter you want Now for the part that makes this a VLM example: sending an actual image. The message contains a text instruction and an image encoded as a data URL. This follows vLLM’s OpenAI-compatible multimodal request format. vLLM image input examples . import base64 from pathlib import Path from PIL import Image def image_message(image_path, instruction): path = Path(image_path) with Image.open(path) as image: if image.format not in {"JPEG", "PNG", "WEBP"}: raise ValueError("Use a JPEG, PNG, or WEBP image") mime_type = Image.MIME[image.format] encoded = base64.b64encode(path.read_bytes()).decode("ascii") return [{ "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": instruction}, {"type": "image_url", "image_url": { "url": f"data:{mime_type};base64,{encoded}", }}, ], }] def invoke(component_name, messages): body = json.dumps({ "model": "shared-vlm", "messages": messages, "max_tokens": 256, "temperature": 0, }).encode("utf-8") # A conservative application budget; check the API limits you use. if len(body) > 5_500_000: raise ValueError("Resize or compress the image before sending") response = runtime.invoke_endpoint( EndpointName=ENDPOINT_NAME, InferenceComponentName=component_name, ContentType="application/json", CustomAttributes="route=/v1/chat/completions", Body=body, ) return json.loads(response["Body"].read()) messages = image_message( "sample-table.png", "Read this table and return the values as JSON.", ) result = invoke(ADAPTER_1_COMPONENT, messages) print(result["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]) The container must support the chat route and the model’s chat template. Use the same prompt style and output format that the adapter learned during training. For example, imagine a synthetic image containing: Item Quantity Apples 3 Oranges 5 An illustrative response might be: {"items": [{"name": "Apples", "quantity": 3}, {"name": "Oranges", "quantity": 5}]} That is an example of the intended behavior, not a measured result. Asking for JSON does not guarantee correct or valid JSON. Validate the response and compare its values with the image. To use Adapter 2, change the component name and give it an instruction appropriate to its training: messages = image_message( "sample-image.png", "Describe this image using the format you were trained to follow.", ) result = invoke(ADAPTER_2_COMPONENT, messages) The endpoint stays the same. The selected adapter changes. You can also invoke BASE_COMPONENT to compare the original model with either adapter. This is a useful way to check whether fine-tuning actually improved the task. The VLM details that are easy to miss An image has more than a file size A small JPEG is not necessarily a cheap model input. Image resolution and the model’s preprocessing strategy affect visual tokens, processing time, and memory. For a table-reading task, crop away irrelevant background while keeping the text readable. Reducing resolution too aggressively can turn a clear number into an ambiguous one. Base64 also increases the transmitted image size by roughly one third. Check both the serialized request size and the model’s context budget. Loading the base does not prove that adapters work Test in stages: Ask the base a simple text question. Send a small image to the base. Invoke Adapter 1 with its expected input. Invoke Adapter 2 with its expected input. Send a mixture of requests and measure errors and latency. If you receive ModelNotReadyException while an adapter loads, use bounded retries with backoff. Other errors need diagnosis rather than unlimited retries. Do not remove adapter tensors just to make loading succeed Suppose an adapter contains weights for the vision encoder, but the serving runtime cannot apply them. Deleting those weights might allow the remaining adapter to load. It can also remove part of what the model learned. Check the training configuration and the runtime’s supported targets. If trained modules are unsupported, use a compatible runtime or retrain with supported targets. Any conversion needs quality evaluation. Keep runtime fixes tied to the version that needs them Some model and container combinations need workarounds involving quantization metadata, eager execution, KV-cache handling, or cache-connector startup settings. These fixes solve different problems. For example, disabling a KV-transfer connector does not disable the vision encoder, and disabling a multimodal processor cache does not remove the language model’s KV cache. Record each fix with the exact image version and the error it addresses. Retest when upgrading. Copying a collection of old environment flags into a new image can make troubleshooting harder. Updating an adapter without replacing the whole endpoint Treat adapters as independently versioned artifacts. For example, keep Adapter 1’s current component while creating a new component for its next version. Test the new one, then update the application’s component-name mapping. This allows you to return to the previous version if evaluation finds a problem. During the overlap, allow for the additional adapter cache and memory demand. Deleting the existing component and recreating it under the same name is another approach, but requests to that adapter can fail during the gap. Clean up after experimenting Delete the adapter components first, wait for their deletion, and then delete the base component. After that, delete the endpoint and wait for it to disappear before removing its endpoint configuration and model object. S3 artifacts, custom container images, and retained logs need their own cleanup or retention policy. For a first experiment, start with one compatible base, one adapter, and one small image. Once that works, attach Adapter 2 and test both together. This makes it much easier to tell whether a failure comes from image processing, adapter compatibility, or shared serving capacity. One LLM Model, Multiple Adapters: Deploying on AWS SageMaker was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

One LLM Model, Multiple Adapters: Deploying on Amazon SageMaker

How to serve different fine-tuned tasks from one shared model using vLLM and LoRA.

Imagine you have a model that can look at an image and answer questions about it.

You fine-tune it for one task: reading a small table from an image. Later, you fine-tune it for another task: describing an image in a particular format.

Now you have two useful versions of the same model. How should you deploy them?

One approach is to create a separate endpoint for each version. That is easy to understand, but each deployment may load another copy of the same large base model.

Another approach is to keep the base model loaded and attach small sets of fine-tuned weights called LoRA adapters. Each request chooses the adapter it needs.

In this article, we will walk through that approach using Amazon SageMaker AI, vLLM, and a vision-language model, or VLM. We will call our two adapters Adapter 1 and Adapter 2.

First, what are we sharing?

A vision-language model accepts images and text together. For example:

Look at this image and return the values in the table as JSON.

A typical image request follows this path:

Image + question
       ↓
Image processor
       ↓
Vision encoder
       ↓
Multimodal connector
       ↓
Language model
       ↓
Answer

The image processor prepares the image. The vision encoder turns it into features. The connector makes those features usable by the language model, which generates the answer.

A LoRA adapter contains a relatively small set of learned changes to selected layers. It works together with the base model it was trained for.

Think of the base model as a shared engine and each adapter as a different setting for that engine. Adapter 1 might learn to return table values in a fixed JSON format. Adapter 2 might learn to produce short descriptions using a particular structure.

These are illustrative tasks. In your deployment, use adapters trained for your own requirements.

The important requirement is compatibility: both adapters must match the base model and the serving runtime.

What the deployment looks like

SageMaker uses inference components to represent the base and its adapters:

One SageMaker endpoint
          |
          +-- Base inference component
                  |
                  +-- Shared VLM running in vLLM
                  |
                  +-- Adapter 1
                  |
                  +-- Adapter 2

The base component has the compute allocation. Each adapter component points to that base and to an adapter archive in Amazon S3. This relationship is defined by SageMaker’s BaseInferenceComponentName setting. AWS inference component reference.

A request selects Adapter 1 or Adapter 2 through InferenceComponentName.

This does not combine both adapters into one answer. Each request in our example selects one specialization.

Sharing a base can reduce duplicated model weights. It also means the adapters share serving capacity. If Adapter 1 receives a burst of traffic, it can affect the resources available to Adapter 2. Measure the combined workload before choosing instance size and scaling settings.

Before starting: choose the model and container together

For a VLM, checking that the container supports “LoRA” is not enough.

You need support for the particular combination of:

  • Model architecture and image processor.
  • Base checkpoint and tokenizer.
  • Adapter targets and rank.
  • Weight precision, such as BF16 or BitsAndBytes 4-bit.
  • vLLM version and SageMaker container integration.

An adapter can modify only the language layers while still answering image questions through the base model’s vision encoder. Alternatively, training may modify vision or connector layers too. Those cases have different serving requirements.

vLLM documents experimental support for multimodal tower and connector LoRA. Check support for your exact model and pinned runtime before deployment. vLLM LoRA documentation.

The following walkthrough assumes that you have already checked this compatibility. It provides a deployment pattern, rather than claiming that any VLM and adapter pair will work together. The snippets have not been run against an AWS account for this article.

Step 1: prepare the model files

We need three archives in S3:

s3://YOUR_BUCKET/models/base-model.tar.gz
s3://YOUR_BUCKET/adapters/adapter-1.tar.gz
s3://YOUR_BUCKET/adapters/adapter-2.tar.gz

The base archive must contain the complete VLM checkpoint. Include its model configuration, weight files, tokenizer, image processor configuration, and chat template where supplied by the model repository.

A common mistake is to package only the language-model weights. A VLM also needs the files that explain how to process images.

For a conventional PEFT LoRA adapter, the archive commonly contains these files at its root:

adapter-1.tar.gz
├── adapter_config.json
└── adapter_model.safetensors

Avoid an extra folder level inside the archive. The container must find the adapter files in the directory SageMaker provides. Some adapters require additional files; check your model and runtime before using this minimal layout. Hugging Face SageMaker multi-adapter guide.

Here is a simple packaging example for an adapter you have already downloaded:

import tarfile
from pathlib import Path
adapter_folder = Path("adapter-1")
with tarfile.open("adapter-1.tar.gz", "w:gz") as archive:
    for filename in ["adapter_config.json", "adapter_model.safetensors"]:
        path = adapter_folder / filename
        if not path.is_file():
            raise FileNotFoundError(path)
        archive.add(path, arcname=filename, recursive=False)

Keep a record of the exact base and adapter revisions. When you release a new adapter, upload it under a new S3 key so that you can identify and restore the previous version.

Step 2: set up SageMaker

Use your AWS environment’s authentication and a SageMaker execution role. Keep credentials out of notebook cells and published examples.

The role needs access to the model artifacts, container image, logs, and any encryption keys used by the deployment. Your deployment identity also needs the necessary SageMaker permissions and permission to pass the role.

import json
import os
import time
import uuid
import boto3
from botocore.config import Config
REGION = os.environ.get("AWS_REGION", "us-east-1")
ROLE_ARN = os.environ["SAGEMAKER_EXECUTION_ROLE_ARN"]
IMAGE_URI = os.environ["VALIDATED_VLLM_IMAGE_URI"]
BASE_MODEL_S3 = os.environ["BASE_MODEL_S3_URI"]
ADAPTER_1_S3 = os.environ["ADAPTER_1_S3_URI"]
ADAPTER_2_S3 = os.environ["ADAPTER_2_S3_URI"]
INSTANCE_TYPE = os.environ["SAGEMAKER_INSTANCE_TYPE"]
session = boto3.Session(region_name=REGION)
sm = session.client("sagemaker")
runtime = session.client(
    "sagemaker-runtime",
    config=Config(read_timeout=70, connect_timeout=10),
)
suffix = uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]
MODEL_NAME = f"vlm-model-{suffix}"
ENDPOINT_NAME = f"vlm-endpoint-{suffix}"
ENDPOINT_CONFIG_NAME = f"vlm-config-{suffix}"
BASE_COMPONENT = f"vlm-base-{suffix}"
ADAPTER_1_COMPONENT = f"adapter-1-{suffix}"
ADAPTER_2_COMPONENT = f"adapter-2-{suffix}"

Use S3 artifacts in the deployment region. Select the instance based on measured memory needs, and check its regional availability and your SageMaker quota.

VALIDATED_VLLM_IMAGE_URI should identify a container you have tested with your VLM. Pin its image digest so a later image change does not silently change your deployment.

Step 3: configure vLLM for images and adapters

The following environment variables use the Hugging Face vLLM container’s SM_VLLM_ interface. Confirm that your selected image supports that interface.

environment = {
    "SM_VLLM_MODEL": "/opt/ml/model",
    "SM_VLLM_SERVED_MODEL_NAME": "shared-vlm",
    "SM_VLLM_HOST": "0.0.0.0",
    "SM_VLLM_MAX_MODEL_LEN": "4096",
    "SM_VLLM_GPU_MEMORY_UTILIZATION": "0.80",
    "SM_VLLM_ENABLE_LORA": "true",
    "SM_VLLM_MAX_LORA_RANK": "32",
    "SM_VLLM_MAX_LORAS": "2",
    "SM_VLLM_MAX_CPU_LORAS": "2",
    "SM_VLLM_LIMIT_MM_PER_PROMPT": json.dumps({
        "image": 1,
        "audio": 0,
        "video": 0,
    }),
    "VLLM_ALLOW_RUNTIME_LORA_UPDATING": "true",
}

Here is what the main settings mean:

  • ENABLE_LORA: Enable adapter serving
  • MAX_LORA_RANK: Accept adapters up to rank 32
  • MAX_LORAS: Allow up to two different adapters in a batch
  • LIMIT_MM_PER_PROMPT: Accept one image per request; disable audio and video
  • MAX_MODEL_LEN: Set the model's context limit to 4,096 tokens
  • ALLOW_RUNTIME_LORA_UPDATING: Enable runtime adapter registration

The runtime registration setting supports the adapter lifecycle used by SageMaker’s integration. Hugging Face container configuration example.

The rank limit must cover both adapters. Check r and any per-layer rank overrides in their configurations.

Also, MAX_LORAS=2 does not mean “only two requests at a time.” It controls the number of different adapters that can participate in a batch.

What if the base uses 4-bit weights?

For a compatible prequantized BitsAndBytes checkpoint, the serving configuration may also need:

# Add only for a validated BitsAndBytes deployment.
environment.update({
    "SM_VLLM_QUANTIZATION": "bitsandbytes",
    "SM_VLLM_LOAD_FORMAT": "bitsandbytes",
    "SM_VLLM_DTYPE": "bfloat16",
})

These settings tell the runtime how to load and compute with the checkpoint. They do not convert an arbitrary checkpoint into a compatible 4-bit model.

The weights can be stored in 4-bit form while computation uses BF16. This reduces weight memory, but images, activations, adapters, and the KV cache still need memory.

Step 4: create the endpoint and load the base

First, register the model and create the endpoint:

sm.create_model(
    ModelName=MODEL_NAME,
    ExecutionRoleArn=ROLE_ARN,
    PrimaryContainer={
        "Image": IMAGE_URI,
        "ModelDataUrl": BASE_MODEL_S3,
        "Environment": environment,
    },
)
sm.create_endpoint_config(
    EndpointConfigName=ENDPOINT_CONFIG_NAME,
    ExecutionRoleArn=ROLE_ARN,
    ProductionVariants=[{
        "VariantName": "AllTraffic",
        "InstanceType": INSTANCE_TYPE,
        "InitialInstanceCount": 1,
        "RoutingConfig": {
            "RoutingStrategy": "LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS",
        },
    }],
)
sm.create_endpoint(
    EndpointName=ENDPOINT_NAME,
    EndpointConfigName=ENDPOINT_CONFIG_NAME,
)
sm.get_waiter("endpoint_in_service").wait(
    EndpointName=ENDPOINT_NAME,
    WaiterConfig={"Delay": 30, "MaxAttempts": 120},
)

This step creates a billable endpoint. Some containers also require a particular inference AMI or driver combination; set a compatible InferenceAmiVersion in the production variant when your selected image requires it.

Next, add the base inference component:

def wait_for_component(name, timeout=3600):
    deadline = time.monotonic() + timeout
    while time.monotonic() < deadline:
        info = sm.describe_inference_component(
            InferenceComponentName=name,
        )
        status = info["InferenceComponentStatus"]
        if status == "InService":
            return
        if status in {"Failed", "UpdateFailed", "Deleting"}:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"{name}: {status}: {info.get('FailureReason', '')}"
            )
        time.sleep(15)
    raise TimeoutError(f"Timed out waiting for {name}")
sm.create_inference_component(
    InferenceComponentName=BASE_COMPONENT,
    EndpointName=ENDPOINT_NAME,
    VariantName="AllTraffic",
    Specification={
        "ModelName": MODEL_NAME,
        "ComputeResourceRequirements": {
            "NumberOfAcceleratorDevicesRequired": 1,
            "MinMemoryRequiredInMb": 8192,
        },
        "StartupParameters": {
            "ModelDataDownloadTimeoutInSeconds": 1800,
            "ContainerStartupHealthCheckTimeoutInSeconds": 1800,
        },
    },
    RuntimeConfig={"CopyCount": 1},
)
wait_for_component(BASE_COMPONENT)

The 8,192 MB value is an example host-memory reservation, not GPU memory. Adjust it to your container and model-loading requirements.

This example creates one serving copy of the base. If you scale to multiple copies, each copy needs its own model weights.

Step 5: attach Adapter 1 and Adapter 2

Once the base is ready, attach both adapters:

adapters = {
    ADAPTER_1_COMPONENT: ADAPTER_1_S3,
    ADAPTER_2_COMPONENT: ADAPTER_2_S3,
}
for component_name, artifact_uri in adapters.items():
    sm.create_inference_component(
        InferenceComponentName=component_name,
        EndpointName=ENDPOINT_NAME,
        Specification={
            "BaseInferenceComponentName": BASE_COMPONENT,
            "Container": {"ArtifactUrl": artifact_uri},
        },
    )
    wait_for_component(component_name)

Notice that we do not request another GPU for each adapter. We link each child component to the existing base. AWS adapter deployment example.

Save these resource names and artifact versions in a deployment manifest. You will need them for updates, troubleshooting, and cleanup.

Step 6: send an image to the adapter you want

Now for the part that makes this a VLM example: sending an actual image.

The message contains a text instruction and an image encoded as a data URL. This follows vLLM’s OpenAI-compatible multimodal request format. vLLM image input examples.

import base64
from pathlib import Path
from PIL import Image
def image_message(image_path, instruction):
    path = Path(image_path)
    with Image.open(path) as image:
        if image.format not in {"JPEG", "PNG", "WEBP"}:
            raise ValueError("Use a JPEG, PNG, or WEBP image")
        mime_type = Image.MIME[image.format]
    encoded = base64.b64encode(path.read_bytes()).decode("ascii")
    return [{
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {"type": "text", "text": instruction},
            {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {
                "url": f"data:{mime_type};base64,{encoded}",
            }},
        ],
    }]
def invoke(component_name, messages):
    body = json.dumps({
        "model": "shared-vlm",
        "messages": messages,
        "max_tokens": 256,
        "temperature": 0,
    }).encode("utf-8")
    # A conservative application budget; check the API limits you use.
    if len(body) > 5_500_000:
        raise ValueError("Resize or compress the image before sending")
    response = runtime.invoke_endpoint(
        EndpointName=ENDPOINT_NAME,
        InferenceComponentName=component_name,
        ContentType="application/json",
        CustomAttributes="route=/v1/chat/completions",
        Body=body,
    )
    return json.loads(response["Body"].read())
messages = image_message(
    "sample-table.png",
    "Read this table and return the values as JSON.",
)
result = invoke(ADAPTER_1_COMPONENT, messages)
print(result["choices"][0]["message"]["content"])

The container must support the chat route and the model’s chat template. Use the same prompt style and output format that the adapter learned during training.

For example, imagine a synthetic image containing:

Item       Quantity
Apples     3
Oranges    5

An illustrative response might be:

{"items": [{"name": "Apples", "quantity": 3}, {"name": "Oranges", "quantity": 5}]}

That is an example of the intended behavior, not a measured result. Asking for JSON does not guarantee correct or valid JSON. Validate the response and compare its values with the image.

To use Adapter 2, change the component name and give it an instruction appropriate to its training:

messages = image_message(
    "sample-image.png",
    "Describe this image using the format you were trained to follow.",
)
result = invoke(ADAPTER_2_COMPONENT, messages)

The endpoint stays the same. The selected adapter changes.

You can also invoke BASE_COMPONENT to compare the original model with either adapter. This is a useful way to check whether fine-tuning actually improved the task.

The VLM details that are easy to missAn image has more than a file size

A small JPEG is not necessarily a cheap model input. Image resolution and the model’s preprocessing strategy affect visual tokens, processing time, and memory.

For a table-reading task, crop away irrelevant background while keeping the text readable. Reducing resolution too aggressively can turn a clear number into an ambiguous one.

Base64 also increases the transmitted image size by roughly one third. Check both the serialized request size and the model’s context budget.

Loading the base does not prove that adapters work

Test in stages:

  1. Ask the base a simple text question.
  2. Send a small image to the base.
  3. Invoke Adapter 1 with its expected input.
  4. Invoke Adapter 2 with its expected input.
  5. Send a mixture of requests and measure errors and latency.

If you receive ModelNotReadyException while an adapter loads, use bounded retries with backoff. Other errors need diagnosis rather than unlimited retries.

Do not remove adapter tensors just to make loading succeed

Suppose an adapter contains weights for the vision encoder, but the serving runtime cannot apply them.

Deleting those weights might allow the remaining adapter to load. It can also remove part of what the model learned.

Check the training configuration and the runtime’s supported targets. If trained modules are unsupported, use a compatible runtime or retrain with supported targets. Any conversion needs quality evaluation.

Keep runtime fixes tied to the version that needs them

Some model and container combinations need workarounds involving quantization metadata, eager execution, KV-cache handling, or cache-connector startup settings.

These fixes solve different problems. For example, disabling a KV-transfer connector does not disable the vision encoder, and disabling a multimodal processor cache does not remove the language model’s KV cache.

Record each fix with the exact image version and the error it addresses. Retest when upgrading. Copying a collection of old environment flags into a new image can make troubleshooting harder.

Updating an adapter without replacing the whole endpoint

Treat adapters as independently versioned artifacts.

For example, keep Adapter 1’s current component while creating a new component for its next version. Test the new one, then update the application’s component-name mapping.

This allows you to return to the previous version if evaluation finds a problem. During the overlap, allow for the additional adapter cache and memory demand.

Deleting the existing component and recreating it under the same name is another approach, but requests to that adapter can fail during the gap.

Clean up after experimenting

Delete the adapter components first, wait for their deletion, and then delete the base component. After that, delete the endpoint and wait for it to disappear before removing its endpoint configuration and model object.

S3 artifacts, custom container images, and retained logs need their own cleanup or retention policy.

For a first experiment, start with one compatible base, one adapter, and one small image. Once that works, attach Adapter 2 and test both together. This makes it much easier to tell whether a failure comes from image processing, adapter compatibility, or shared serving capacity.
